title: Scalable continuous-space crystal optimality certificates
open: Can we certify that a proposed crystal structure is within a stated energy tolerance of the true global minimum, when atoms sit at continuous positions and the cell geometry itself may vary? The goal is a computationally practical certificate for a stated class of realistic many-body potentials and bounded cell sizes, with discretization error explicitly controlled.
status: Gusev et al. (2023) demonstrated integer-programming optimality guarantees and assumption-dependent relaxed structures. Practical scaling, grid-to-continuum error bounds, and wider potential classes remain open extension targets.
solved_when: A method exists that, for a stated class of realistic many-body potentials and bounded cell sizes, produces a certificate that a candidate lies within a chosen energy tolerance of the global minimum over continuous atomic positions and variable cell geometry, with grid-to-continuum (discretization) error explicitly bounded.
why: It separates reliable ground-state predictions from the particular preferences of whatever search algorithm happened to be run, so materials-discovery pipelines can trust their predicted structures.
key_works: Oganov, Pickard, Zhu and Needs (2019), “Structure prediction drives materials discovery,” [DOI:10.1038/s41578-019-0101-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-019-0101-8); V. V. Gusev et al. (2023), “Optimality guarantees for crystal structure prediction,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06071-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06071-y).

title: Three-dimensional Kauzmann transition
open: Do realistic three-dimensional glass formers undergo a true thermodynamic ideal-glass transition at positive temperature, in which the liquid's excess entropy vanishes and an equilibrium glass phase appears with controlled thermodynamic and equilibration limits?
status: Posed by Kauzmann (1948), "The Nature of the Glassy State and the Behavior of Liquids at Low Temperatures" ([DOI:10.1021/cr60135a002](https://doi.org/10.1021/cr60135a002)). Jung et al. (2025; journal 2026), "Numerical investigation of the equilibrium Kauzmann transition in a two-dimensional atomistic glass" ([arXiv:2507.03590](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03590)), find a zero-temperature transition in a two-dimensional model, which leaves the three-dimensional question unresolved.
solved_when: A demonstration — analytical or numerical with controlled limits — that a realistic three-dimensional glass former either has or does not have an ideal-glass transition at positive temperature, with the thermodynamic limit and equilibration procedures under control.
why: It settles whether ordinary glass formation conceals an underlying equilibrium phase transition rather than being a purely dynamical slowdown.
key_works: Kauzmann (1948), “The Nature of the Glassy State and the Behavior of Liquids at Low Temperatures,” [DOI:10.1021/cr60135a002](https://doi.org/10.1021/cr60135a002); Jung et al. (2025; journal 2026), “Numerical investigation of the equilibrium Kauzmann transition in a two-dimensional atomistic glass,” [arXiv:2507.03590](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03590).

title: Gardner transition in physical dimensions
open: Does the mean-field Gardner transition — the splitting of a glass basin into a hierarchy of marginally stable sub-basins — persist as a genuine thermodynamic transition in three-dimensional glasses, or is it smeared into a crossover or pre-empted by localized defects?
status: The transition was proposed in spin-glass theory in 1985; mean-field amorphous-solid results and finite-system signatures exist, with dimensional and preparation dependence unresolved. Key work: Berthier et al. (2019), "Gardner physics in amorphous solids and beyond," [DOI:10.1063/1.5097175](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5097175).
solved_when: A criterion (analytic, numerical, or experimental) establishes whether the Gardner transition in three dimensions is a true phase transition or a crossover, resolving its dependence on dimension and preparation protocol.
why: It decides whether mean-field marginal stability genuinely controls glass stability and anomalous elasticity in physical dimensions, or is an artifact confined to infinite dimension.
key_works: Berthier et al. (2019), “Gardner physics in amorphous solids and beyond,” [DOI:10.1063/1.5097175](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5097175).

title: Chemical identity of tunnelling defects
open: What are the tunnelling two-level systems in glasses, atom by atom? The goal is to identify the specific atomic rearrangements responsible for tunnelling two-level systems in representative amorphous oxides, and to predict their density and coupling from the glass's preparation history.
status: Phenomenological tunnelling models date to the 1970s; individual defects are measurable, but no universal microscopic account spans glass chemistries. Yu and Carruzzo (2021), "Two-Level Systems and the Tunneling Model: A Critical View," [arXiv:2101.02787](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.02787).
solved_when: The microscopic defects behind tunnelling two-level systems in representative amorphous oxides are identified, and their density and coupling are predicted as a function of preparation history.
why: A microscopic account would let materials be engineered for reduced dielectric loss, mechanical noise, and quantum-device decoherence.
key_works: Yu and Carruzzo (2021), “Two-Level Systems and the Tunneling Model: A Critical View,” [arXiv:2101.02787](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.02787).

title: Heat transport beyond weak anharmonicity
open: Can we predict thermal conductivity in strongly anharmonic, dynamically disordered solids, where well-defined phonon quasiparticles and perturbative scattering no longer suffice? A satisfactory theory would compute conductivity from first principles in this regime without relying on quasiparticle or weak-scattering assumptions.
status: Wigner transport, as formulated by Simoncelli, Marzari and Mauri (2022) in “Wigner Formulation of Thermal Transport in Solids” ([DOI:10.1103/PhysRevX.12.041011](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.12.041011)), unifies particle-like and coherence contributions to thermal conductivity. Strongly nonperturbative, temperature-changing structures remain a demanding frontier beyond its reach.
solved_when: A predictive, nonperturbative framework yields first-principles conductivities for strongly anharmonic, dynamically disordered solids — including structures whose character changes with temperature — with accuracy validated against experiment.
why: It would enable reliable, first-principles design of complex thermal barriers and thermoelectric materials, where current quasiparticle-based methods fail.
key_works: Simoncelli, Marzari and Mauri (2022), “Wigner Formulation of Thermal Transport in Solids,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevX.12.041011](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.12.041011).

title: Atomic tomography of intact buried interfaces
open: Can we determine the three-dimensional positions of metal and oxygen atoms across an intact buried metal–oxide interface inside a micrometre-thick specimen, without cutting the sample apart? The problem further demands that atom-recovery rates, false-assignment probabilities, and probe-induced structural changes be independently bounded and validated.
status: Y. Yang et al. (2017), "Deciphering chemical order/disorder and material properties at the single-atom level" ([DOI:10.1038/nature21042](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature21042)), mapped 23,196 Fe/Pt atom positions and species in a nanoparticle, and Chen et al. (2021), "Electron ptychography achieves atomic-resolution limits set by lattice vibrations" ([DOI:10.1126/science.abg2533](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abg2533)), reached lattice-vibration-limited resolution in 2021. Intact thick mixed-element interfaces, however, impose substantially stronger penetration, inversion, and dose constraints than these achievements address.
solved_when: A three-dimensional atomic map of metal and oxygen positions across an intact buried metal–oxide interface in a micrometre-thick specimen is obtained without sectioning, together with independently validated bounds on atom recovery, false assignment, and probe-induced structural change.
why: It would measure the actual atomic structures that underlie materials properties at the interfaces where those properties are often determined.
key_works: Y. Yang et al. (2017), “Deciphering chemical order/disorder and material properties at the single-atom level,” [DOI:10.1038/nature21042](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature21042); Chen et al. (2021), “Electron ptychography achieves atomic-resolution limits set by lattice vibrations,” [DOI:10.1126/science.abg2533](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abg2533).

title: Atomic chemistry below the damage threshold
open: Can beam-sensitive materials be chemically mapped at useful local resolution before the probe alters the very structure being measured? Formally: measure local bonding and composition with independently quantified uncertainty, strictly below the damage threshold.
status: Low-dose, cryogenic, and dose-fractionated methods currently mitigate damage, but damage-free information acquisition at useful resolution remains specimen dependent. See Egerton (2019), "Radiation damage to organic and inorganic specimens in the TEM," [DOI:10.1016/j.micron.2019.01.005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.micron.2019.01.005).
solved_when: A measurement of local bonding and composition in a beam-sensitive specimen is reported at useful resolution, together with an independently quantified uncertainty, obtained before the probe changes the structure being measured.
why: It would make electron-microscopy observations of polymers, soft interfaces, and reactive solids trustworthy rather than artifacts of beam damage.
key_works: Egerton (2019), “Radiation damage to organic and inorganic specimens in the TEM,” [DOI:10.1016/j.micron.2019.01.005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.micron.2019.01.005).

title: Identifiable electric-field and strain maps
open: Can local electric fields and strain be recovered from scanning diffraction data in a way that is provably identifiable — that is, with thickness, tilt, dynamical scattering, probe aberrations, and charging separated out rather than confounded? A complete answer would deliver validated uncertainty estimates alongside the inferred field and strain maps.
status: 4D-STEM currently provides multiple quantitative imaging modes (Ophus 2019, "Four-Dimensional Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (4D-STEM): From Scanning Nanodiffraction to Ptychography and Beyond," DOI:10.1017/S1431927619000497), but the identifiability problem remains open: distinct physical causes can still generate similar measured contrast, so fields and strain cannot yet be unambiguously separated from confounders.
solved_when: An inversion method exists that recovers electric-field and strain maps from 4D-STEM scanning diffraction data while explicitly separating thickness, tilt, dynamical scattering, probe aberrations, and charging, with uncertainty estimates that are validated against ground truth.
why: Distinct physical causes can produce similar measured contrast, so without identifiability a structural or electrostatic artifact can be reported as a real mechanism — false mechanism claims are the failure mode this prevents.
key_works: Ophus (2019), “Four-Dimensional Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (4D-STEM): From Scanning Nanodiffraction to Ptychography and Beyond,” [DOI:10.1017/S1431927619000497](https://doi.org/10.1017/S1431927619000497).

title: Copper removal from scrap-derived steel at industrial throughput
open: Can dissolved copper be removed from realistic scrap-steel melts to the purity specification demanded by high-value sheet products, at industrial throughput and cost? Success means economically qualifying a removal route that maintains throughput, iron yield, reagent recycling, and cost competitiveness against the fallback of diluting scrap with primary iron.
status: Copper accumulation remains a circular-steel bottleneck. Souza Filho et al. demonstrated a promising oxygen-controlled metallurgical removal route in 2024; economically qualified industrial operation across variable scrap streams remains open. Key work: I. R. Souza Filho et al. (2024), "Sustainable Ironmaking Toward a Future Circular Steel Economy: Exploiting a Critical Oxygen Concentration for Metallurgical Cu Removal from Scrap-Based Melts," [DOI:10.1002/srin.202300785](https://doi.org/10.1002/srin.202300785).
solved_when: A metallurgical copper-removal process is demonstrated on realistic scrap-steel melts under economically qualified industrial operation across variable scrap streams, achieving sheet-product copper specifications while preserving industrial throughput, iron yield, reagent recycling, and cost competitiveness with dilution by primary iron.
why: It removes the copper-accumulation bottleneck that currently limits circular steel, allowing high-value steel recycling without continually adding primary iron.
key_works: I. R. Souza Filho et al. (2024), “Sustainable Ironmaking Toward a Future Circular Steel Economy: Exploiting a Critical Oxygen Concentration for Metallurgical Cu Removal from Scrap-Based Melts,” [DOI:10.1002/srin.202300785](https://doi.org/10.1002/srin.202300785).

title: Site-resolved martensite nucleation under deformation
open: Can we predict, from the measured defect structure of a metastable stainless steel alone, which defects will nucleate martensite under deformation, which crystallographic variants will be selected, and at what onset stresses — across changes in temperature and strain rate — without seeding the model with embryos taken from the microstructure that is ultimately observed?
status: Atomic observations and simulations in 316L stainless steel at 15 and 173 K (reported in 2025) identified different transformation pathways and defect associations, but prospectively selecting actual nucleation sites remains harder than explaining observed ones; see S. Li, P. J. Withers, W. Chen, K. Yan (2025), “Atomic-scale investigation of the mechanisms of deformation-induced martensitic transformation at ultra-cryogenic temperatures,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jmst.2024.04.067](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mst.2024.04.067).
solved_when: A predictive method identifies the actual nucleation sites, selected variants, and onset stresses in metastable stainless steel prospectively, across temperature and strain-rate conditions, with no input derived from the observed post-transformation microstructure.
why: It would make transformation-induced strengthening and ductility reliably designable rather than explained after the fact.
key_works: S. Li, P. J. Withers, W. Chen, K. Yan (2025), “Atomic-scale investigation of the mechanisms of deformation-induced martensitic transformation at ultra-cryogenic temperatures,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jmst.2024.04.067](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmst.2024.04.067).

title: Closure of three-dimensional dislocation-network dynamics
open: Can the three-dimensional dynamics of a dislocation network be replaced by closed continuum evolution equations that faithfully carry dislocation topology and predict multiplication, junction formation, annihilation, and pattern length scales from the initial microstructure? In formal terms, the goal is a closure — correlation and reaction terms of broad validity derived rather than fitted — that reproduces these features without regime-specific calibrated rules.
status: Phase-field formulations with conserved dislocation variables demonstrated pattern formation in 2025 (Y. Zhang, R. Wu, M. Zaiser (2025), "Continuum dislocation dynamics as a phase field theory with conserved order parameters: formulation and application to dislocation patterning," [DOI:10.1088/1361-651X/adc31f](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-651X/adc31f); [arXiv:2410.17177](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17177)); however, deriving broadly valid correlation and reaction closures remains distinct from demonstrating selected patterns and is still open.
solved_when: A set of tractable continuum evolution equations is obtained that preserves dislocation topology and predicts multiplication, junction formation, annihilation, and pattern length scales from initial microstructure, with no regime-specific fitted closure rules.
why: It would connect microscopic dislocation motion to component-scale constitutive models, replacing phenomenological plasticity inputs with derivable ones.
key_works: Y. Zhang, R. Wu, M. Zaiser (2025), “Continuum dislocation dynamics as a phase field theory with conserved order parameters: formulation and application to dislocation patterning,” [DOI:10.1088/1361-651X/adc31f](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-651X/adc31f); [arXiv:2410.17177](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17177).

title: Slip transmission through chemically complex grain boundaries
open: Can we predict, from the measured three-dimensional structure of a grain boundary — its chemistry, segregation state, and local stress — whether an incident dislocation will be absorbed, transmitted, or re-emitted, and if so on which outgoing slip system? A successful theory should be verifiable against in situ observation of the outgoing slip.
status: Stricker and Weygand implemented explicit physical dislocation transmission through planar boundaries in 2024 (M. Stricker and D. Weygand (2024), "A model for physical dislocation transmission through grain boundaries and its implementation in a discrete dislocation dynamics tool," DOI:10.1186/s41313-024-00065-7). Curved, chemically heterogeneous boundaries and evolving boundary dislocation content extend beyond that controlled setting and remain open.
solved_when: A predictive criterion exists that, given a measured three-dimensional boundary with its segregation state and local stress, correctly determines the fate of an incident dislocation (absorbed, transmitted, or re-emitted) and identifies the outgoing slip system, validated by in situ observation of that slip system.
why: It would connect grain-boundary design directly to strain localization and crack initiation, turning boundary chemistry into a controllable lever against failure.
key_works: M. Stricker and D. Weygand (2024), “A model for physical dislocation transmission through grain boundaries and its implementation in a discrete dislocation dynamics tool,” [DOI:10.1186/s41313-024-00065-7](https://doi.org/10.1186/s41313-024-00065-7).

title: Hydrogen-trap protection after saturation and cycling
open: When do deliberately introduced hydrogen traps keep protecting a metal under repeated charging, unloading, and temperature cycling — and when do they instead saturate or release hydrogen into crack-critical regions? A satisfying answer gives predictive limits for actual microstructures rather than idealized ones.
status: Atomic-scale trapping measurements and interface-engineering strategies exist, but they do not establish lifetime protection: a reduction in initial hydrogen uptake — including the approximately twofold reduction reported by G. Hachet et al. (2025), "Protection of metal interfaces against hydrogen-assisted cracking," [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6) — does not establish it.
solved_when: A predictive criterion, validated on real microstructures, identifies the conditions under which traps retain their protective function through repeated charge–unload and temperature cycles versus saturating or releasing hydrogen; demonstrated for actual microstructures.
why: It prevents mitigation strategies from failing in service after apparently successful short tests.
key_works: G. Hachet et al. (2025), “Protection of metal interfaces against hydrogen-assisted cracking,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6).

title: Material-specific onset of dynamic crack microbranching
open: Can the onset velocity, branch spacing, and three-dimensional morphology of dynamic crack microbranching be predicted a priori from independently measured dissipation and process-zone physics, across classes of brittle materials? A successful theory would take those inputs and output material-specific onset and length scales, rather than parameters fitted to the branching event itself.
status: Controlled experiments established microbranching in the 1990s (E. Sharon, S. P. Gross, J. Fineberg (1995), "Local crack branching as a mechanism for instability in dynamic fracture," [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.5096](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.5096); E. Sharon and J. Fineberg (1996), "Microbranching instability and the dynamic fracture of brittle materials," [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.54.7128](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.54.7128)). Contemporary simulations generate branching, but reproducing it does not by itself validate transferable onset and length-scale predictions.
solved_when: A predictive framework reproduces the measured onset velocity, branch spacing, and three-dimensional microbranch morphology for brittle material classes using only independently characterized dissipation and process-zone properties, with no fitting to the branching phenomena it predicts.
why: It would determine rapid-fracture resistance and fragmentation behavior beyond what quasistatic toughness can capture, grounding material selection under dynamic failure.
key_works: E. Sharon, S. P. Gross, J. Fineberg (1995), “Local crack branching as a mechanism for instability in dynamic fracture,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.5096](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.5096); E. Sharon and J. Fineberg (1996), “Microbranching instability and the dynamic fracture of brittle materials,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.54.7128](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.54.7128).

title: Preventing keyhole pores by closed-loop control
open: Can a closed-loop controller detect the onset of keyhole instability in laser powder-bed fusion and adjust process parameters in time to prevent pore entrapment — robustly across scan turns, accumulating heat, and varying surface angles?
status: A 2025 acoustic study (L. Galiègue et al. (2025), "Acoustic emission monitoring reveals keyhole formation and evolution," [DOI:10.1038/s41598-025-27232-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-27232-1)) correlated frequency signatures with keyhole depth and porosity onset across several alloys, but this is detection only; generalized prevention requires control action and full-build validation beyond detection.
solved_when: A control scheme demonstrates measurably lower keyhole-pore defect rates on entire builds, with false-alarm rates quantified, operating across scan turns, accumulated heat, and changing surface angles.
why: It would prevent internal defects during manufacture rather than catching them later, reducing reliance on post-build inspection.
key_works: L. Galiègue et al. (2025), “Acoustic emission monitoring reveals keyhole formation and evolution,” [DOI:10.1038/s41598-025-27232-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-27232-1).

title: Oxidation-tolerant crack-deflecting CMC interphases
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can an interphase be designed that stays weak enough to deflect cracks and allow fiber pull-out, yet survives the oxidizing, volatilizing environment that enters through matrix cracks during service?
status: SiC/BN/SiBCN studies in 2025 show that steam can consume BN and form glassy products that bond fibers to the matrix, so initial toughness does not guarantee retained toughness after exposure. Z. Li, Z. Gao, X. Zhang, Y. Liu, P. J. Withers, P. Xiao (2025), “Oxidation behavior and subsequent mechanical properties of SiC/BN/SiBCN composite after exposure to steam at high temperature,” [institutional paper record](https://research.manchester.ac.uk/en/publications/oxidation-behavior-and-subsequent-mechanical-properties-of-sicbns/).
solved_when: A fiber–matrix interphase is demonstrated that both maintains crack deflection and fiber pull-out (toughness) and resists oxidation and volatilization after exposure to steam at high temperature, with toughness retained after exposure rather than only initially.
why: It preserves the damage tolerance that makes ceramic-matrix composites useful; without it, initial toughness is lost as steam consumes the interphase and bonds fibers to the matrix.
key_works: Z. Li, Z. Gao, X. Zhang, Y. Liu, P. J. Withers, P. Xiao (2025), “Oxidation behavior and subsequent mechanical properties of SiC/BN/SiBCN composite after exposure to steam at high temperature,” [institutional paper record](https://research.manchester.ac.uk/en/publications/oxidation-behavior-and-subsequent-mechanical-properties-of-sicbns/).

title: Rapid uniform densification of thick CMC preforms
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Achieve a specified near-full matrix density throughout thick, complex fiber preforms in a single short infiltration campaign without prematurely sealing outer pores or damaging fibers, verified by three-dimensional porosity and mechanical measurements.
status: Venkatachalam et al. reported 90% theoretical density in 24 hours using radio-frequency-assisted CVI in 2024, at least ten times faster than their conventional comparison. Higher density, complex geometry, and validated properties remain separate hurdles.
why: Reduces a major time and cost barrier in ceramic-composite manufacturing.
key_works: V. Venkatachalam, B. Esser, J. Binner (2024), “Processing and performance of ultra high temperature ceramic matrix composite (UHTCMCs) using radio frequency assisted chemical vapour infiltration (RF-CVI),” [DLR paper record](https://elib.dlr.de/205288/).

title: Repeated autonomous concrete healing with structural recovery
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Can concrete heal its own cracks again and again — not just once — while genuinely recovering structural performance? Specifically, can repeated autonomous healing restore both permeability and mechanical properties after multiple damage events under realistic wet–dry exposure, without the healing capacity being exhausted or causing harmful expansion?
status: Seymour et al.'s 2023 experiments support lime-clast-mediated healing inspired by Roman concrete. Repeatable recovery in reinforced structural service remains beyond one-time laboratory crack closure. Key work: L. M. Seymour et al. (2023), "Hot mixing: Mechanistic insights into the durability of ancient Roman concrete," [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.add1602](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.add1602).
solved_when: A demonstration shows healing that recurs after multiple damage events under realistic wet–dry exposure, restoring the specified permeability and mechanical performance each time, without exhausting the healing capacity or producing harmful expansion.
why: It would cut concrete repair needs and extend service life of structures, moving self-healing from a laboratory curiosity to a maintenance-free structural material.
key_works: L. M. Seymour et al. (2023), “Hot mixing: Mechanistic insights into the durability of ancient Roman concrete,” [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.add1602](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.add1602).

title: Operando accounting of inactive lithium
open: Can we track, while a cell is running and without disturbing the buried electrode, how much lithium sits as electronically isolated metal versus how much is chemically bound in interphase products — and where each sits within the electrode?
status: Fang et al. (2019), “Quantifying inactive lithium in lithium metal batteries,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1481-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1481-z), introduced destructive titration–gas chromatography. Later imaging and recovery studies establish that isolated lithium can move or reconnect; a generally applicable operando inventory remains a distinct target.
solved_when: A spatially resolved, operando accounting of inactive lithium that separates isolated metal from interphase-bound lithium without perturbing the electrode, and that closes the lithium mass balance in realistic multilayer cells.
why: It identifies which loss process an electrolyte or charging intervention actually fixes, so mitigation strategies can be targeted rather than guessed.
key_works: C. Fang et al. (2019), “Quantifying inactive lithium in lithium metal batteries,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1481-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1481-z).

title: Stripping-induced void suppression at solid–lithium interfaces
open: Can we keep a solid–lithium interface in contact while lithium is stripped faster than interfacial creep and diffusion can replenish it, at practically useful currents, capacities, and low external pressure — and, beyond mitigation, predict the safe operating window from measured interface properties?
status: Kasemchainan et al. (2019), "Critical stripping current leads to dendrite formation on plating in lithium anode solid electrolyte cells," [DOI:10.1038/s41563-019-0438-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-019-0438-9), directly connected stripping-current limits, voids, and subsequent dendrites. Applied pressure and interlayers mitigate particular interfaces, but transferable criteria across electrolyte, temperature, and lithium thickness remain incomplete.
solved_when: A design operates at useful current and capacity with low external pressure while suppressing void formation at the stripping interface, together with a transferable criterion that predicts the safe operating window across electrolyte choice, temperature, and lithium thickness from measured interface properties.
why: Void formation during stripping is a failure mechanism that can precede short circuits even when lithium plating initially appears uniform, so suppressing it is a prerequisite for durable solid-state lithium batteries.
key_works: J. Kasemchainan et al. (2019), “Critical stripping current leads to dendrite formation on plating in lithium anode solid electrolyte cells,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-019-0438-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-019-0438-9).

title: Reversible oxygen redox without cumulative voltage loss
open: Can a battery cathode sustain substantial capacity from oxygen redox over many cycles without oxygen loss, irreversible cation rearrangement, or growing charge–discharge voltage hysteresis? More precisely, are there structural design rules, valid across compositions rather than for a single special material, that yield reversible anionic redox with stable energy efficiency over practical cycling?
status: Oxygen-redox cathodes have been developed for decades. House et al. demonstrated superstructure control of first-cycle hysteresis in 2020, but first-cycle improvements do not by themselves establish stable lifetime energy efficiency. Key work: R. A. House et al. (2020), "Superstructure control of first-cycle voltage hysteresis in oxygen-redox cathodes," [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1854-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1854-3).
solved_when: A cathode material (or a composition-independent structural rule) is identified that delivers substantial anionic-redox capacity over practical cycling while suppressing oxygen release, avoiding irreversible cation rearrangement, and showing no cumulative growth of charge–discharge hysteresis.
why: It unlocks cathode capacity beyond what transition-metal redox alone can provide, without sacrificing the delivered energy over the battery's lifetime.
key_works: R. A. House et al. (2020), “Superstructure control of first-cycle voltage hysteresis in oxygen-redox cathodes,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1854-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1854-3).

title: Magnesium interfaces compatible with high-energy full cells
open: Can a single electrolyte sustain both efficient magnesium metal cycling at the anode and a high-voltage, high-loading cathode at the other electrode? Formally, the goal is an interphase that is electronically passivating yet selectively conducts Mg ions, and that tolerates realistic impurity levels in a practical full cell.
status: Son et al. demonstrated an artificial interphase enabling reversible magnesium chemistry in carbonate electrolyte in 2018 (S.-B. Son et al. (2018), “An artificial interphase enables reversible magnesium chemistry in carbonate electrolytes,” [DOI:10.1038/s41557-018-0019-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-018-0019-6)). This resolves a proof-of-principle incompatibility; a broadly practical cathode–electrolyte–anode combination remains unfinished.
solved_when: An interface is demonstrated that is electronically passivating while conducting Mg ions, supports efficient metal cycling and a high-voltage, high-loading cathode in the same electrolyte, and functions under realistic impurity tolerance.
why: It would let abundant magnesium compete on full-cell energy and cost, which current proof-of-principle chemistries cannot yet deliver.
key_works: S.-B. Son et al. (2018), “An artificial interphase enables reversible magnesium chemistry in carbonate electrolytes,” [DOI:10.1038/s41557-018-0019-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-018-0019-6).

title: Regenerable organic flow-battery molecules
open: Can we design inexpensive organic redox molecules for flow batteries whose main degradation products can be converted back into active material in situ, with little energy or reagent consumption and no buildup of irreversible contaminants?
status: Organic-electrolyte decomposition has constrained the field for years. Jing et al. demonstrated electrochemical recomposition of a decomposed anthraquinone electrolyte in 2022 ("In situ electrochemical recomposition of decomposed redox-active species in aqueous organic flow batteries," DOI:10.1038/s41557-022-00967-4); broadly applicable regeneration across both electrolytes and repeated aging remains open.
solved_when: A redox-active organic electrolyte is demonstrated whose dominant degradation products are regenerable to active material in situ over repeated aging cycles, without significant energy or reagent input and without accumulation of irreversible contaminants.
why: It would make electrolyte lifetime repairable in place rather than requiring continual chemical replacement.
key_works: Y. Jing et al. (2022), “In situ electrochemical recomposition of decomposed redox-active species in aqueous organic flow batteries,” [DOI:10.1038/s41557-022-00967-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-022-00967-4).

title: Singlet-oxygen-resistant lithium–oxygen chemistry
open: Can a lithium–oxygen cell be made chemically immune to the singlet oxygen it generates — suppressing or harmlessly quenching singlet oxygen during oxygen reduction and evolution without sacrificing useful capacity or adding consumable scavengers? In formal terms, the target is reversible aprotic oxygen cycling with closed oxygen and electrolyte mass balances over extended operation.
status: Mahne et al. identified singlet oxygen as a major parasitic-reaction source in 2017. Quenchers and mediator redesign help individual pathways, but reversible aprotic oxygen cycling with durable components remains unresolved. Key work: N. Mahne et al. (2017), “Singlet oxygen generation as a major cause for parasitic reactions during cycling of aprotic lithium–oxygen batteries,” [DOI:10.1038/nenergy.2017.36](https://doi.org/10.1038/nenergy.2017.36).
solved_when: Singlet oxygen is suppressed or harmlessly quenched during oxygen reduction and evolution, useful capacity is retained, no consumable scavengers are added, and closed oxygen and electrolyte mass balances are demonstrated over extended cycling.
why: Singlet oxygen drives parasitic chemistry that destroys cell components while masquerading as rechargeable oxygen capacity, so solving it is what makes genuinely rechargeable aprotic lithium–oxygen batteries possible.
key_works: N. Mahne et al. (2017), “Singlet oxygen generation as a major cause for parasitic reactions during cycling of aprotic lithium–oxygen batteries,” [DOI:10.1038/nenergy.2017.36](https://doi.org/10.1038/nenergy.2017.36).

title: Lead immobilization through damage and end of life
open: Can we design lead-binding materials for perovskite photovoltaics that keep the lead immobilized under realistic breakage, weathering, and end-of-life disposal scenarios, yet still allow the module to be recycled efficiently? Success requires quantifying capture saturation and the leaching products that form, rather than measuring leakage from intact modules alone.
status: Adsorption, complexation, grain isolation, and encapsulation approaches were assessed comprehensively in 2023 (H. Zhang et al., 2023, “Lead immobilization for environmentally sustainable perovskite solar cells,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-05938-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-05938-4)). Lead sorbents are known to exist; the unresolved target is durable containment across failure modes with demonstrated recovery.
solved_when: A lead-capture material is demonstrated to durably contain released lead across failure modes — breakage, weathering, and disposal — while showing quantified capture saturation, characterized leaching products, and demonstrated recovery through module recycling.
why: It cuts the environmental release of lead from lead-containing absorbers and makes their responsible deployment, and eventual recycling, straightforward.
key_works: H. Zhang et al. (2023), “Lead immobilization for environmentally sustainable perovskite solar cells,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-05938-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-05938-4).

title: Useful bulk p-type conductivity in beta-gallium oxide
open: Can bulk beta-Ga2O3 be made to conduct via mobile holes — genuine p-type behavior — at the temperatures and carrier densities useful for devices? Alternatively, if it cannot, can the material-specific limits imposed by hole self-trapping and acceptor energetics be established quantitatively?
status: Self-trapped holes were identified as a fundamental obstacle to p-type conductivity in wide-band-gap oxides by Varley and colleagues in 2012 (J. B. Varley, A. Janotti, C. Franchini and C. G. Van de Walle, “Role of self-trapping in luminescence and p-type conductivity of wide-band-gap oxides,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.85.081109](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.85.081109)). Existing reports of p-type behavior remain ambiguous and require distinguishing true band transport from defect, surface, and secondary-phase conduction.
solved_when: Reproducible bulk p-type conduction in beta-Ga2O3 is demonstrated at device-useful temperatures and densities, with compensation and parasitic (defect, surface, and secondary-phase) conduction channels experimentally excluded; or, alternatively, a definitive account of the limits set by self-trapping and acceptor energetics is established.
why: It would enable native bipolar device architectures in an ultrawide-bandgap power material, which the absence of p-type conduction currently forecloses.
key_works: J. B. Varley, A. Janotti, C. Franchini and C. G. Van de Walle (2012), “Role of self-trapping in luminescence and p-type conductivity of wide-band-gap oxides,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.85.081109](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.85.081109).

title: Efficient room-temperature electron doping of diamond
open: Can diamond be given practical n-type character at room temperature — donors introduced into device-quality material that actually release electrons under normal operating conditions? Formally, the goal is a doping process yielding electrically active donors with sufficiently shallow activation, low compensation, and controlled spatial profiles, so that low-resistance electron transport is achieved without cooling.
status: Diamond n-type doping has been pursued for decades and is not wholly absent: phosphorus-doped material exists. The 2025 review by M. Sultana, S. Karmakar and A. Haque (2025), ["N- and P-type doping of diamonds: A review"](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S136980012400920X), emphasizes deep levels, incorporation limitations, and room-temperature conductivity as continuing obstacles.
solved_when: Device-quality diamond exhibits room-temperature electron transport with low resistance, via donors that are shallow enough to activate, electrically uncompensated, and spatially controllable in profile.
why: It would complement diamond's established hole conduction and enable high-power bipolar devices, which currently lack a usable electron-conducting side.
key_works: M. Sultana, S. Karmakar and A. Haque (2025), [“N- and P-type doping of diamonds: A review”](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S136980012400920X).

title: High-conductivity p-type aluminum nitride
open: Can aluminum nitride be made to conduct holes usefully — that is, doped p-type in a stable, reproducible way that does not succumb to acceptor compensation, optical absorption, or contact resistance — and can the mechanism be validated in a functioning AlN-based bipolar structure?
status: Deep acceptors have constrained AlN devices for decades. Ma et al. reported Mg-doped p-type films in 2025, while identifying limited activation and mobility; detecting p-type character does not settle useful device conductivity. Key work: Y. Ma et al. (2025), “Mg-Doped P-Type AlN Thin Film Prepared by Magnetron Sputtering Using Mg-Al Alloy Targets,” [DOI:10.3390/mi16091035](https://doi.org/10.3390/mi16091035).
solved_when: Stable, reproducible hole injection and conduction is demonstrated in high-quality AlN without excessive compensation, optical absorption, or contact resistance, and the mechanism is validated in a working AlN-based bipolar device.
why: It underpins deep-ultraviolet emitters and ultrawide-bandgap bipolar electronics, both of which are blocked without practical p-type AlN.
key_works: Y. Ma et al. (2025), “Mg-Doped P-Type AlN Thin Film Prepared by Magnetron Sputtering Using Mg-Al Alloy Targets,” [DOI:10.3390/mi16091035](https://doi.org/10.3390/mi16091035).

title: Wafer-scale 2D single crystals without stitched-boundary penalties
open: Can two-dimensional materials be grown as true single crystals spanning an entire manufacturing wafer, so that aligned domains merge without electrically harmful translation boundaries? Concretely, this means device-grade monolayers with uniform thickness, orientation, and defect density over wafer-scale areas, with reproducible yield across batches and substrates.
status: Jiang et al. (2025) demonstrated centimetre-scale single-domain MoS2 through two-dimensional Czochralski growth. Extending single-domain quality to manufacturing-scale wafers and compatible substrates remains open.
solved_when: Wafer-scale monolayer single crystals of a 2D semiconductor are demonstrated with uniform thickness, orientation, and defect density, no electrically harmful stitched translation boundaries at merging domains, and reproducible yield across batches and on manufacturing-compatible substrates.
why: It would make large-area two-dimensional electronics predictable at the individual-device level, so device performance no longer depends on where on the wafer a device happens to sit.
key_works: H. Jiang et al. (2025), “Two-dimensional Czochralski growth of single-crystal MoS2,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-02069-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-02069-7).

title: Continuous electrically pumped colloidal-quantum-dot lasing
open: Can a solution-processable colloidal-quantum-dot device be made to lase continuously under electrical pumping, with unambiguous cavity-mode and coherence signatures? Formally, this demands simultaneous control of Auger recombination, charge imbalance, Joule heating, and optical loss during sustained operation.
status: Ahn et al. achieved electrically driven amplified spontaneous emission in 2023, establishing electrical gain; however, continuous laser operation and durable devices impose additional materials constraints.
solved_when: Continuous electrically pumped lasing from a colloidal-quantum-dot device is demonstrated, with clear evidence of a cavity mode and coherence, under control of Auger recombination, charge imbalance, Joule heating, and optical loss.
why: It would yield chemically tunable, integrated laser sources fabricated from colloidal materials.
key_works: N. Ahn et al. (2023), “Electrically driven amplified spontaneous emission from colloidal quantum dots,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-05855-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-05855-6).

title: The superconducting order parameter of Sr2RuO4
open: What is the superconducting order parameter of Sr2RuO4? A full answer must reconcile the spin susceptibility, strain response, time-reversal-symmetry tests, gap structure, and thermodynamics measured on comparably characterized samples, resolving the conflicting interpretations these probes currently support.
status: Unsettled since superconductivity was discovered in 1994. A. Pustogow et al. (2019), "Constraints on the superconducting order parameter in Sr2RuO4 from oxygen-17 nuclear magnetic resonance," [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1596-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1596-2), challenged the long-favored spin-triplet interpretation; a universally consistent experimental identification remains open.
solved_when: A single order parameter is identified that is consistent with spin susceptibility, strain response, time-reversal-symmetry tests, gap structure, and thermodynamics in comparably characterized samples, and the conflicting interpretations among these probes are resolved.
why: A definitive identification would test how multiorbital electronic correlations create unconventional superconductivity, with Sr2RuO4 as the paradigmatic case.
key_works: A. Pustogow et al. (2019), “Constraints on the superconducting order parameter in Sr2RuO4 from oxygen-17 nuclear magnetic resonance,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1596-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1596-2).

title: Arbitrary-sequence synthetic polymers at production scale
open: Can we synthesize nonbiological-backbone polymers whose monomers are placed one by one in a fully specified sequence, at meaningful scale? Formally, produce long, individually specified monomer sequences with simultaneous control of chain length, stereochemistry, and sequence defects.
status: Sequence control has advanced substantially since the 2000s through iterative synthesis, controlled polymerization, and biological templates, as surveyed in J.-F. Lutz, M. Ouchi, D. R. Liu, and M. Sawamoto (2013), “Sequence-Controlled Polymers,” [DOI:10.1126/science.1238149](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1238149), and J.-F. Lutz (2017), “Defining the Field of Sequence-Controlled Polymers,” [DOI:10.1002/marc.201700582](https://doi.org/10.1002/marc.201700582); however, these capabilities do not establish the combined length–fidelity–throughput target for arbitrary synthetic backbones.
solved_when: Kilogram batches of prescribed 1,000-unit chains are produced with independently measured whole-chain sequence fidelity above 99%.
why: It would enable reproducible synthetic catalysts, molecular information storage, and protein-like materials built from chemistries beyond what biology offers.
key_works: J.-F. Lutz, M. Ouchi, D. R. Liu, and M. Sawamoto (2013), “Sequence-Controlled Polymers,” [DOI:10.1126/science.1238149](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1238149); J.-F. Lutz (2017), “Defining the Field of Sequence-Controlled Polymers,” [DOI:10.1002/marc.201700582](https://doi.org/10.1002/marc.201700582).

title: Repeated autonomous restoration of elastomer fatigue resistance
open: Can an elastomer that has accumulated fatigue damage regain its resistance to cyclic crack growth — not merely its tensile strength — through repeated autonomous repair at ambient conditions, even when interfaces are contaminated and load is sustained throughout, all without loss of dimensional stability?
status: Self-healing materials have progressed from soft networks to stiff composites; Liu et al. reported an approximately 8.23 kJ/m² fatigue threshold and rapid near-infrared-triggered healing in 2025. Autonomous repair under realistic continuing service remains a stronger combined target. Key work: T. Liu et al. (2025), "Multiscale interlinked structures limit fatigue crack propagation in a MXene-polyurethane composite," [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-64611-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64611-8).
solved_when: A damaged elastomer demonstrates restoration of its fatigue threshold repeatedly under ambient conditions, with contaminated interfaces and sustained load present, while retaining dimensional stability; recovery of tensile strength alone does not qualify.
why: It would enable load-bearing soft components that repair themselves in service, yielding measurable service-life gains rather than single-shot laboratory demonstrations.
key_works: T. Liu et al. (2025), “Multiscale interlinked structures limit fatigue crack propagation in a MXene-polyurethane composite,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-64611-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64611-8).

title: Device-quality colloidal diamond
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
open: Can colloidal particles be assembled into diamond-structured crystals that are large, orientationally controlled, and clean enough — with sufficiently low vacancy, stacking-fault, and grain-boundary defect densities — to exhibit a complete three-dimensional photonic bandgap, and then converted into a high-index material without losing the structure, yielding reproducible optical device performance?
status: Colloidal diamond itself was experimentally assembled by He et al. in 2020 after decades of effort; scalable, defect-controlled assembly plus device-material conversion is the remaining integrated problem. Key work: M. He et al. (2020), "Colloidal diamond," [DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2718-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2718-6).
solved_when: Colloidal-diamond domains are assembled with controlled orientation and defect densities (vacancies, stacking faults, grain boundaries) low enough to realize a specified complete photonic bandgap, and the architecture is preserved through conversion into a useful high-index material with demonstrated reproducible optical performance.
why: It would provide an inexpensive route to three-dimensional photonic materials with complete bandgaps.

title: Inverse design of assembly pathways
subfield: Colloids, liquid crystals, gels, and active soft materials
open: Can we go from a desired colloidal structure straight to the protocol that builds it — choosing temperature, concentration, or field schedules so that finite-time yield is maximized while competing structures are suppressed? Equivalently, given a target structure and physically realizable interactions, construct a protocol whose prediction includes kinetic failure modes, not just the favorable equilibrium phase.
status: Established as a distinct problem by the 2010s; simulations and selected controlled protocols outperform fixed conditions, but transferable inverse design for realistic hydrodynamics and polydispersity remains limited. Key works: S. Whitelam and R. L. Jack (2015), “The Statistical Mechanics of Dynamic Pathways to Self-Assembly,” [DOI:10.1146/annurev-physchem-040214-121215](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-physchem-040214-121215); W. M. Jacobs, A. Reinhardt, and D. Frenkel (2015), “Rational design of self-assembly pathways for complex multicomponent structures,” [arXiv:1502.01351](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.01351).
solved_when: A method exists that, given a target colloidal structure and practical interactions, outputs a temperature, concentration, or field protocol that maximizes finite-time yield while avoiding competing structures, and predicts kinetic failures rather than only identifying a favorable equilibrium phase.
why: It would turn self-assembly from a hit-or-miss phenomenon into a reliable manufacturing route for complex structures.
key_works: S. Whitelam and R. L. Jack (2015), “The Statistical Mechanics of Dynamic Pathways to Self-Assembly,” [DOI:10.1146/annurev-physchem-040214-121215](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-physchem-040214-121215); W. M. Jacobs, A. Reinhardt, and D. Frenkel (2015), “Rational design of self-assembly pathways for complex multicomponent structures,” [arXiv:1502.01351](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.01351).

title: Predicting the foreign-body response from material design
open: Can we predict, from a material's design alone — its chemistry, mechanics, and geometry, together with implantation site and host condition — the long-term foreign-body response, namely capsule formation and inflammatory cell states? Such a model must generalize across species and must separate the immune consequences of surgical injury from those genuinely induced by the material.
status: The problem has been studied for decades; material size and shape are known to affect the response (O. Veiseh et al. (2015), "Size- and shape-dependent foreign body immune response to materials implanted in rodents and non-human primates," [DOI:10.1038/nmat4290](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat4290)). Adhesive interfaces prevented observable capsules for 12 weeks in several animal settings in 2024 (J. Wu et al. (2024), "Adhesive anti-fibrotic interfaces on diverse organs," [DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07426-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07426-9)). General host- and site-transferable prediction remains open.
solved_when: A validated predictive model exists that forecasts long-term capsule formation and inflammatory cell states from material chemistry, mechanics, geometry, implantation site, and host condition, transfers across species and implantation sites, and distinguishes material-induced immune responses from surgical injury effects.
why: It would reduce the failure of implants, biosensors, and drug-delivery devices, whose long-term function is defeated by fibrotic encapsulation and chronic inflammation.
key_works: O. Veiseh et al. (2015), “Size- and shape-dependent foreign body immune response to materials implanted in rodents and non-human primates,” [DOI:10.1038/nmat4290](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat4290); J. Wu et al. (2024), “Adhesive anti-fibrotic interfaces on diverse organs,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07426-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07426-9).

title: Long-lived small-diameter vascular grafts
open: Can we engineer a clinically practical small-diameter vascular graft that stays open and functional for years in humans? Such a graft must sustain physiological compliance and endothelial function without progressive thrombosis, intimal hyperplasia, or aneurysm, including in anatomically and hemodynamically demanding configurations.
status: This is a decades-old challenge. Zhang et al. reported 100% patency in their allogeneic rhesus-macaque experiment in 2025 (J. Zhang et al. (2025), “Small-diameter artery grafts engineered from pluripotent stem cells maintain 100% patency in an allogeneic rhesus macaque model,” [DOI:10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.102002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.102002)), but that study-specific result does not establish universal or multiyear clinical durability.
solved_when: A readily available small-diameter graft demonstrates patency, compliance, and endothelial function — without progressive thrombosis, intimal hyperplasia, or aneurysm — in long-term comparative human studies across demanding graft configurations.
why: It would supply durable vascular replacements for patients who lack suitable autologous vessels, a common and limiting situation in cardiovascular surgery.
key_works: J. Zhang et al. (2025), “Small-diameter artery grafts engineered from pluripotent stem cells maintain 100% patency in an allogeneic rhesus macaque model,” [DOI:10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.102002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.102002).

title: Defined dynamic matrices across organoid lineages
open: Can chemically defined, fully synthetic matrices replace variable animal-derived matrices in supporting the complete developmental program — expansion, differentiation, and maturation — of human organoids across multiple lineages? In particular, which time-dependent changes in matrix mechanics and ligand presentation are required at each developmental transition?
status: Gjorevski et al. demonstrated dynamic synthetic matrices for intestinal organoids in 2016 (N. Gjorevski et al. (2016), "Designer matrices for intestinal stem cell and organoid culture," [DOI:10.1038/nature20168](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature20168)); later matrices extend selected tissue systems, but a transferable recipe covering diverse lineages and mature function remains open.
solved_when: A transferable recipe exists for chemically defined dynamic matrices that supports reproducible expansion, differentiation, and maturation across diverse specified human organoid lineages, with the necessary time-dependent mechanical and ligand changes identified for each developmental transition.
why: It would remove batch-to-batch variability from organoid culture, improving the reliability of disease models, drug testing, and the manufacture of transplantable tissues.
key_works: N. Gjorevski et al. (2016), “Designer matrices for intestinal stem cell and organoid culture,” [DOI:10.1038/nature20168](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature20168).

title: Practical broadband three-dimensional elastic cloaking
open: Can an architected material cloak a finite-sized object from elastic waves of all polarizations — longitudinal and shear alike — across a specified finite frequency band and range of incidence directions, while using only finite, manufacturable constitutive parameters? A complete answer would require the demonstrated performance to hold under realistic support loads, material losses, and fabrication imperfections.
status: Transformation elasticity gives exact idealized designs, and restricted-wave demonstrations exist, following A. N. Norris and A. L. Shuvalov (2011), “Elastic cloaking theory,” [arXiv:1103.6045](https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.6045). Simultaneous three-dimensional, multipolarization, broadband performance under practical constitutive constraints remains unresolved; unlimited perfect passive cloaking is not the target.
solved_when: A three-dimensional cloak simultaneously reduces longitudinal and shear scattering over the specified finite band and incidence range, with finite material parameters, and its measured or simulated performance specification explicitly includes support loads, losses, and imperfections.
why: It enables practical vibration protection and structurally useful yet wave-unobtrusive supports — cloaks that work in real engineered structures rather than idealized geometries.
key_works: A. N. Norris and A. L. Shuvalov (2011), “Elastic cloaking theory,” [arXiv:1103.6045](https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.6045).

title: Active metasurfaces with joint efficiency, speed, and endurance
open: Can an actively addressable metasurface be built that delivers large reversible optical modulation while simultaneously achieving useful switching speed, low loss, low energy consumption, and high cycle life over a large area? A complete answer must report aging behavior and pixel-to-pixel drift alongside the initial optical response.
status: Electrical, thermal, mechanical, and phase-change tuning mechanisms are established, but the speed, modulation depth, loss, and integration tradeoffs identified in 2019 continue to motivate distinct material platforms, and no single tuning mechanism settles the combined specification. Key work: A. M. Shaltout, V. M. Shalaev, and M. L. Brongersma (2019), "Spatiotemporal light control with active metasurfaces," [DOI:10.1126/science.aat3100](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aat3100).
solved_when: A large-area, addressable metasurface material demonstrates large reversible optical modulation together with useful switching speed, low loss, low energy, and high cycle life, with measured aging and pixel-to-pixel drift reported alongside the initial optical response.
why: Such a material would make dynamic holography, beam steering, and adaptive optics practical rather than laboratory demonstrations.
key_works: A. M. Shaltout, V. M. Shalaev, and M. L. Brongersma (2019), “Spatiotemporal light control with active metasurfaces,” [DOI:10.1126/science.aat3100](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aat3100).

title: Chemistry-based closure of moving-contact-line dynamics
subfield: Surfaces, wetting, adhesion, and functional coatings
open: Can the dynamics of a moving liquid contact line be predicted from independently measured surface chemistry and molecular dynamics alone, rather than by refitting an effective parameter for each experiment? In full, such a theory should reproduce the speed-dependent contact angle and the transition to film deposition by bridging microscopic slip, adsorption, and contact-line friction to macroscopic flow.
status: Slip and diffuse-interface models regularize the classical moving-contact-line singularity. The 2013 review by Snoeijer and Andreotti documents established regimes and remaining microscopic-to-continuum matching questions; real heterogeneous surfaces add unresolved history dependence.
solved_when: A predictive closure exists that derives macroscopic contact-line motion — including speed-dependent contact angle and transitions to film deposition — from independently measured surface chemistry and molecular-scale physics, without refitting effective parameters for each experiment.
why: It would make coating, printing, immersion lithography, and fluid deposition quantitatively predictable.
key_works: J. H. Snoeijer and B. Andreotti (2013), “Moving Contact Lines: Scales, Regimes, and Dynamical Transitions,” [DOI:10.1146/annurev-fluid-011212-140734](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-fluid-011212-140734).

title: Long-lived submerged gas layers on superhydrophobic surfaces
subfield: Surfaces, wetting, adhesion, and functional coatings
open: Can a superhydrophobic surface keep a useful gas layer submerged for a full service interval, despite water depth, gas undersaturation, turbulence, abrasion, and contamination? The problem is to predict when gas dissolution or wetting nucleation forces failure, and to quantify any energy needed to replenish the gas.
status: Jones et al. connected roughness scale to submerged gas/vapor stability in 2015 [P. R. Jones et al. (2015), "Sustaining dry surfaces under water," DOI:10.1038/srep12311], but thermodynamic stability arguments and laboratory plastron retention do not alone establish durability under combined field conditions.
solved_when: A surface design retains a specified gas-covered fraction under the specified combined conditions (depth, undersaturation, turbulence, abrasion, contamination) for the intended service interval, with a validated failure prediction and a quantified gas-replenishment energy.
why: It would make submerged drag reduction and corrosion isolation dependable enough for real service rather than short-lived laboratory demonstrations.
key_works: P. R. Jones et al. (2015), “Sustaining dry surfaces under water,” [DOI:10.1038/srep12311](https://doi.org/10.1038/srep12311).

title: Catalyst-tolerant processing of dirty mixed plastic waste
open: Can a chemical or biological processing route be designed that tolerates real, unsorted mixed plastic waste — polymers, dyes, stabilizers, fillers, food residues, and halogen-containing contaminants — while keeping catalyst activity and useful product selectivity? The goal extends to quantifying contaminant tolerance limits and catalyst regenerability using representative waste rather than only clean model mixtures.
status: Sullivan et al. (2022) combined chemical oxidation and biological funneling for mixed plastics, but sustained operation under realistic impurity distributions, separation demands, and feed changes remains a distinct, unsolved scale-up problem. Key work: K. P. Sullivan et al. (2022), “Mixed plastics waste valorization through tandem chemical oxidation and biological funneling,” [DOI:10.1126/science.abo4626](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abo4626).
solved_when: A process operates on representative dirty mixed plastic waste, retains catalyst activity and product selectivity in the presence of the contaminant classes listed, and reports quantitative tolerance limits and regeneration performance over realistic impurity distributions and feed changes.
why: It would eliminate expensive presorting of plastic waste and prevent contamination from being carried into recycled products.
key_works: K. P. Sullivan et al. (2022), “Mixed plastics waste valorization through tandem chemical oxidation and biological funneling,” [DOI:10.1126/science.abo4626](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abo4626).

title: Predicting resumption of waste-glass alteration
subfield: Radiation, nuclear materials, and extreme environments
open: Under what conditions does the formation of secondary phases destabilize the protective alteration layer on nuclear waste glass and cause dissolution to accelerate again? A predictive treatment should yield induction times and acceleration magnitudes for independently specified water chemistry, temperature, and surface-area-to-solution conditions.
status: Forty years of standardized durability testing were reviewed in 2021 (C. L. Thorpe et al. (2021), “Forty years of durability assessment of nuclear waste glass by standard methods,” [DOI:10.1038/s41529-021-00210-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41529-021-00210-4)); resumption of alteration is observed under some conditions and absent under others, so it cannot be treated as a universal fixed stage of glass alteration.
solved_when: A validated prediction exists for the onset (induction time) and magnitude of resumption of alteration as a function of independently specified water chemistry, temperature, and surface-area conditions, consistent with the observed cases where resumption occurs and where it does not.
why: It identifies the conditions under which simple long-term durability extrapolations for nuclear waste glass become invalid, which is essential for confident repository performance assessment.
key_works: C. L. Thorpe et al. (2021), “Forty years of durability assessment of nuclear waste glass by standard methods,” [DOI:10.1038/s41529-021-00210-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41529-021-00210-4).

title: Phason-entropy stabilization of decagonal Al–Co–Cu
open: Does phason entropy actually stabilize decagonal Al–Co–Cu against its crystalline approximants in the converged quasiperiodic limit, and by how much? The question asks for a decomposition of phason, chemical, and vibrational entropy and a prediction of the equilibrium stability window with no fitting to the observed transition temperature.
status: Huang, Widom, and Mihalkovič’s 2024 calculations (DOI:10.1103/PhysRevResearch.6.033145) place their quasicrystal approximants at least about 3 meV per atom above crystalline competitors at zero temperature and predict entropy stabilization around 600–800 K. Experimental validation remains open; 2025 ground-state calculations for other binary quasicrystals (Baek et al., DOI:10.1038/s41567-025-02925-6) also show why entropy stabilization should not be assumed universal.
solved_when: The three entropy channels are cleanly separated, the stability window is predicted without fitting the transition temperature, and the prediction is confirmed against experiment in the converged quasiperiodic limit.
why: It would establish which microscopic disorder stabilizes a real quasiperiodic solid and make its thermal processing predictable.
key_works: Y. Huang, M. Widom, and M. Mihalkovič (2024), “Simulated structure and thermodynamics of decagonal Al-Co-Cu quasicrystals,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevResearch.6.033145](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevResearch.6.033145); W. Baek et al. (2025), “Quasicrystal stability and nucleation kinetics from density functional theory,” [DOI:10.1038/s41567-025-02925-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-025-02925-6).

title: Same-specimen reconciliation of MXene hydroxyl assignments
open: How much of the hydrogen-bearing signal on Ti₃C₂Tₓ is truly terminating hydroxyl, and how much belongs to intercalated water, adsorbed water, or oxidation products? Answer this by reconciling isotope-sensitive solid-state NMR with photoelectron spectroscopy measured on matched specimens with controlled hydration histories and a closed hydrogen inventory.
status: A 2020 NMR–DFT study (T. Kobayashi et al. (2020), "Nature of Terminating Hydroxyl Groups and Intercalating Water in Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXenes: A Study by ¹H Solid-State NMR and DFT Calculations," DOI:10.1021/acs.jpcc.0c04744) assigned terminating hydroxyls and distinct water environments, while a 2021 UPS/XPS study (L.-Å. Näslund et al. (2021), "Chemical Bonding of Termination Species in 2D Carbides Investigated through Valence Band UPS/XPS of Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene," DOI:10.1088/2053-1583/ac1ea9) concluded that hydroxyls were not inherent terminations of its Ti₃C₂Tₓ surfaces. Reconciling these assignments through measured preparation and measurement histories remains open.
solved_when: The terminating-hydroxyl abundance and geometry on Ti₃C₂Tₓ are determined separately from intercalated water, adsorbed water, and oxidation products, and the NMR and photoelectron-spectroscopy assignments agree on matched specimens with controlled hydration histories and a closed hydrogen inventory.
why: Surface proton identity changes interfacial reactions, ion binding, and the interpretation of computational MXene models, so unresolved assignments leave both experiments and theory on uncertain footing.
key_works: T. Kobayashi et al. (2020), “Nature of Terminating Hydroxyl Groups and Intercalating Water in Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXenes: A Study by ¹H Solid-State NMR and DFT Calculations,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpcc.0c04744](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.0c04744); L.-Å. Näslund et al. (2021), “Chemical Bonding of Termination Species in 2D Carbides Investigated through Valence Band UPS/XPS of Ti₃C₂Tₓ MXene,” [DOI:10.1088/2053-1583/ac1ea9](https://doi.org/10.1088/2053-1583/ac1ea9).

title: Prescribing zeolite aluminum sites and aluminum pairs
open: Can a zeolite be synthesized whose aluminum atoms occupy a pre-chosen distribution among inequivalent tetrahedral sites, with a pre-chosen population of aluminum pairs, while the framework topology and bulk Si/Al ratio are held fixed? In other words, can site populations and pair separations be selected prospectively rather than only measured after synthesis?
status: This longstanding synthesis-control problem became more sharply measurable through Rzepka et al.'s 2025 anomalous X-ray diffraction determination of aluminum distributions in ZSM-5. Site mapping is a major advance, but it does not provide arbitrary control over occupancy, pairing, or redistribution during later treatment. Key works: P. Rzepka et al. (2025), “Aluminum distribution and active site locations in the structures of zeolite ZSM-5 catalysts,” [DOI:10.1126/science.ads7290](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ads7290).
solved_when: A zeolite is synthesized in which the aluminum distribution over inequivalent tetrahedral sites and the aluminum-pair population match specified target values, with framework topology and bulk Si/Al ratio fixed.
why: Zeolites of identical bulk composition can contain different acid-site arrangements and thereby support different catalytic pathways, so control over the arrangement would give access to catalytic behavior that composition alone cannot prescribe.
key_works: P. Rzepka et al. (2025), “Aluminum distribution and active site locations in the structures of zeolite ZSM-5 catalysts,” [DOI:10.1126/science.ads7290](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.ads7290).

title: Strong intrinsic argon-over-oxygen recognition
open: Can a physisorbent be designed that, at ambient temperature, preferentially takes up argon over oxygen strongly enough to matter, while still releasing the gas reversibly? A proposed census target is Ar/O₂ selectivity of at least ten at 298–310 K and at least 0.5 mmol g⁻¹ argon working capacity between 1 and 0.1 bar — proposed thresholds, not community benchmarks.
status: The state of the art is modest recognition: Yan et al.'s 2025 amino-functionalized ultra-micropore MOF reports Ar/O₂ selectivity around 1.4 and argon uptake around 10 cm³ g⁻¹ at 308 K and 1 bar [DOI:10.1016/j.jiec.2025.01.013](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jiec.2025.01.013). Zhao et al. already demonstrate oxygen product purity above 99.99% with AlFUM under ambient conditions [DOI:10.1016/j.ces.2025.122130](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ces.2025.122130), though purity must be distinguished from recovery yield.
solved_when: An ambient-temperature physisorbent is demonstrated with reversible argon uptake, Ar/O₂ selectivity of at least ten at 298–310 K, and at least 0.5 mmol g⁻¹ argon working capacity between 1 and 0.1 bar.
why: Strong intrinsic recognition of argon over oxygen would shrink sorbent inventories and reduce gas-recycling burdens in air-separation processes.
key_works: F. Yan et al. (2025), “An amino-functionalized ultra-micropore metal–organic framework using for argon/oxygen adsorption separation,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jiec.2025.01.013](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jiec.2025.01.013); S. Zhao et al. (2025), “Selective recognition of argon by an aluminum-based MOF for oxygen recovery from Ar/O₂ mixture under ambient conditions,” [DOI:10.1016/j.ces.2025.122130](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ces.2025.122130).

title: GeTe resistance drift beyond a single structural-relaxation clock
open: What microscopic processes govern resistance drift in melt-quenched GeTe when a single structural-relaxation clock cannot capture the data — specifically the temperature-independent early drift and the accelerated late drift near the glass transition? A successful theory should predict resistance from 10 ns to 1,000 s across temperature and quench rate, including the increased drift coefficients observed after slower quenching.
status: Ballmaier, Walfort, and Salinga's 2025 measurements span eleven time decades and approximately room temperature to 460 K. Submicrosecond behavior and late acceleration near the glass transition depart from familiar power-law models; the authors identify deficiencies in existing descriptions. Key work: J. Ballmaier, S. Walfort, and M. Salinga (2025), "Resistance Drift of Phase Change Materials Beyond the Power Law," [DOI:10.1002/aelm.202400905](https://doi.org/10.1002/aelm.202400905).
solved_when: A microscopic account identifies the processes producing both temperature-independent early drift and accelerated late drift, and yields quantitative predictions of resistance over the full window from 10 ns to 1,000 s, across the measured temperature range and quench rates, reproducing the larger drift coefficients after slower quenches.
why: Predictive drift physics would improve analog-memory reliability and distinguish genuinely stable resistance states from those that merely appear stable over short observation windows.
key_works: J. Ballmaier, S. Walfort, and M. Salinga (2025), “Resistance Drift of Phase Change Materials Beyond the Power Law,” [DOI:10.1002/aelm.202400905](https://doi.org/10.1002/aelm.202400905).

title: Stable coherent NV centres within two nanometres of diamond surfaces
open: Can a nitrogen-vacancy centre located just 0.5–2 nm below a diamond surface be made to keep both its useful charge state and the coherence predicted to survive in this regime through surface-induced strain combined with a weak static magnetic field? Any demonstration must independently verify the depth and characterize the surface electric- and magnetic-noise spectra.
status: Pershin et al.’s 2025 first-principles study (A. Pershin, A. Tárkányi, V. Verkhovlyuk, V. Ivády, and A. Gali, 2025, "A coherence-protection scheme for quantum sensors based on ultra-shallow single nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond," DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-64771-7) proposes protection even near 1 nm depth, but its favorable limits assume strong isotopic purification and sufficiently weak electric-field noise. Existing coherence demonstrations at larger shallow depths do not establish this ultrasmall stand-off regime.
solved_when: A single NV centre is experimentally shown at a verified depth of 0.5–2 nm below the surface, with independently established depth and measured surface electric- and magnetic-noise spectra, retaining its useful charge state and the coherence protection predicted for surface-induced strain plus a weak static magnetic field.
why: NV centres this close to the surface would couple far more strongly to individual external nuclear spins and to molecular-scale magnetic structure, extending nanoscale sensing to single-molecule resolution.
key_works: A. Pershin, A. Tárkányi, V. Verkhovlyuk, V. Ivády, and A. Gali (2025), “A coherence-protection scheme for quantum sensors based on ultra-shallow single nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-64771-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64771-7).

title: Experimental Purcell refrigeration below the rare-earth thermal-population limit
open: Can a rare-earth-doped crystal be laser-cooled below the temperature any bulk rare-earth solid has reached, by placing it in an optical cavity that preferentially enhances higher-energy fluorescence? Formally, this means demonstrating net laser refrigeration below liquid-nitrogen temperature, with parasitic absorption, surface quenching, optical escape, and a calibrated heat load all accounted for in the measurement.
status: A 2026 calculation by P. Ju et al. (“Purcell-enhanced optical refrigeration,” [DOI:10.1103/d7pk-hsry](https://doi.org/10.1103/d7pk-hsry), [arXiv:2404.19142](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.19142)), using measured Yb:YLF coefficients, predicts approximately 38 K for a nanocrystal near a cavity, compared with an experimental rare-earth refrigeration baseline of 87 K cited in that work; the lower temperature remains a theoretical projection.
solved_when: A cavity-enhanced rare-earth-doped crystal shows net laser refrigeration below liquid-nitrogen temperature, beating the 87 K experimental baseline, with the demonstration including parasitic absorption, surface quenching, optical escape, and a calibrated heat load.
why: It would extend vibration-free optical refrigeration to detectors and quantum devices requiring deeper cryogenic cooling.
key_works: P. Ju et al. (2026), “Purcell-enhanced optical refrigeration,” [DOI:10.1103/d7pk-hsry](https://doi.org/10.1103/d7pk-hsry), [arXiv:2404.19142](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.19142).

title: Distinguishing bulk-flexoelectric boundary layers from surface piezoelectricity
open: Can an experiment distinguish a true surface piezoelectric layer from a surface-localized response that bulk flexoelectricity generates? The challenge is to design a measurement that independently varies sample size, surface termination, and electrical boundary conditions while resolving strain or field profiles near the surface.
status: Mohammadi et al.'s 2025 closed-form solutions show that finite flexoelectric bodies can respond near surfaces even under homogeneous loading, and such boundary layers resemble surface piezoelectric effects — creating the experimental attribution problem. The continuum boundary-layer calculation itself is already solved. Key work: H. Mohammadi, F. Greco, D. Codony, and I. Arias (2025), “Flexoelectricity causes surface piezoelectric-like effects in dielectrics,” [DOI:10.1016/j.ijmecsci.2025.110162](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijmecsci.2025.110162), [arXiv:2501.17626](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17626).
