solved_when: A measurement protocol exists that separates genuine surface piezoelectricity from bulk-flexoelectric boundary layers, using independent variation of sample size, surface termination, and electrical boundary conditions with resolved strain or field profiles, yielding unambiguous attribution of the observed surface response.
why: Without reliable attribution, large nanoscale coupling coefficients cannot be confidently transferred to devices or used to infer material symmetry.
key_works: H. Mohammadi, F. Greco, D. Codony, and I. Arias (2025), “Flexoelectricity causes surface piezoelectric-like effects in dielectrics,” [DOI:10.1016/j.ijmecsci.2025.110162](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijmecsci.2025.110162), [arXiv:2501.17626](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.17626).

title: Three-dimensional trap geography in SrAl₂O₄:Eu,Dy afterglow
open: Can we determine the actual three-dimensional spatial distribution and connectivity of Eu emitters, Dy electron traps, and competing defects in SrAl₂O₄:Eu,Dy, and from that measured structure alone predict charging, afterglow, and thermoluminescence — without separately refitting arbitrary trap-energy distributions or hopping networks to each experiment?
status: Optical work published in 2025 directly supports trapping at lanthanide codopants, including Dy: D. Van der Heggen, J. J. Joos, and P. F. Smet (2025), "Optical Evidence of Charge Trapping at Lanthanide Codopants in SrAl₂O₄:Eu,Ln (Ln = Nd, Sm, Dy) Persistent Phosphors," [DOI:10.1002/adom.202402153](https://doi.org/10.1002/adom.202402153). Koizumi et al.'s 2025 random-walk model ("Visualization of trap distribution in SrAl₂O₄:Eu²⁺,Dy³⁺ … based on a random walk model," [DOI:10.1039/D5CP01232E](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5CP01232E)) reproduces several luminescence processes using an inferred one-dimensional trap landscape; connecting these effective models to independently measured three-dimensional geometry remains open.
solved_when: A measured three-dimensional trap geometry exists, and a single model built on it reproduces charging, afterglow, and thermoluminescence behavior without separately refitting trap-energy distributions or hopping networks to each experiment.
why: It would make brightness, charging speed, and persistence jointly designable rather than independently tuned.
key_works: D. Van der Heggen, J. J. Joos, and P. F. Smet (2025), “Optical Evidence of Charge Trapping at Lanthanide Codopants in SrAl₂O₄:Eu,Ln (Ln = Nd, Sm, Dy) Persistent Phosphors,” [DOI:10.1002/adom.202402153](https://doi.org/10.1002/adom.202402153); R. Koizumi et al. (2025), “Visualization of trap distribution in SrAl₂O₄:Eu²⁺,Dy³⁺ … based on a random walk model,” [DOI:10.1039/D5CP01232E](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5CP01232E).

title: Linear-contamination threshold in ring-melt viscosity
open: At what concentration of linear chains does a ring polymer melt develop a rubbery plateau or lose its intrinsic zero-shear viscosity, and how does that threshold depend on the molecular weights of both the rings and the contaminant chains? A quantitative answer would also let the intrinsic viscosity of a pure ring melt be recovered with quantified uncertainty, whenever contamination stays below the threshold.
status: A 2024 reassessment of moderately entangled ring melts — K. Peponaki, D. Tsalikis, N. Patelis, G. Sakellariou, T. Chang, and D. Vlassopoulos (2024), "Revisiting the Viscosity of Moderately Entangled Ring Polymer Melts," [DOI:10.1021/acs.macromol.4c00601](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.macromol.4c00601) — identifies remaining purity and analytical-detection limits as the main obstacles to accurate viscosity measurements. Trace linear chains can obscure the terminal response precisely where competing descriptions of ring relaxation would need stringent tests.
solved_when: The linear-chain concentration threshold for plateau onset or viscosity dominance is determined as a function of both ring and contaminant molecular weights, and the intrinsic ring-melt viscosity is recovered with quantified uncertainty at contamination below that threshold.
why: A calibrated threshold would make ring-rheology measurements comparable across labs and prevent impurity-controlled relaxation from being mistaken for intrinsic topology.
key_works: K. Peponaki, D. Tsalikis, N. Patelis, G. Sakellariou, T. Chang, and D. Vlassopoulos (2024), “Revisiting the Viscosity of Moderately Entangled Ring Polymer Melts,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.macromol.4c00601](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.macromol.4c00601).

title: Experimental realization of colloidal-ring topological bigels
open: Can a bicomponent gel of polymers threaded through colloidal rings be realized in the laboratory, in which network connectivity is set by topological threading rather than by attractive aggregation? The goal is to measure the ring-radius threshold for gelation, the resulting connectivity, and the terminal rheology, and to show that network lifetime follows threading constraints rather than uncontrolled attractive aggregation.
status: Bonato, Marenduzzo, and Orlandini’s 2025 simulations (A. Bonato, D. Marenduzzo, and E. Orlandini (2025), “Formation of Topological Bigels in Mixtures of Colloidal Rings and Polymers,” DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.188203) predict a fluid-to-gel-like transition above a critical ring radius, with an analytical threshold estimate and slowed entanglement mobility. Experimental realization and finite-lifetime limits remain the next tests.
solved_when: An experimental bicomponent gel of polymers and colloidal rings is realized and its measured ring-radius threshold (against the analytical threshold estimate from simulation), connectivity, and terminal rheology are characterized, with network lifetime demonstrably governed by threading constraints rather than uncontrolled aggregation; finite-lifetime limits also assessed.
why: Such gels could obtain connectivity from removable geometric constraints without permanent cross-links, enabling transient networks whose architecture can be undone rather than fixed.
key_works: A. Bonato, D. Marenduzzo, and E. Orlandini (2025), “Formation of Topological Bigels in Mixtures of Colloidal Rings and Polymers,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.188203](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.188203).

title: Predicting knot-specific mechanochemical scission
open: Can we predict where and how fast a polymer chain under tension will break, given its knot type, how tightly the knot is tied, and the chemistry of its backbone? A successful theory would compare different knot topologies against unknotted controls sharing the same chemical linkages and loading histories, and would separate the contributions of geometric stress concentration, knot friction, and intrinsic bond reactivity.
status: Zhang et al. (2024) demonstrated mechanical weakening by a molecular knot, resolving the basic existence question for their architecture, but no transferable law exists that distinguishes geometric stress concentration, knot friction, and intrinsic bond reactivity (M. Zhang, R. Nixon, F. Schaufelberger, L. Pirvu, G. De Bo, and D. A. Leigh, 2024, "Mechanical scission of a knotted polymer," [DOI:10.1038/s41557-024-01510-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-024-01510-3)).
solved_when: A transferable predictive law exists that determines scission location and force-dependent scission rate as a joint function of knot type, tightness, and backbone chemistry, validated across compared knot topologies and unknotted controls with matched chemical linkages and loading histories.
why: It would turn molecular knots from uncontrolled weak points into predictable mechanophores — load-bearing chemical features whose scission behavior can be designed rather than suffered.
key_works: M. Zhang, R. Nixon, F. Schaufelberger, L. Pirvu, G. De Bo, and D. A. Leigh (2024), “Mechanical scission of a knotted polymer,” [DOI:10.1038/s41557-024-01510-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-024-01510-3).

title: Autophobic dewetting versus core–ligand chemical mismatch
open: Can autophobic dewetting, driven by matrix-chain entropy and particle curvature, be cleanly distinguished from core–ligand chemical mismatch as the cause of demixing in polymer-grafted nanoparticles when these variables are independently controlled — and can we then predict whether raising the matrix-to-graft chain-length ratio induces aggregation?
status: Koh et al.’s 2020 simulations of roughly 5 nm particles show no demixing at chain-length ratio ten without suitable attractions, whereas experiments on roughly 10–20 nm particles commonly demix above ratios around four; introducing chemical-mismatch interactions reproduces behavior otherwise attributed to autophobicity. Key work: C. Koh, G. S. Grest, and S. K. Kumar (2020), “Assembly of Polymer-Grafted Nanoparticles in Polymer Matrices,” [DOI:10.1021/acsnano.0c05495](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.0c05495).
solved_when: An experiment or simulation independently controls matrix-chain entropy, particle curvature, and core–ligand chemical mismatch, and yields a predictive criterion for aggregation as a function of matrix-to-graft chain-length ratio — in particular, explaining why roughly 5 nm particles show no demixing at chain-length ratio ten without suitable attractions while roughly 10–20 nm particles commonly demix above ratios around four.
why: Resolving the attribution replaces empirical compatibility rules with reliable nanocomposite design, since chemical-mismatch interactions can reproduce behavior otherwise attributed to autophobicity.
key_works: C. Koh, G. S. Grest, and S. K. Kumar (2020), “Assembly of Polymer-Grafted Nanoparticles in Polymer Matrices,” [DOI:10.1021/acsnano.0c05495](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.0c05495).

title: Entanglement threshold for nanotetrapod-promoted polymer flow
open: At what molecular weight and entanglement density do dispersed nanotetrapods switch from inert to viscosity-reducing additives in a polymer melt? A sharp answer would locate the crossover — including its dependence on tetrapod arm length and loading — and validate it through independently measured chain dynamics across matched polymer series.
status: A 2025 study (J. Sarkar et al., "Nanotetrapods promote polymer flow through confinement induced packing frustration," DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63555-3) reports approximately an order-of-magnitude viscosity reduction in ultrahigh-molecular-weight polystyrene, while 9 kDa polystyrene shows no comparable enhancement. The authors identify chain-length dependence as future work and report an approximately tenfold absolute-viscosity discrepancy between dewetting analysis and rheometry.
solved_when: A predictive molecular-weight and entanglement-density crossover is established, with its dependence on arm length and loading quantified, and the crossover confirmed by independent chain-dynamics measurements on matched polymer series.
why: A predictive crossover would let processors use the additive across a range of conditions while preserving the mechanical performance that comes from long chains.
key_works: J. Sarkar et al. (2025), “Nanotetrapods promote polymer flow through confinement induced packing frustration,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63555-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63555-3).

title: Temperature-dependent mechanisms of cellulose hornification
open: Which molecular changes make the loss of cellulose swelling during drying irreversible, and why do water retention and accessible surface shift their relationship with drying temperature? A satisfying answer must disentangle kinetic trapping, fibril coalescence, and chemical cross-linking as distinct, temperature-dependent mechanisms.
status: Hornification has been recognized since the 1940s. F. A. Sellman et al. (2023), "Hornification of cellulose-rich materials – A kinetically trapped state," [DOI:10.1016/j.carbpol.2023.121132](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.carbpol.2023.121132) frames the phenomenon as kinetic trapping, while 2025 pulp experiments by C. Moser and B. Sjöstrand, "Hornification of Softwood and Hardwood Pulps Correlating with a Decrease in Accessible Surfaces," [DOI:10.1021/acsomega.5c03470](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.5c03470) find different water-retention–surface-accessibility correlations below and above 100 °C — evidence that multiple mechanisms operate, though none has been uniquely identified.
solved_when: The mechanism (or combination of mechanisms) responsible for hornification is identified such that the different water-retention–surface-accessibility correlations observed below and above 100 °C are explained, with kinetic trapping, fibril coalescence, and chemical cross-linking separately accounted for.
why: Mechanistic control would make it possible to preserve accessibility through drying, directly affecting paper recycling, nanocellulose processing, and biomass conversion.
key_works: F. A. Sellman et al. (2023), “Hornification of cellulose-rich materials – A kinetically trapped state,” [DOI:10.1016/j.carbpol.2023.121132](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.carbpol.2023.121132); C. Moser and B. Sjöstrand (2025), “Hornification of Softwood and Hardwood Pulps Correlating with a Decrease in Accessible Surfaces,” [DOI:10.1021/acsomega.5c03470](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.5c03470).

title: Aqueous identity and lifetime of Posner-type calcium-phosphate clusters
open: Do the classic neutral Posner clusters, Ca₉(PO₄)₆, actually exist as persistent, appreciable species in aqueous solution? The task is to measure their abundance and lifetime under relevant aqueous conditions, relative to protonated and compositionally variable aggregates, without inferring solution structures solely from dried solids.
status: The Posner-cluster hypothesis is longstanding. Revised calcium–phosphate association constants reported in 2024 substantially change speciation predictions, and evidence for calcium-phosphate association alone does not uniquely establish the classic neutral cluster. Key work: D. P. McDonogh, J. D. Gale, P. Raiteri, and D. Gebauer (2024), "Redefined ion association constants have consequences for calcium phosphate nucleation and biomineralization," [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-47721-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47721-7).
solved_when: A direct solution-phase measurement establishes whether neutral Ca₉(PO₄)₆ clusters persist in appreciable abundance under relevant aqueous conditions, and quantifies their lifetime relative to protonated and compositionally variable aggregates.
why: Correct solution species are essential to predictive models of bone mineralization, pathological calcification, and calcium-phosphate precipitation; they also underpin the structural premises of proposed phosphate-spin mechanisms in quantum biology.
key_works: D. P. McDonogh, J. D. Gale, P. Raiteri, and D. Gebauer (2024), “Redefined ion association constants have consequences for calcium phosphate nucleation and biomineralization,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-47721-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47721-7).

title: Reproducing enamel crystallites’ defect sandwich
open: Can we artificially make apatite crystallites that reproduce the internal "defect sandwich" of human enamel — magnesium-rich layers flanking a sodium-, fluoride-, and carbonate-enriched core — and then measure how these chemical gradients drive residual stress and preferential acid dissolution?
status: The 2020 discovery (K. A. DeRocher et al. (2020), “Chemical gradients in human enamel crystallites,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2433-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2433-3)) established intracrystallite chemical heterogeneity and connected gradients to stress. Enamel-like crystal platforms reported in 2025 (J. Chang et al. (2025), “Biomimetic Enamel-like Crystals: A Versatile Platform for Unraveling the Basic Mechanisms of Demineralization and Remineralization,” [DOI:10.1021/acsami.5c13544](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.5c13544)) improve experimental access, but reproducing the complete gradient and isolating its mechanical–chemical effects remain distinct targets.
solved_when: Synthetic crystallites are produced with controlled magnesium-rich layers surrounding the enriched core, at morphology and overall composition matched to human enamel, and gradient-driven residual stress and preferential acid dissolution are measured in them.
why: Gradient-controlled crystallites would clarify the nanoscale origins of caries susceptibility and guide the design of restorative minerals.
key_works: K. A. DeRocher et al. (2020), “Chemical gradients in human enamel crystallites,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-020-2433-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2433-3); J. Chang et al. (2025), “Biomimetic Enamel-like Crystals: A Versatile Platform for Unraveling the Basic Mechanisms of Demineralization and Remineralization,” [DOI:10.1021/acsami.5c13544](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.5c13544).

title: A falsifiable test of spinorial hastatic order in URu₂Si₂
open: Can an experiment on URu₂Si₂ find and measure an observable that distinguishes spinorial (hastatic) hybridization from competing multipolar explanations of its hidden order — in particular across the pressure-induced antiferromagnetic transition? A successful test would explain the observed symmetry breaking and elusive magnetic signatures within a single parameter-consistent model.
status: The parent hidden-order problem dates to 1985. Kornjača and Flint’s 2023 theory (M. Kornjača and R. Flint (2023), “Unified theory of hastatic order and antiferromagnetism in URu₂Si₂,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.108.085133](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.108.085133)) unifies candidate hastatic and antiferromagnetic phases and identifies additional vector observables, but remains a discriminating proposal rather than experimental identification.
solved_when: An observable unique to the hastatic scenario is identified and measured, both in the hidden-order phase and across the pressure-induced transition to antiferromagnetism, with the results either confirming or excluding a one-parameter-consistent spinorial-hybridization description against multipolar alternatives.
why: It would establish or exclude an unusual form of spinorial order in a long-standing puzzle and constrain correlated-electron hybridization theories more broadly.
key_works: M. Kornjača and R. Flint (2023), “Unified theory of hastatic order and antiferromagnetism in URu₂Si₂,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.108.085133](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.108.085133).

title: Species-resolved pair breaking by UTe₂ interstitial defects
open: Can a specific defect species be causally linked to UTe₂'s superconducting behavior — its transition temperature, residual quasiparticle density, and split transitions? Doing so requires controlled introduction or removal of defects that separates the effect of interstitials from uranium vacancies, strain, and compositional gradients.
status: Sample dependence has persisted since superconductivity was reported in 2019. Kengle et al. (2025) find interstitial defects in Te2 layers and no uranium vacancies in the examined samples; the resulting explanation needs quantitative, independently controlled validation. Key work: C. S. Kengle, N. Schnitzer, M. M. Bordelon, S. M. Thomas, and P. F. S. Rosa (2025), "What causes the variation in superconducting properties of UTe₂?", [arXiv:2509.20298](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.20298).
solved_when: A controlled defect intervention (introduction or removal) demonstrates a quantitative, species-resolved correspondence between interstitial defects and the transition temperature, residual quasiparticle density, and split transitions, with interstitial effects distinguished from uranium vacancies, strain, and compositional gradients.
why: It would turn sample quality into a defined physical variable and sharpen unconventional pair-breaking tests.
key_works: C. S. Kengle, N. Schnitzer, M. M. Bordelon, S. M. Thomas, and P. F. S. Rosa (2025), “What causes the variation in superconducting properties of UTe₂?”, [arXiv:2509.20298](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.20298).

title: FFLO modulation versus triplet pair-density waves in CeCoIn₅’s Q phase
open: Can experiments on CeCoIn₅'s Q phase directly measure the condensate's spatial modulation and spin structure well enough to tell whether it is an FFLO-modulated d-wave state or one hosting a triplet pair-density wave? Reproducing magnetic-domain switching alone does not discriminate between the theories.
status: The interpretation has been contested since at least the 2014 domain-switching experiment. Gerber et al. (2014), "Switching of magnetic domains reveals spatially inhomogeneous superconductivity," [DOI:10.1038/nphys2833](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys2833), infer inhomogeneous triplet pairing; Hatakeyama and Ikeda (2015), "Antiferromagnetic order oriented by Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov superconducting order," [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.91.094504](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.91.094504), reproduce the switching with FFLO modulation and no triplet component.
solved_when: A direct measurement of the condensate's spatial modulation and spin structure unambiguously distinguishes an FFLO-modulated d-wave state from a triplet pair-density wave.
why: It would identify the pairing response to strong paramagnetic pair breaking in a bulk superconductor.
key_works: S. Gerber et al. (2014), “Switching of magnetic domains reveals spatially inhomogeneous superconductivity,” [DOI:10.1038/nphys2833](https://doi.org/10.1038/nphys2833); Y. Hatakeyama and R. Ikeda (2015), “Antiferromagnetic order oriented by Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov superconducting order,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.91.094504](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.91.094504).

title: A phase-sensitive sign test for nodeless CeCu₂Si₂
open: Does the fully open gap of CeCu₂Si₂ reverse sign between the relevant electronic states? A phase-sensitive junction experiment, or a calibrated impurity-interference measurement that does not presuppose the impurity potential, should decide among sign-preserving s wave, sign-changing s± wave, and matrix-pairing interpretations of the order parameter.
status: The modern nodeless-gap controversy has developed over the past decade. Zhao et al. (2022) predict a quasiparticle-interference test for s± pairing, and the 2023 review by Smidman et al. documents why a full gap alone does not settle the order parameter.
solved_when: An experiment directly determines whether the nodeless superconducting gap changes sign between relevant electronic states, distinguishing sign-preserving s wave, sign-changing s wave, and matrix-pairing scenarios without assuming the impurity potential.
why: It would resolve a central ambiguity in the first heavy-fermion superconductor.
key_works: S. Zhao et al. (2022), “Revealing sign-reversal s±-wave pairing by quasiparticle interference in the heavy-fermion superconductor CeCu₂Si₂,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.105.014501](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.105.014501); M. Smidman et al. (2023), “Colloquium: Unconventional fully gapped superconductivity in the heavy-fermion metal CeCu₂Si₂,” [DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.95.031002](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.95.031002).

title: Identifying the one-ninth plateau state in YCOB
open: What is the true nature of the one-ninth magnetization plateau in YCu₃(OH)₆Br₂[Brₓ(OH)₁₋ₓ] — its order and excitation statistics? Formally, one seeks to discriminate among Dirac-spinon, chiral topological, and translation-breaking interpretations using thermodynamics, spectroscopy, and disorder dependence.
status: The plateau was reported in 2024. Zheng et al. (2025) measured heat capacity to 41.5 T and 0.46 K and found behavior consistent with fermionic excitations, but the evidence does not uniquely establish topological order.
solved_when: The order and excitation statistics of the one-ninth plateau are determined, and the Dirac-spinon, chiral topological, and translation-breaking interpretations are discriminated through thermodynamics, spectroscopy, and disorder dependence.
why: This small plateau provides a precise material test of fractionalization in frustrated magnets.
key_works: S. Jeon et al. (2024), “One-ninth magnetization plateau stabilized by spin entanglement in a kagome antiferromagnet,” [DOI:10.1038/s41567-023-02318-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-023-02318-7); G. Zheng et al. (2025), “Thermodynamic Evidence of Fermionic Behavior in the Vicinity of One-Ninth Plateau in a Kagome Antiferromagnet,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevX.15.021076](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.15.021076).

title: The dmit-131 residual thermal-conductivity discrepancy
open: Why do nominally equivalent β′-EtMe₃Sb[Pd(dmit)₂]₂ crystals yield incompatible conclusions about mobile gapless excitations? A specimen-exchange experiment — quantifying thermal contacts, cooling history, disorder, and low-temperature extrapolation on shared samples — should resolve the conflict.
status: A large residual heat conduction reported in 2010 conflicts with two 2019 studies reporting no such term. Kato et al. (2022) test the cooling-rate explanation and find no corresponding changes in structure, resistivity, or NMR; a generally accepted reconciliation remains lacking. Key work: R. Kato, M. Uebe, S. Fujiyama, and H. Cui (2022), “A Discrepancy in Thermal Conductivity Measurement Data of Quantum Spin Liquid β′-EtMe₃Sb[Pd(dmit)₂]₂,” [DOI:10.3390/cryst12010102](https://doi.org/10.3390/cryst12010102), [arXiv:2201.07073](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07073).
solved_when: A single set of shared samples, measured with controlled thermal contacts, cooling histories, and disorder levels and analyzed under explicit low-temperature extrapolation schemes, yields concordant residual thermal-conductivity values (whether a residual term is present or absent) that are accepted across the groups involved.
why: The discrepancy determines whether a leading organic spin-liquid candidate carries mobile neutral quasiparticles, so its resolution directly decides the interpretation of the low-temperature transport in this material.
key_works: R. Kato, M. Uebe, S. Fujiyama, and H. Cui (2022), “A Discrepancy in Thermal Conductivity Measurement Data of Quantum Spin Liquid β′-EtMe₃Sb[Pd(dmit)₂]₂,” [DOI:10.3390/cryst12010102](https://doi.org/10.3390/cryst12010102), [arXiv:2201.07073](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.07073).

title: The positive thermal Hall mechanism in GdZnPO
open: What excitations generate the positive transverse heat transport observed in GdZnPO, a honeycomb spiral-spin-liquid candidate? A successful identification must distinguish spin and momentum vortices from weak anisotropic-exchange effects and reproduce the measured field and temperature dependence quantitatively.
status: Zhao et al. (2025) report magnetic heat conduction down to approximately 50 mK and a positive thermal Hall response at higher temperatures. Idealized ordered-state spin-wave models yield zero Chern numbers, leaving vortices, weak perturbations, and quantum effects as possible missing ingredients. Key work: Y. Zhao et al. (2025), “Itinerant and topological excitations in a honeycomb spiral spin liquid candidate,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63620-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63620-x), [arXiv:2508.18795](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18795).
solved_when: A microscopic mechanism is identified that quantitatively reproduces the observed positive thermal Hall response and its field and temperature dependence, down to the experimentally accessed range of approximately 50 mK.
why: It would tie a directly measured transport coefficient to the topology of a spiral manifold in a real material, turning an anomalous signal into evidence for specific topological excitations.
key_works: Y. Zhao et al. (2025), “Itinerant and topological excitations in a honeycomb spiral spin liquid candidate,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63620-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63620-x), [arXiv:2508.18795](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18795).

title: Equilibrium order versus arrested proton disorder in ice XIX
open: Does ice XIX possess a unique equilibrium proton-ordered state, or is the partial order we observe a frozen-in artifact of slow proton rearrangement? Separately determine the equilibrium proton configuration and configurational entropy of ice XIX versus kinetically arrested disorder, using convergent annealing protocols, isotope-controlled calorimetry, and diffraction to test whether observed partial order converges to a well-defined equilibrium state.
status: Structural models of ice XIX already exist. Gasser et al. (2024) recover about 25 ± 3% of the Pauling entropy and show strong isotope-dependent kinetics, including small H₂O additions enabling ordering in D₂O samples that otherwise fail to transform under the tested anneals. Key work: T. M. Gasser, A. V. Thoeny, A. D. Fortes, and T. Loerting (2024), "Configurational entropy of ice XIX and its isotope effect," [DOI:10.1038/s41598-024-61250-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-61250-9).
solved_when: Convergent annealing, isotope-controlled calorimetry, and diffraction jointly establish whether the observed partial ordering approaches a unique equilibrium proton configuration, quantitatively separating the equilibrium configurational entropy from kinetic arrest — with the isotope-dependence of the kinetics accounted for.
why: It would cleanly separate thermodynamic residual entropy from kinetic arrest in a defined hydrogen-bond network, telling us which part of ice XIX's disorder is a property of the phase itself and which is a frozen accident of its preparation.
key_works: T. M. Gasser, A. V. Thoeny, A. D. Fortes, and T. Loerting (2024), “Configurational entropy of ice XIX and its isotope effect,” [DOI:10.1038/s41598-024-61250-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-61250-9).

title: Microscopic trigger of light-erased clay hydration hysteresis
open: What microscopic excitation lets near-infrared light unlock metastable hydration states in swelling clay? The goal is to identify the energy-transfer channel, distinguishing mere local heating from direct excitation of confined water, and to predict the action spectrum, absorbed-power threshold, isotope dependence, and accompanying layer-spacing transition.
status: Teng and colleagues eliminated hydration hysteresis in synthetic Laponite in 2025 using 785 nm illumination with bulk-temperature control; their measurements support optically activated nucleation, but the microscopic energy-transfer channel and the wavelength-dependent rate law remain follow-up targets. Key work: Y. Teng, C. Chen, L. Zheng, and M. L. Whittaker (2025), “Optically Triggered Nucleation Eliminates Hydration Hysteresis in Swelling Minerals,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.langmuir.4c04468](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.langmuir.4c04468).
solved_when: A microscopic mechanism is identified that accounts for the observed light-erased hysteresis and correctly predicts the action spectrum, the absorbed-power threshold, the isotope dependence, and the layer-spacing transition, with local heating cleanly separated from direct excitation of confined water.
why: A mechanism would make optical control of mineral hydration predictable and would test how confined water crosses metastable free-energy barriers.
key_works: Y. Teng, C. Chen, L. Zheng, and M. L. Whittaker (2025), “Optically Triggered Nucleation Eliminates Hydration Hysteresis in Swelling Minerals,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.langmuir.4c04468](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.langmuir.4c04468).

title: Equilibrium versus drying-induced interstratification at the clay swelling crossover
open: Are the mixed nematic, crystalline, and interstratified states observed between osmotic and crystalline swelling genuine equilibrium coexistence phases, or are they structures selected by the drying protocol? A resolution should determine their reversibility, phase boundaries, and relaxation times under independently controlled water activity and counterion composition.
status: Hotton and colleagues followed the complete crossover in levitated beidellite droplets in 2025, observing layer separations that decreased continuously to approximately 30 Å before entering a mixed regime; determining equilibrium versus protocol-dependent selection is a further question arising from the continuously drying geometry. Key work: C. Hotton, T. Bizien, C. Hamon, É. Ferrage, and E. Paineau (2025), "Bridging the Gap between Osmotic and Crystalline Swelling in 2D Layered Materials Using Levitated Droplets," [DOI:10.1002/smll.202505038](https://doi.org/10.1002/smll.202505038).
solved_when: The reversibility, phase boundaries, and relaxation times of the mixed nematic, crystalline, and interstratified states at the osmotic-to-crystalline swelling crossover have been determined under independently controlled water activity and counterion composition, establishing whether these states are equilibrium coexistence or drying-induced.
why: It would establish when clay water-retention curves describe equilibrium and when they encode processing history.
key_works: C. Hotton, T. Bizien, C. Hamon, É. Ferrage, and E. Paineau (2025), “Bridging the Gap between Osmotic and Crystalline Swelling in 2D Layered Materials Using Levitated Droplets,” [DOI:10.1002/smll.202505038](https://doi.org/10.1002/smll.202505038).

title: Experimental proton conduction along montmorillonite edges
open: Can proton transport along hydrated montmorillonite edges be measured as a distinct channel, cleanly separated from interlayer conduction and dissolved-electrolyte transport? In particular, does it exhibit the pH dependence, magnesium-substitution sensitivity, edge-connectivity effects, and hydrogen–deuterium exchange signatures predicted by simulation?
status: Feng and colleagues' 2026 simulations (Y. Feng, X. R. Advincula, H. Fang, and C. Schran (2026), "Clay Edges Are Dynamic Proton-Conducting Networks Modulated by Structure and pH," DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.5c03748; arXiv:2508.15401) found direct and water-assisted proton transfer along clay edges, with connectivity and barriers controlled by local chemistry. Nanosecond molecular trajectories establish a candidate mechanism, but whether these exchanges generate a measurable edge-specific conduction channel remains experimentally unresolved.
solved_when: An experimental measurement isolates edge-specific proton conduction in hydrated montmorillonite and tests the predicted dependence on pH, magnesium substitution, edge connectivity, and hydrogen–deuterium exchange.
why: It would connect mineral acid–base chemistry at clay surfaces to macroscopic electrical transport, anchoring a simulated nanoscale mechanism in measurable bulk behavior.
key_works: Y. Feng, X. R. Advincula, H. Fang, and C. Schran (2026), “Clay Edges Are Dynamic Proton-Conducting Networks Modulated by Structure and pH,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.5c03748](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.5c03748); [arXiv:2508.15401](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15401).

title: Dissolved-gas enhancement of compacted-clay swelling pressure
open: Does dissolved gas raise the swelling pressure of compacted clay by partitioning preferentially into interlayers, even when water activity, external pressure, and counterion chemistry are held fixed? A convincing answer must isolate this effect from confounders such as gas bubbles, desaturation, and gas-induced chemical reactions.
status: Molecular simulations by Owusu and colleagues (2026) predict gas-dependent swelling-pressure increases of approximately 1.5 MPa under their modeled conditions (J. P. Owusu, K. Karalis, N. I. Prasianakis, A. Ferrari, and S. V. Churakov (2026), “Swelling of Na-montmorillonite in the presence of dissolved gas molecules,” [DOI:10.1016/j.clay.2025.108058](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clay.2025.108058)). This is a calculated increment, and its contribution to the response of a compacted specimen containing both interlayer and interparticle porosity still requires experimental isolation.
solved_when: An experiment under controlled water activity, external pressure, and counterion chemistry demonstrates a dissolved-gas contribution to swelling pressure that is cleanly separated from bubbles, desaturation, and chemical reactions — allowing comparison against the predicted gas-dependent increment of roughly 1.5 MPa from molecular simulation.
why: It would sharpen predictions for gas-generating waste barriers and underground gas-storage seals, where swelling pressure controls seal performance.
key_works: J. P. Owusu, K. Karalis, N. I. Prasianakis, A. Ferrari, and S. V. Churakov (2026), “Swelling of Na-montmorillonite in the presence of dissolved gas molecules,” [DOI:10.1016/j.clay.2025.108058](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clay.2025.108058).

title: Location and fate of tetrahedral iron during ferrihydrite aging
open: Where does tetrahedrally coordinated Fe(III) actually reside in ferrihydrite, and what happens to it as the mineral ages? A resolution should distinguish particle-interior motifs, hydrated surface sites, and defects, identify the atomic rearrangements that reduce the tetrahedral population during aging, and establish whether dehydration drives the coordination change.
status: M. Sassi et al. (2024), "Influence of time and ageing conditions on the properties of ferrihydrite" (DOI:10.1039/D3EN00828B), compared fresh ferrihydrite with material aged for five years; spectroscopy linked aging and dehydration to a decreasing tetrahedral-to-octahedral iron ratio, but the measurements neither uniquely locate the sites nor establish the atomic transformation pathway.
solved_when: Tetrahedral Fe(III) sites are uniquely located among interior, surface, and defect environments, and the transformation pathway that converts them to octahedral coordination during aging — including whether dehydration is the cause — is established.
why: Reliable site assignments would sharpen predictions of contaminant binding, iron exchange, and mineral transformation in a mineral whose behavior changes with age.
key_works: M. Sassi et al. (2024), “Influence of time and ageing conditions on the properties of ferrihydrite,” [DOI:10.1039/D3EN00828B](https://doi.org/10.1039/D3EN00828B).

title: Operando charge compensation and branch selection in vivianite oxidation
open: How do electron loss, water deprotonation, hydrogen defects, and lattice rearrangement couple when hydrated vivianite oxidizes? In particular, under which conditions does oxidation proceed through a metavivianite intermediate and which conditions bypass it, as revealed by simultaneous iron-valence, proton-release, and structural measurements?
status: M. Sassi and K. M. Rosso (2025), "Insights into the Oxidation Mechanism of Vivianite to Metavivianite from First-Principles Calculations," [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpcc.4c07790](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.4c07790), predict metavivianite stabilization over an intermediate range of approximately 66–33% residual Fe(II). K. Chiba et al. (2020), "The synthesis of metavivianite and the oxidation sequence of vivianite," [DOI:10.2465/jmps.200417](https://doi.org/10.2465/jmps.200417), experimentally demonstrated oxidation paths that bypass metavivianite. The remaining question is conditional pathway selection and charge compensation.
solved_when: A mechanism is established that identifies the conditions selecting a metavivianite intermediate versus those bypassing it, grounded in simultaneous iron-valence, proton-release, and structural measurements, and consistent with the predicted stabilization of metavivianite over the residual Fe(II) range of approximately 66–33%.
why: It would clarify phosphorus retention and the stability of recovered iron-phosphate products.
key_works: M. Sassi and K. M. Rosso (2025), “Insights into the Oxidation Mechanism of Vivianite to Metavivianite from First-Principles Calculations,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpcc.4c07790](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.4c07790); K. Chiba et al. (2020), “The synthesis of metavivianite and the oxidation sequence of vivianite,” [DOI:10.2465/jmps.200417](https://doi.org/10.2465/jmps.200417).

title: Atomic identity of clay-stabilized labile Fe(III)
open: What is the atomic identity — coordination environment, nuclearity, and physical location — of the reactive Fe(III) that montmorillonite retains during Fe(II)-catalyzed ferrihydrite transformation? A satisfying answer would assign the operationally defined labile fraction to specific molecular species and quantify exchange among interlayer sites, external adsorption sites, and nascent iron-oxide structures.
status: Wei and colleagues showed in 2025 that clay–ferrihydrite interactions alter recrystallization and can suppress magnetite formation while retaining reactive iron. Selective extraction establishes an operationally defined labile fraction; assigning that fraction to specific molecular species is the narrower remaining target.
solved_when: The labile Fe(III) fraction is assigned to identified molecular species with specified coordination and nuclearity, located either in the clay interlayer, on external adsorption sites, or within nascent iron oxides, and the exchange among these reservoirs has been measured.
why: It would connect measured reactive-iron inventories to mechanisms of contaminant mobilization.
key_works: H. Wei et al. (2025), “Nano-Scale Insights into Clay Minerals Regulating the Fe(II)-Catalyzed Ferrihydrite Transformation under Anoxic Conditions,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.4c11232](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c11232).

title: Electron acceptor in emerald-green photooxidation
open: What species accepts the electrons when light converts arsenic(III) to arsenic(V) in emerald-green pigment, and through what intermediate sequence? Formally, the answer should close electron and atom balances across oxygen, acetate ligands, possible transient Cu(I), arsenolite, and the final arsenic(V)-rich material.
status: Carboni Marri and colleagues established distinct light- and humidity-driven degradation pathways in 2025, but their paper explicitly leaves the oxidative reaction partner and intermediate sequence unresolved; because the final products are predominantly Cu(II), they cannot establish whether transient Cu(I) participates. Key work: S. Carboni Marri et al. (2025), "Discovering the dual degradation pathway of emerald green in oil paints: The effects of light and humidity," [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.ady1807](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ady1807).
solved_when: The electron acceptor is identified and a reaction sequence is established that closes electron and atom balances among oxygen, acetate ligands, transient Cu(I) (confirmed or ruled out), arsenolite, and the final arsenic(V)-rich product.
why: Identifying the partner reveals which environmental or binder controls can suppress arsenic migration from degraded pigment.
key_works: S. Carboni Marri et al. (2025), “Discovering the dual degradation pathway of emerald green in oil paints: The effects of light and humidity,” [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.ady1807](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ady1807).

title: Dark dissolution versus photocorrosion in cadmium–zinc sulfide pigments
open: How much of the degradation of Cd–Zn sulfide pigments in aged paint is caused by dark dissolution, and how much by light-driven photocorrosion? In formal terms, the task is to quantify these pathway fractions while closing the metal and sulfur balances and independently controlling composition, polymorph, particle size, water activity, and binder ligands.
status: Castagnotto and colleagues' 2025 study found strong light-driven activity in nanosized cubic compositions containing 20% or 40% zinc, together with lower but measurable dark ion release. The unresolved extension is quantitative pathway partitioning within a binder-confined historical paint layer. Key work: E. Castagnotto, S. Alberti, M. Campolucci, P. Manfrinetti, M. Ferretti, and F. Locardi (2025), "Photocorrosion Stability of CdxZn1–xS Yellow-Orange Pigments," [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemmater.4c03274](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemmater.4c03274).
solved_when: A quantitative partitioning of pigment loss between dark dissolution and light-driven oxidation is achieved within a binder-confined historical paint layer, with closed metal and sulfur balances and independent control of composition, polymorph, particle size, water activity, and binder ligands.
why: It would establish whether limiting light exposure addresses the dominant degradation route, or whether dark processes make light mitigation insufficient.
key_works: E. Castagnotto, S. Alberti, M. Campolucci, P. Manfrinetti, M. Ferretti, and F. Locardi (2025), “Photocorrosion Stability of CdxZn1–xS Yellow-Orange Pigments,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemmater.4c03274](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemmater.4c03274).

title: Interdiffusion-driven cavitation inside liquid solder pockets
open: Does interdiffusion-induced tension actually nucleate cavities inside liquid solder before the liquid is fully consumed — and can this mechanism be cleanly distinguished from expansion of oxide films or entrained defects, and from vacancy-driven voiding in solid intermetallics?
status: Kuziora and Aasmundtveit’s 2025 model predicts a cavitation criterion near −29 MPa for one 5 μm³ Ni–Sn solder pocket, reached after approximately six seconds under specified growth conditions; these are model outputs only, as actual liquid pressure and the operative void-initiation mechanism remain unmeasured. Key work: S. L. Kuziora and K. E. Aasmundtveit (2025; online 2024), “Solid–Liquid Diffusion Stresses Leading to Voiding,” [DOI:10.1007/s11661-024-07618-y](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11661-024-07618-y).
solved_when: The liquid pressure inside a solder pocket is measured and the operative void-initiation mechanism is identified, testing whether cavitation occurs near the predicted −29 MPa threshold within approximately six seconds in a 5 μm³ Ni–Sn pocket under the specified growth conditions.
why: It determines whether void suppression efforts should target diffusion kinetics, liquid connectivity, or oxide cleanliness.
key_works: S. L. Kuziora and K. E. Aasmundtveit (2025; online 2024), “Solid–Liquid Diffusion Stresses Leading to Voiding,” [DOI:10.1007/s11661-024-07618-y](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11661-024-07618-y).

title: Chunky graphite after high-superheat remelting
open: Why does remelting a low-sulfur ductile iron and then chill casting it produce chunky graphite? Formally, determine whether the graphite nuclei survive the melt or form anew — disentangling nucleant memory, magnesium fading, inoculant fading, and carbon supersaturation.
status: Adhiwiguna, Plück, and Deike's 2025 study found strong thermal-history dependence over 1300–1500 °C remelting conditions; magnesium and inoculant fading alone could not explain the resulting graphite sequence, and the disappearance of visible graphite does not establish removal of all heterogeneous precursors.
solved_when: A mechanism is identified that accounts for the observed chunky-graphite formation across the 1300–1500 °C remelting conditions, with a determination of whether heterogeneous nucleant precursors persist through remelting or arise de novo.
why: It would make recycled ductile-iron melt treatment more predictable.
key_works: I. B. G. S. Adhiwiguna, L. Plück, and R. Deike (2025; online 2024), “Vermicular and Chunky Graphite Nucleation during Chill Casting: Study on the Dynamics of Ductile Iron Recycling,” [DOI:10.1007/s40962-024-01473-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40962-024-01473-8).

title: Stress-free zero-temperature ground state of PbZrO₃
open: Does ideal, unstrained bulk PbZrO₃ adopt the conventional Pbam antiferroelectric ground state, or does a lower-energy ferrielectric arrangement prevail once nuclear zero-point effects and kinetic trapping are properly resolved?
status: The question sharpened in 2021 when calculations placed competing structures within small energy differences (H. Aramberri et al. (2021), “On the possibility that PbZrO3 not be antiferroelectric,” [DOI:10.1038/s41524-021-00671-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-021-00671-w)). Ferrielectric–antiferroelectric coexistence was stabilized experimentally through strain in 2024 (Z. Yu et al. (2024), “Room-temperature stabilizing strongly competing ferrielectric and antiferroelectric phases in PbZrO3 by strain-mediated phase separation,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-47776-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47776-6)), but strained-film accessibility does not identify the equilibrium zero-stress bulk ground state.
solved_when: The zero-stress, zero-temperature equilibrium structure of bulk PbZrO₃ is determined with an energy ranking robust beyond a single density functional, and with zero-point and kinetic-trapping effects explicitly accounted for.
why: The actual ground state of this reference antiferroelectric directly affects how switching and energy-storage pathways in PbZrO₃ are interpreted.
key_works: H. Aramberri et al. (2021), “On the possibility that PbZrO3 not be antiferroelectric,” [DOI:10.1038/s41524-021-00671-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-021-00671-w); Z. Yu et al. (2024), “Room-temperature stabilizing strongly competing ferrielectric and antiferroelectric phases in PbZrO3 by strain-mediated phase separation,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-47776-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-47776-6).

title: Hundreds-second structural relaxation in magnetocaloric La(Fe,Si)₁₃
open: What governs the hundreds-of-seconds structural relaxation observed in La(Fe,Si)₁₃ after a magnetic-field sweep stops — intrinsic nonthermal transformation kinetics, thermal lag, or their coupling? A satisfactory answer should predict the pronounced asymmetry between the field-application and field-removal branches using independently measured local temperatures and phase fractions.
status: Time-resolved synchrotron measurements in 2024 found relaxation lasting hundreds of seconds. Free-energy analysis revealed asymmetric barriers and behavior suggestive of nonthermal activation, but a mechanism-discriminating account of that inference remains open. Key work: A. Azevedo Beleza et al. (2024), “Structural dynamics of first-order phase transition in giant magnetocaloric La(Fe,Si)13: The free energy landscape,” [DOI:10.1016/j.mtphys.2024.101388](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mtphys.2024.101388).
solved_when: A mechanism-discriminating account identifies which of nonthermal kinetics, thermal lag, or their coupling controls the relaxation, and quantitatively predicts the difference between the field-application and field-removal branches from independently measured local temperatures and phase fractions, matching relaxation on the observed hundreds-of-seconds timescale.
why: Slow structural response can prevent a large equilibrium caloric effect from delivering useful cooling power.
key_works: A. Azevedo Beleza et al. (2024), “Structural dynamics of first-order phase transition in giant magnetocaloric La(Fe,Si)13: The free energy landscape,” [DOI:10.1016/j.mtphys.2024.101388](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mtphys.2024.101388).

title: Reversed odd–even acoustic selection rules in ultrathin lithium niobate
open: What depth-dependent polarization and piezoelectric profile causes the thickness-mode selection rules to reverse in approximately 67 nm lithium-niobate films? A successful answer should distinguish graded surface damage from domain inversion and predict the coupling expected after controlled surface treatments.
status: Xie and colleagues demonstrated resonances up to 220 GHz in 2025. Even-order modes became dominant as films thinned; surface measurements suggested a graded altered region, with approximately 5–6 nm indicated by reflectivity and approximately 20 nm affected by etching. Its piezoelectric profile remains undetermined.
solved_when: The depth profile causing the reversed odd–even selection rules in approximately 67 nm films is identified, graded surface damage is distinguished from domain reversal, and the model predicts coupling after controlled surface treatments.
why: It would enable deliberate sub-terahertz mode selection in these resonators and pinpoint which fabrication steps damage the film.
key_works: J. Xie, W. Wu, M. Shen, P. Fay, and H. X. Tang (2025), “Towards terahertz nanomechanics,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63561-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63561-5).

title: Carbon site versus growth-rate origin of the β-Ga₂O₃ 1.6 eV compensator
open: Is the Eᶜ−1.6 eV compensating acceptor in rapidly grown β-Ga₂O₃ caused by carbon itself — on oxygen site I or site III — or by some other defect that merely correlates with fast growth? The question calls for experiments that independently vary carbon supply and growth rate, which current precursor-flow studies cannot decouple.
status: Ghadi and colleagues reported in June 2026 that this state accounts for more than 90% of compensation in their high-growth-rate series. Its concentration follows SIMS carbon, but precursor flow changes both carbon incorporation and growth rate; the paper explicitly leaves definitive assignment to experiments decoupling them (H. Ghadi et al. (2026), “Defect evolution and carrier compensation in high-growth rate MOCVD-grown β-Ga2O3,” [DOI:10.1063/5.0325051](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0325051)).
solved_when: A defect assignment is made — carbon on oxygen site I, carbon on site III, or another growth-correlated defect — supported by experiments in which carbon supply and growth rate are varied independently.
why: A definitive assignment would allow faster growth of thick drift layers in β-Ga₂O₃ without compensating away their donors.
key_works: H. Ghadi et al. (2026), “Defect evolution and carrier compensation in high-growth rate MOCVD-grown β-Ga2O3,” [DOI:10.1063/5.0325051](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0325051).

title: Predicting the crystallite-size cutoff for negative gas adsorption in DUT-49
open: Can we predict, from first principles, when a DUT-49 crystallite becomes too small to exhibit negative gas adsorption? A successful theory would take independently determined microscopic parameters and predict how crystallite size, shape, and surface termination suppress the effect, including the quantity of gas expelled and whether phase coexistence survives.
status: Size-dependent pressure amplification was measured in 2018 by S. Krause et al. (2018), "The effect of crystallite size on pressure amplification in switchable porous solids," [DOI:10.1038/s41467-018-03979-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-03979-2). By 2024, simulations — as surveyed by J. D. Evans and F.-X. Coudert (2024), "Challenges and Opportunities of Molecular Simulations for Negative Gas Adsorption," [DOI:10.1021/accountsmr.4c00071](https://doi.org/10.1021/accountsmr.4c00071) — described bulk thermodynamics and some finite MOF crystallites, while chemically accurate external surfaces and quantitative transfer between length scales remained explicit gaps.
solved_when: A quantitative finite-crystal nucleation and propagation model, built from independently measured microscopic parameters, reproduces the observed size-dependent suppression of negative gas adsorption in DUT-49, predicting expelled-gas quantities and phase coexistence as functions of crystallite size, shape, and surface termination.
why: It would determine whether pressure amplification survives particle manufacture and miniaturization — the practical prerequisite for using switchable porous solids as actuators or sensors at device-relevant scales.
key_works: S. Krause et al. (2018), “The effect of crystallite size on pressure amplification in switchable porous solids,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-018-03979-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-03979-2); J. D. Evans and F.-X. Coudert (2024), “Challenges and Opportunities of Molecular Simulations for Negative Gas Adsorption,” [DOI:10.1021/accountsmr.4c00071](https://doi.org/10.1021/accountsmr.4c00071).

title: Rapid bulk tetrataenite synthesis after the phosphorus-casting retraction
open: Can an L1₀-ordered FeNi (tetrataenite) bulk magnet be produced with a high volume fraction of well-ordered phase on practical manufacturing timescales, now that the claimed rapid phosphorus-casting route has been retracted? In particular, can ordering and magnetic properties be established by independent measurements that rule out phosphide diffraction peaks and surface-oxidation artifacts?
status: The 2022 rapid-casting claim was retracted; Houghton and colleagues' 2025 reinterpretation found no supporting evidence for tetrataenite in those castings (O. S. Houghton et al. (2025), "Reinterpretation of Report of Tetrataenite in Bulk Alloy Castings," [DOI:10.1002/advs.202408796](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202408796)). Other work, reported by L. H. Lewis et al. (2024) in "Accelerating Nature: Induced Atomic Order in Equiatomic FeNi" [DOI:10.1002/advs.202302696](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202302696), achieved local ordering up to approximately 22 vol% after six weeks, leaving rapid extensive bulk ordering unresolved.
solved_when: A bulk L1₀ FeNi magnet is demonstrated with high volume fraction and well-established long-range order on practical manufacturing timescales, with ordering and magnetic properties verified independently while excluding phosphide diffraction and surface-oxidation artifacts — materially exceeding the reported local ordering of approximately 22 vol% achieved after six weeks.
why: A successful route would deliver an iron–nickel permanent magnet free of rare-earth critical minerals, reducing dependence on scarce rare-earth supplies for permanent-magnet applications.
key_works: O. S. Houghton et al. (2025), “Reinterpretation of Report of Tetrataenite in Bulk Alloy Castings,” [DOI:10.1002/advs.202408796](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202408796); L. H. Lewis et al. (2024), “Accelerating Nature: Induced Atomic Order in Equiatomic FeNi,” [DOI:10.1002/advs.202302696](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.202302696).

title: Molecular origin of locked compressive maturation stress in conifer wood
open: How do galactan, xylan, lignin, and bound water in the cell wall jointly generate and lock in the compressive maturation stress of conifer wood? More precisely, can wall chemistry or hydration be manipulated at matched microfibril angle so that the sign and magnitude of the resulting stress are predicted from the resulting wall architecture?
status: R. Cresswell et al. (2025), "The molecular architecture distinctions between compression, opposite and normal wood of Pinus radiata," [DOI:10.3389/fpls.2025.1576928](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2025.1576928), found reduced water content, porosity, and molecular mobility in compression wood, with disordered galactan. Their proposed combination of high microfibril angle, lignification, and dehydration does not yet apportion causal stress generation among those components.
solved_when: A mechanism is established that apportions causal stress generation among galactan, xylan, lignin, and bound water, and that predicts the sign and magnitude of compressive maturation stress from wall architecture measured after manipulating chemistry or dehydration at matched microfibril angle.
why: It would explain timber warping and supply design principles for prestressed plant-derived composites.
key_works: R. Cresswell et al. (2025), “The molecular architecture distinctions between compression, opposite and normal wood of Pinus radiata,” [DOI:10.3389/fpls.2025.1576928](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpls.2025.1576928).

title: Thickness and chemistry of lignin welds in hot-pressed paper
open: What is actually happening at the molecular scale when hot pressing makes paper water-resistant — how thick are the lignin junctions that carry load, how far do the polymers interpenetrate, and what chemistry binds them? Answering this means separating the roles of polymer flow, interdiffusion, and chemical bonding, so that wet strength can be predicted from measured junction properties.
status: Mattsson and colleagues’ 2026 tomography study examined pressing at 200 °C and 3.5 MPa for 0.05–30 seconds, finding that longer pressing improved wet mechanical response; the authors explicitly identify molecular bonding mechanisms and lignin-interface thickness as future work.
solved_when: The thickness, interpenetration depth, and chemistry of load-bearing lignin junctions are measured after hot pressing; polymer flow and interdiffusion are distinguished from chemical bonding as mechanisms; and wet strength is predictable from the measured junction properties.
why: It would enable water-resistant paper with controlled strength at lower processing severity, by grounding hot-pressing conditions in measured junction behavior rather than trial and error.
key_works: A. Mattsson, A. Miettinen, T. Joelsson, G. Pettersson, P. Engstrand, and J. A. Ketoja (2026), “Stress-strain behavior and microstructural evolution of hot-pressed paper webs revealed by x-ray tomography,” [DOI:10.15376/biores.21.2.3718-3732](https://doi.org/10.15376/biores.21.2.3718-3732).

title: Nonmicellar DMPE templating of cocoa-butter Form V
open: How does a dimyristoylphosphoethanolamine surface select cocoa-butter Form V during simple cooling? Concretely, what headgroup arrangement and triacylglycerol adsorption geometry give this additive its polymorph specificity?
status: Stobbs and colleagues achieved suitable crystallization with 0.1 wt% DMPE under simple cooling without shear in 2025; see J. A. Stobbs et al. (2025), “Dimyristoylphosphoethanolamine Addition During Chocolate Manufacture Promotes Proper Tempering under Simple Cooling Conditions without Shear,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00575](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00575). Neutron scattering found no DMPE micelles, and infrared measurements did not establish a strong specific interaction, so successful templating currently precedes any resolved molecular mechanism.
solved_when: The molecular surface structure of DMPE responsible for Form V selection is identified — specifically the headgroup arrangement and the triacylglycerol adsorption geometry underlying its additive specificity.
why: It would make low-energy tempering transferable across variable cocoa-butter supplies and alternative fats.
key_works: J. A. Stobbs et al. (2025), “Dimyristoylphosphoethanolamine Addition During Chocolate Manufacture Promotes Proper Tempering under Simple Cooling Conditions without Shear,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00575](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00575).

title: Molecular and geometrical origin of hagfish-skein peeling resistance
open: How much of the resistance that keeps a hagfish skein from unwinding comes from molecular adhesive contacts between thread coils, and how much from the geometry of the coiled bundle itself? A satisfying answer identifies the adhesive molecule and its spatial distribution, and yields a peeling law — depending on salt concentration and loading rate — that predicts the discrete force barriers observed during unwinding.
status: Hossain and colleagues directly measured peeling forces in 2025, with a typical value near 6.8 nN, and showed that mucus is not required to initiate unwinding; the molecular identity and spatial distribution of the adhesive barriers remain unresolved. Key works: M. T. Hossain et al. (2025), "Physics of unravelling and micromechanics of hagfish threads," [DOI:10.1098/rsif.2025.0503](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2025.0503); [arXiv:2506.07243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07243).
solved_when: The adhesive responsible for peeling resistance is molecularly identified and its spatial distribution mapped, and a salt- and rate-dependent peeling law is derived that quantitatively predicts the discrete force barriers, consistent with directly measured peeling forces near the typical value of 6.8 nN.
why: It would enable compactly stored fibers that deploy rapidly under controlled flow.
key_works: M. T. Hossain et al. (2025), “Physics of unravelling and micromechanics of hagfish threads,” [DOI:10.1098/rsif.2025.0503](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2025.0503); [arXiv:2506.07243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07243).

title: Cavitation-controlled size limit for ambient-dried silica monoliths
open: When does internal solvent cavitation relieve drying stresses in an ambient-pressure-dried silica gel, and when does spatially heterogeneous cavitation instead promote cracking? The goal is a predictive account of maximum crack-free monolith size and drying schedules built from measured stiffening, transport, cavitation, and fracture properties.
status: Gonthier and colleagues’ 2024 tomography and scattering experiments detected vapor formation before maximum shrinkage, beginning near a 50% reduction in pore volume. The event is observed; the coupled nucleation, stress-redistribution, and size-scaling law remains unresolved. Key work: J. Gonthier, E. Scoppola, T. Rilling, A. Gurlo, P. Fratzl, and W. Wagermaier (2024), “Solvent Cavitation during Ambient Pressure Drying of Silica Aerogels,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.langmuir.4c00497](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.langmuir.4c00497).
solved_when: A validated model predicts the maximum crack-free monolith size and drying schedules from measured stiffening, transport, cavitation, and fracture properties, resolving the coupled nucleation, stress-redistribution, and size-scaling law.
why: Controlled cavitation would expand production of large aerogel components by ambient-pressure drying, avoiding the cost and scale limits of alternative drying routes.
key_works: J. Gonthier, E. Scoppola, T. Rilling, A. Gurlo, P. Fratzl, and W. Wagermaier (2024), “Solvent Cavitation during Ambient Pressure Drying of Silica Aerogels,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.langmuir.4c00497](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.langmuir.4c00497).

title: Chemical ordering of recovered cubic BC₂N
open: What is the actual arrangement of boron, carbon, and nitrogen atoms in recovered cubic BC₂N — do apparently cubic specimens host an ordered network, chemical disorder, or nanoscale intergrowths? Any assignment must jointly account for the observed chemical contrast, diffuse scattering, and mechanical properties.
status: Synthesis has preceded unambiguous atomic assignment by decades. Rao et al.’s 2024 paper, published online in 2023 (Y. Rao, Y. Wu, C. Y. Zhao, and S. Ju, “Heterogeneous C–C bonding induced anomalous phonon transport in superhard BC₂N polymorphs,” *Acta Materialia* 262, 119454, [DOI:10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119454](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119454)), explicitly identified the elusive experimental structure as a limitation while calculating sharply different bonding and phonon transport in candidate polymorphs. Discriminating experimental assignment remains the target.
solved_when: An experimentally verified B/C/N occupation pattern for recovered cubic BC₂N is established that simultaneously explains the chemical contrast, the diffuse scattering, and the mechanical properties.
why: Without a verified structure, it is impossible to determine which combination of hardness, heat conduction, and dopant incorporation this material can actually support.
key_works: Y. Rao, Y. Wu, C. Y. Zhao, and S. Ju (2024), “Heterogeneous C–C bonding induced anomalous phonon transport in superhard BC₂N polymorphs,” *Acta Materialia* 262, 119454, [DOI:10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119454](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119454).

title: Freestanding boroxol B₂O₃ monolayers
open: Can a crystalline boroxol-network B₂O₃ monolayer be released from its growth substrate and survive as an intact freestanding membrane, and does the predicted rippled state persist once suspended? A decisive answer would pair successful transfer with measurements that distinguish intrinsic rippling and membrane elasticity from damage introduced by the transfer itself.
status: Zio et al. (2025) synthesized the supported two-dimensional polymorph ("Two-dimensional diboron trioxide crystal composed by boroxol groups," *Science* 390, 95–99). Zhang, Lei, Zhang, and He (2026) predicted that a flat freestanding sheet is dynamically unstable, while a rippled configuration is stable, lowering the calculated energy by approximately 8 meV per B₂O₃ unit ("Rippling-induced stabilization and property modulation in freestanding two-dimensional B₂O₃," DOI:10.1063/5.0324393). Experimental release and validation of the rippled state remain the open follow-up implied by these results.
solved_when: A supported boroxol B₂O₃ monolayer is experimentally detached as an intact suspended membrane, and its corrugation and elastic properties are measured in a way that separates intrinsic rippling from transfer-induced damage, testing whether the rippled configuration predicted to be stable survives.
why: Success would establish a chemically distinct oxide membrane and provide a direct test of whether atomically thin networks can be stabilized by their ring topology.
key_works: T. Zio et al. (2025), “Two-dimensional diboron trioxide crystal composed by boroxol groups,” *Science* 390, 95–99, [institutional record](https://iris.cnr.it/handle/20.500.14243/578781); X. Zhang, Y. Lei, Y. Zhang, and C. He (2026), “Rippling-induced stabilization and property modulation in freestanding two-dimensional B₂O₃,” [DOI:10.1063/5.0324393](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0324393).

title: An alteration-free Curie temperature for greigite
open: What is the true Curie temperature of greigite, measured in a way that proves Fe₃S₄ itself is still the magnetic phase at the moment of the transition? In particular, a measurement must settle whether previously reported transitions belong to greigite or to thermally generated alteration products, and how the answer depends on composition.
status: Wang et al. (2010) reported approximately 677 K [arXiv:1012.2364], but greigite commonly alters at around 220–350 °C before the anticipated transition, so A. P. Roberts (2026 online, *Mineral Magnetism*, DOI:10.1017/9781108935630.016) still treats the intrinsic value as unknown. Reconciling the positive report with phase-resolved thermal stability remains the open gap.
solved_when: A Curie temperature for Fe₃S₄ is determined with phase-resolved evidence that greigite remains the magnetic phase throughout the measurement, resolving whether reported transitions (including the approximately 677 K value) belong to greigite or to thermal alteration products, and establishing the compositional dependence.
why: The value governs how sedimentary magnetic records containing greigite are interpreted and informs assessments of sulfide magnetic materials.
key_works: J. Wang, S.-H. Cao, W. Wu, and G.-M. Zhao (2010), “The Curie temperature and exchange energy between two sublattices in half-metallic greigite Fe₃S₄,” [arXiv:1012.2364](https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.2364); A. P. Roberts (2026 online), “The Iron Sulphides: Greigite,” *Mineral Magnetism*, [DOI:10.1017/9781108935630.016](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108935630.016).

title: The predicted Besnus-like transition of 6C pyrrhotite
open: Does phase-pure antiferromagnetic 6C pyrrhotite actually undergo the proposed low-temperature symmetry-lowering transition? A resolution requires either measurement of the transition's order parameter and atomic displacements, or the identification of energetic and compositional constraints that prevent this symmetry-allowed transition.
status: Haines et al.'s analysis, first posted in 2019, predicted a Besnus-like transition specifically in 6C pyrrhotite, distinct from the familiar 4C transition and the proposed spin-flop behavior of 3C/5C. The phase-specific experimental test remains the outstanding target; symmetry analysis alone does not establish that a transition occurs.
solved_when: The proposed Besnus-like transition in 6C pyrrhotite has been definitively established or ruled out — via measurement of its order parameter and atomic displacements in phase-pure samples, or by identifying the energetic and compositional constraints that block it.
why: A solution would test the coupling between vacancy order and magnetic symmetry and improve low-temperature mineral identification.
key_works: C. R. S. Haines, C. J. Howard, R. J. Harrison, and M. A. Carpenter (2019/2020), “Group-theoretical analysis of structural instability, vacancy ordering and magnetic transitions in the system troilite (FeS)–pyrrhotite (Fe₁₋ₓS),” [arXiv:1901.04756](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04756), [DOI:10.1107/S2052520619014197](https://doi.org/10.1107/S2052520619014197).

title: Matrix-solute-controlled incubation of tin pest
open: Can we predict, from solute concentrations inside the tin matrix, residual stress, and second-phase partitioning, how long a β-Sn sample will incubate before transforming to α-Sn? Formally, this asks for a validated model of the incubation-time distribution that explains why nominally similar alloys transform after very different delays and supports long service-life prediction.
status: Michalcová et al. followed five historical-organ-pipe analogues for up to 100 days in 2026: retained stress accelerated transformation, and substantial bulk Pb did not guarantee protection when alloy constituents partitioned into separate phases; their proposed low-level Zn segregation could not be resolved by EDS, leaving matrix chemistry and long-latency prediction incompletely connected. Key works: A. Michalcová, Š. Msallamová, E. Gavel, D. Fink, and P. Jánošíková (2026), “Influence of Low Zn Concentrations on Behavior of Historical Organ Pipes and Its Model Analogs,” [DOI:10.3390/met16020241](https://doi.org/10.3390/met16020241); D. Hillman, R. Wilcoxon, and A. Wieland (2022), “An Examination of the Tin Pest Phenomenon Over a 10-Year Period,” *Journal of Electronic Materials* 51, 6492–6502; University of Maryland CALCE, [“Tin Pests”](https://calce.umd.edu/tin-pests).
solved_when: A predictive theory of incubation-time distributions exists that takes matrix solute concentrations, residual stress, and second-phase partitioning as inputs, accounts for the observed scatter among similar alloys, and supports long-latency (long service-life) predictions.
why: It would improve preservation of tin artifacts and the cold-storage reliability of tin-rich electronics.
key_works: A. Michalcová, Š. Msallamová, E. Gavel, D. Fink, and P. Jánošíková (2026), “Influence of Low Zn Concentrations on Behavior of Historical Organ Pipes and Its Model Analogs,” [DOI:10.3390/met16020241](https://doi.org/10.3390/met16020241); D. Hillman, R. Wilcoxon, and A. Wieland (2022), “An Examination of the Tin Pest Phenomenon Over a 10-Year Period,” *Journal of Electronic Materials* 51, 6492–6502; University of Maryland CALCE, [“Tin Pests”](https://calce.umd.edu/tin-pests).

title: Avoiding reduction arrest in partially molten, gangue-bearing iron ore
open: Can we design ore microstructures and gangue chemistries that keep hydrogen reaching the oxide — and keep the oxide reducible — even as the material passes through the partially molten regime? More formally, the goal is to predict when dense iron and silicate phases arrest reduction, and then to prevent that arrest across realistic feedstock variation.
status: Mohanta et al. (2025) mapped hydrogen reduction from 900 to 1590 °C and found a strong slowdown around 1100–1400 °C, associated with dense metallic product layers and less-reducible gangue-derived phases (R. K. Mohanta, D. Fisher, Y. Korobeinikov, Q. Hong, C. Muhich, S. Sridhar, and N. Leick (2025), "Bridging the Gap in Carbon Free Iron Making: How Hydrogen Affects the Reduction of Iron Ore between 900 and 1590 °C," [DOI:10.1021/acssuschemeng.5c03402](https://doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.5c03402)). A transferable strategy for avoiding this experimentally identified bottleneck remains an engineering follow-up.
solved_when: A design — of microstructure and gangue chemistry — is demonstrated that avoids the reduction slowdown observed in the 1100–1400 °C range, remaining effective across realistic variation in feedstock composition.
why: Without such a strategy, the bottleneck can erase the expected productivity gains from increasing reduction temperature in hydrogen-based ironmaking.
key_works: R. K. Mohanta, D. Fisher, Y. Korobeinikov, Q. Hong, C. Muhich, S. Sridhar, and N. Leick (2025), “Bridging the Gap in Carbon Free Iron Making: How Hydrogen Affects the Reduction of Iron Ore between 900 and 1590 °C,” [DOI:10.1021/acssuschemeng.5c03402](https://doi.org/10.1021/acssuschemeng.5c03402).

title: Tin–oxo insolubility before dense network formation
open: What actually makes an irradiated n-butyltin–oxo cage film stop dissolving once a few butyl groups are lost — is it covalent bridges between cages, physical aggregation, or intact cages trapped in a network? A molecular account of the connectivity and developer interactions at the dissolution threshold is what is being sought.
status: Sadegh et al.’s 2026 TinOH measurements found maximum film retention near 45 mJ cm⁻² and estimated only approximately 2.2 lost butyl groups per cage there, implying that extensive three-dimensional crosslinking is unnecessary; direct structural evidence for the connections between cages remains missing (N. Sadegh, J. Haitjema, Y. Zhang et al. (2026), "Extreme ultraviolet induced reactions of tin–oxo cage photoresists," [DOI:10.1039/D5TC04167H](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5TC04167H)).
solved_when: The intermolecular connectivity and developer interactions responsible for insolubility at the dissolution threshold are identified, with the roles of covalent bridges, aggregation, and trapping of intact cages distinguished — consistent with film retention peaking near 45 mJ cm⁻², where only about 2.2 butyl groups per cage are lost.
why: A molecular dissolution law would make sensitivity improvements in tin–oxo photoresists predictable rather than empirical.
key_works: N. Sadegh, J. Haitjema, Y. Zhang et al. (2026), “Extreme ultraviolet induced reactions of tin–oxo cage photoresists,” [DOI:10.1039/D5TC04167H](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5TC04167H).

title: Residue-free EUV-triggered dry depolymerization of PPA resists
open: Can a polyphthalaldehyde resist be designed so that EUV exposure volatilizes the exposed material completely, leaving patterned features after purely dry development? Formally, the goal is an architecture and exposure/development cycle that removes all exposed material by depolymerization-driven volatilization while preserving unexposed features, suppressing the secondary monomer and radical reactions that generate nonvolatile residue.
status: PPA lithography dates to the 1980s. Naqvi et al. found in 2025 that cyclic PPA and a phthalaldehyde–propanal copolymer respond strongly to EUV, but neither achieved complete dry removal under the tested conditions; spectroscopy supports secondary chemistry and increasing crosslinking at higher doses. (B. A. Naqvi, J. Schwartz, A. Engler, P. A. Kohl, S. De Gendt, and D. De Simone (2025), “Analysis of EUV induced depolymerization and side reactions of polyphthalaldehydes for dry develop EUV resist applications,” [DOI:10.1039/D4TC05250A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4TC05250A).)
solved_when: A PPA-based resist and EUV exposure/development cycle demonstrates complete dry removal of exposed material by volatilization with unexposed features preserved, under conditions where secondary monomer and radical reactions producing nonvolatile residue are suppressed.
why: Complete dry development would eliminate capillary-collapse constraints on high-aspect-ratio features without requiring a separate photoacid component.
key_works: B. A. Naqvi, J. Schwartz, A. Engler, P. A. Kohl, S. De Gendt, and D. De Simone (2025), “Analysis of EUV induced depolymerization and side reactions of polyphthalaldehydes for dry develop EUV resist applications,” [DOI:10.1039/D4TC05250A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4TC05250A).

title: Changed absorption above the amorphous-silicon annealing optimum
