open: What structurally causes the near-infrared absorption trend of amorphous-silicon coatings to change after annealing beyond roughly 400 °C — defect-assisted absorption, incipient crystallization, or altered Urbach-tail disorder? A definitive answer would identify a way to suppress the responsible structural change while preserving the coating's low mechanical loss.
status: Diksha et al.'s 2025 study found correlation between absorption and Urbach energy through approximately 400 °C, followed by a changed trend. Tested substrate hydroxyl content and substantial additional oxygen incorporation were excluded as explanations; the structural mechanism remains undetermined. Key work: D. Diksha, A. Amato, V. Spagnuolo, S. Roorda, M. Chicoine, I. W. Martin, and J. Steinlechner (2025), "Urbach tails and optical absorption of amorphous silicon coatings," [DOI:10.1088/1361-6382/ae153f](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6382/ae153f).
solved_when: The mechanism behind the post-400 °C change in absorption trend is identified and experimentally confirmed, and a process suppressing that structural change while preserving low mechanical loss is demonstrated.
why: Residual absorption heats cryogenic mirrors and can prevent use of otherwise mechanically quiet coatings, so understanding and suppressing it bears directly on cryogenic interferometer heat budgets.
key_works: D. Diksha, A. Amato, V. Spagnuolo, S. Roorda, M. Chicoine, I. W. Martin, and J. Steinlechner (2025), “Urbach tails and optical absorption of amorphous silicon coatings,” [DOI:10.1088/1361-6382/ae153f](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6382/ae153f).

title: Optically usable crystalline titania–tantala with low cryogenic loss
open: Can a crystallized Ti-rich titania–tantala film keep its unusually low cryogenic mechanical loss while also meeting the optical requirements of mirror-grade coatings — specifically, low enough scattering and absorption? A satisfactory answer would identify the phase and grain-size window in a reflective multilayer in which both the mechanical and optical targets hold simultaneously.
status: Murray et al. (2025) reported a large cryogenic loss reduction for their nominally 75%-Ti cation mixture after crystallization at 500 °C; its loss was below that of either separately crystallized constituent, while optical scattering was explicitly left as a potentially decisive limitation. Key work: P. G. Murray, J. Steinlechner, H. N. Isa et al. (2025), "Mechanical loss reduction at low temperature after crystallization in a titania-tantala film," [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevD.111.042005](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.111.042005).
solved_when: A crystallized titania–tantala material is demonstrated that retains low cryogenic mechanical loss while satisfying mirror-grade scattering and absorption requirements, with the phase and grain-size window in which this holds established in a reflective multilayer.
why: It tests whether controlled crystallization can produce useful high-index precision-optics layers; success would open a route to low-loss crystalline coatings for applications such as precision interferometry.
key_works: P. G. Murray, J. Steinlechner, H. N. Isa et al. (2025), “Mechanical loss reduction at low temperature after crystallization in a titania-tantala film,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevD.111.042005](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.111.042005).

title: Reversible mechanical poling of metallic LiOsO₃
open: Can the polar distortion of metallic LiOsO₃ be reversed by applying a calibrated strain gradient, for example through bending, while the material stays metallic? The goal is to demonstrate reversible domain switching, determine its nucleation-and-motion threshold, and distinguish true switching from mere elastic displacement under load.
status: A 2021 first-principles proposal by A. Zabalo and M. Stengel, “Switching a Polar Metal via Strain Gradients” ([DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.127601](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.127601), [arXiv:2007.11857](https://doi.org/abs/2007.11857)), estimated a homogeneous-switching critical bending radius near 118 Å and identified experimental switching as the next target. Domain-wall nucleation and octahedral-tilt-gradient contributions were omitted, so the radius remains a model estimate, and experimental realization of the proposal is unconfirmed.
solved_when: LiOsO₃ exhibits experimentally reversible mechanical switching of its polar distortion under a controlled strain gradient, with metallic conduction retained, the switching threshold (nucleation and motion) characterized, and switching verified as distinct from elastic displacement under load.
why: Electric fields are screened in a metal, so ordinary poling is unavailable; mechanical control would provide a switchable structural state in LiOsO₃ despite that screening.
key_works: A. Zabalo and M. Stengel (2021), “Switching a Polar Metal via Strain Gradients,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.127601](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.127601), [arXiv:2007.11857](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.11857).

title: Is chlorine responsible for GaN’s slow RL1 red luminescence?
open: Which atomic defect gives rise to the approximately 1.8 eV RL1 luminescence band in conductive HVPE-grown GaN, and is chlorine a genuine constituent of that defect or merely a correlate of the growth process? A convincing answer should reproduce the band's characteristic kinetics by introducing the impurity in a controlled way.
status: RL1 was distinguished from fast red centers by at least 2016, and its chemical identity remains unresolved in the 2025 specialist assessment by M. A. Reshchikov (2025), “Luminescence Properties of Defects in GaN: Solved and Unsolved Problems,” [DOI:10.3390/solids6030052](https://doi.org/10.3390/solids6030052). A mean hole-capture coefficient of approximately 2.9 × 10⁻⁷ cm³ s⁻¹ at 100 K is already measured and provides a quantitative constraint, following defect-analysis methods such as M. A. Reshchikov et al. (2017), “Evaluation of the concentration of point defects in GaN,” [DOI:10.1038/s41598-017-08570-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-08570-1).
solved_when: The atomic defect responsible for the approximately 1.8 eV RL1 band is identified, with a determination of whether chlorine is a constituent or only a growth-process correlate, demonstrated by controlled impurity introduction that reproduces the band's kinetics (consistent with the measured mean hole-capture coefficient of approximately 2.9 × 10⁻⁷ cm³ s⁻¹ at 100 K).
why: Chemical identification would make this growth-related recombination channel controllable in conductive HVPE-grown GaN.
key_works: M. A. Reshchikov et al. (2017), “Evaluation of the concentration of point defects in GaN,” [DOI:10.1038/s41598-017-08570-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-08570-1); M. A. Reshchikov (2025), “Luminescence Properties of Defects in GaN: Solved and Unsolved Problems,” [DOI:10.3390/solids6030052](https://doi.org/10.3390/solids6030052).

title: Atomic identity of GaN’s optically generated GL1 giant trap
open: Which atomic defect in GaN gives rise to the excitation-dependent GL1 green luminescence band and its unusually efficient electron capture after optical activation? A complete answer would specify the defect's atomic structure and its charge-state sequence.
status: Work in 2014–2016 established the characteristic kinetics and proposed a carbon assignment, notably M. A. Reshchikov et al. (2016), "Optically generated giant traps in high-purity GaN," [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.93.081202](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.93.081202). Later assessments, including M. A. Reshchikov (2023), "On the Origin of the Yellow Luminescence Band in GaN," [DOI:10.1002/pssb.202200488](https://doi.org/10.1002/pssb.202200488), and work in 2025, nevertheless identify GL1's origin as unresolved; superlinear excitation dependence and temperature-dependent capture remain important constraints.
solved_when: The defect responsible for GL1 is identified, with its atomic structure and charge-state sequence resolved in a way that accounts for the superlinear excitation dependence and temperature-dependent capture kinetics.
why: It would identify a light-activated carrier sink capable of dominating high-purity GaN at low defect concentrations.
key_works: M. A. Reshchikov et al. (2016), “Optically generated giant traps in high-purity GaN,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.93.081202](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.93.081202); M. A. Reshchikov (2023), “On the Origin of the Yellow Luminescence Band in GaN,” [DOI:10.1002/pssb.202200488](https://doi.org/10.1002/pssb.202200488).

title: Chemical identity of GaN’s multiband RY3 center
open: What defect gives rise to GaN’s RY3 center, which produces coupled red and yellow luminescence bands, and is iron involved — as an isolated substitutional impurity or as part of a complex — or not at all?
status: Measurements by M. A. Reshchikov et al. (2019), “Unusual properties of the RY3 center in GaN,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.100.045204](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.100.045204), established dramatically different red and yellow lifetimes of approximately 10 ns and hundreds of microseconds, together with an approximately 0.06 eV redistribution barrier. The 2025 assessment, M. A. Reshchikov (2025), “Luminescence Properties of Defects in GaN…,” [DOI:10.3390/solids6030052](https://doi.org/10.3390/solids6030052), notes correlations of RY3 with Fe, but conductive Fe-containing specimens lacking RY3 leave the chemical assignment tentative.
solved_when: The microscopic and chemical structure of the RY3 center is identified in a way that accounts for the coupled red and yellow emissions with their dramatically different lifetimes (approximately 10 ns for red, hundreds of microseconds for yellow) and the approximately 0.06 eV redistribution barrier, and that resolves whether Fe is required.
why: A firm chemical assignment would convert a distinctive multiband optical fingerprint into a practical tool for controlling defect incorporation during GaN growth and managing compensation.
key_works: M. A. Reshchikov et al. (2019), “Unusual properties of the RY3 center in GaN,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.100.045204](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.100.045204); M. A. Reshchikov (2025), “Luminescence Properties of Defects in GaN…,” [DOI:10.3390/solids6030052](https://doi.org/10.3390/solids6030052).

title: Molecular connectivity behind native suberin lamellae
open: What molecular architecture gives suberin its lamellar repeat? The task is to determine the covalent connections and packing — including links between aliphatic components, aromatics, and the surrounding cell wall — that produce the native lamellar structure, and to predict spacing and barrier properties from a chemically specified architecture.
status: Daraspe et al.’s 2025 cryogenic tomography resolved approximately 5–7 nm lamellae in hydrated Arabidopsis roots without heavy-metal staining (J. Daraspe, E. Bellani, D. De Bellis, C. Genoud, and N. Geldner (2025), “Targeted imaging of specialized plant cell walls by improved cryo-CLEM and cryo-electron tomography,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-66410-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-66410-7)). Opposed hydroxy-fatty-acid units are a proposed explanation of the spacing, while polymer connections and integration into the wall remain explicitly unresolved.
solved_when: A chemically specified architecture for suberin is established that reproduces the approximately 5–7 nm native lamellar repeat and predicts its barrier properties, accounting for the connections among aliphatic components, aromatics, and the cell wall.
why: A molecular design rule for this thin biological barrier could inform drought resilience in plants and the design of degradable barrier films.
key_works: J. Daraspe, E. Bellani, D. De Bellis, C. Genoud, and N. Geldner (2025), “Targeted imaging of specialized plant cell walls by improved cryo-CLEM and cryo-electron tomography,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-66410-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-66410-7).

title: Sequence-mixture synergy in silicatein-mediated nanoceria synthesis
open: Which silicatein variants, alone and in mixtures, are responsible for the enhanced ceria formation seen in evolved sequence populations, and in what ratios do they act? A resolution should disentangle cooperative templating, catalytic chemistry, phase organization, and protein-abundance effects using purified variants in defined mixtures.
status: Vigil et al. screened approximately 100,000 variants and obtained populations producing roughly four times the wild-type ceria yield in 2025. Multiple sequences and truncations persisted in the evolved populations, some catalytic-triad substitutions retained mineralization, and individual-variant characterization was explicitly left unfinished. Key work: T. N. Vigil, M.-J. C. Rowson, A. J. Frost, A. R. Janiga, and B. W. Berger (2025), "Directed Evolution of Silicatein Reveals Biomineralization Synergism between Protein Sequences," [DOI:10.1021/acsomega.4c06359](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.4c06359).
solved_when: Purified individual variants and defined sequence mixtures at specified ratios have been characterized so that the source of the roughly fourfold improvement over wild-type ceria yield is attributed to specific sequences, mixtures, or mechanisms (cooperative templating, catalytic chemistry, phase organization, or protein abundance), closing the explicitly unfinished individual-variant characterization.
why: Resolving whether and how sequences cooperate would make mineral-producing protein systems reproducible and transferable, turning an evolved population-level phenotype into an engineerable design principle.
key_works: T. N. Vigil, M.-J. C. Rowson, A. J. Frost, A. R. Janiga, and B. W. Berger (2025), “Directed Evolution of Silicatein Reveals Biomineralization Synergism between Protein Sequences,” [DOI:10.1021/acsomega.4c06359](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.4c06359).

title: How woven fibrils become a butterfly single gyroid
open: How do the woven fibrillar precursors in the wing scales of *Parides sesostris* transform into the mature single-gyroid photonic network? A complete answer would identify the fibrils' composition and any membrane or protein templates, and explain — or experimentally reproduce — the transition that preserves the gyroid topology.
status: Jessop et al.'s 2025 developmental imaging revealed a woven fibrillar precursor to the adult gyroid, and perturbed development could preserve fibrous structures with blue reflection; however, the weaving rule, the detailed molecular composition, and the conversion mechanism remain open. Key work: A.-L. Jessop, P. L. Clode, M. Saunders et al. (2025), “Hierarchical woven fibrillar structures in developing single gyroids in butterflies,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.2507297122](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2507297122), [arXiv:2504.03459](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03459).
solved_when: The fibril composition and any templating membranes or proteins are identified, and the topology-preserving transition from woven fibrillar precursor to single gyroid is reproduced.
why: An assembly route based on woven fibrils would offer a manufacturing pathway to three-dimensional photonic networks.
key_works: A.-L. Jessop, P. L. Clode, M. Saunders et al. (2025), “Hierarchical woven fibrillar structures in developing single gyroids in butterflies,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.2507297122](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2507297122), [arXiv:2504.03459](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03459).

title: Mechanical function of brominated tyrosine crosslinks in spongin
open: What role do brominated di- and trityrosine crosslinks play in the mechanics of hydrated spongin? Specifically, determine how these crosslinks affect stiffness, dissipation, fatigue resistance, and chemical stability, varying crosslink chemistry while controlling collagen organization well enough to isolate their contribution.
status: A 2025 study (H. Ehrlich, I. Miksik, M. V. Tsurkan et al., "Discovery of mammalian collagens I and III within ancient poriferan biopolymer spongin," DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-57460-y) identified collagen-like components and brominated tyrosine crosslinks and modeled selected crosslinks in collagen-mimetic systems, explicitly leaving open their possible mechanical role in the native fibrous network.
solved_when: A quantitative account exists of how crosslink chemistry modulates hydrated spongin's stiffness, dissipation, fatigue resistance, and chemical stability, with collagen organization controlled so the crosslink contribution is isolated.
why: A solution would explain the durability of a halogen-rich extracellular skeleton and suggest design principles for new wet protein materials.
key_works: H. Ehrlich, I. Miksik, M. V. Tsurkan et al. (2025), “Discovery of mammalian collagens I and III within ancient poriferan biopolymer spongin,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-57460-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57460-y).

title: Durable high-yield particulate solar water splitting
subfield: Catalysts, membranes, and porous energy materials
open: Can a particulate-photocatalyst water-splitting system achieve, over a full year, solar-to-hydrogen energy conversion comparable to today's best photovoltaic-driven electrolyzers while remaining inexpensive and safe? Formally, the target is a system of at least 100 m² with annual solar-to-hydrogen energy conversion of at least 7.6%, scalable catalyst manufacture, safe product separation, and no sacrificial reagents — ten times the 2021 demonstration's reported peak efficiency.
status: Nishiyama et al. demonstrated a 100 m² system operated over several months in 2021, reaching a maximum 0.76% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency [H. Nishiyama et al. (2021), "Photocatalytic solar hydrogen production from water on a 100-m² scale," DOI:10.1038/s41586-021-03907-3]. Peak efficiency and year-long energy yield are different metrics; the proposed combined scale–efficiency–lifetime target remains open.
solved_when: A particulate-photocatalyst system of at least 100 m² operates with annual solar-to-hydrogen energy conversion of at least 7.6%, uses no sacrificial reagents, achieves safe product (gas) separation, and is built from catalysts manufactured by a scalable process.
why: Success would make solar hydrogen production possible with simple, inexpensive semiconductor particle systems, removing the need for complex and costly device architectures.
key_works: H. Nishiyama et al. (2021), “Photocatalytic solar hydrogen production from water on a 100-m² scale,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-021-03907-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03907-3).

title: Sound attenuation near ideal-glass stability
open: Does the ratio of longitudinal to transverse Ioffe–Regel frequencies approach one — or even fall below one — as a glass is driven toward ever greater stability, and can one identify the structural quantity that controls this ratio?
status: A September 2026 preprint reports ratios decreasing to about 2.4 in its three-dimensional models and 1.6 in its two-dimensional models; whether further stabilization reaches or crosses unity remains unresolved. Fu et al. (2026), "On the ratio between longitudinal and transverse Ioffe-Regel frequencies in glasses," [arXiv:2609.22386](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22386).
solved_when: A derivation (analytic or well-supported numerically) establishes whether the ratio tends to, reaches, or crosses unity with increasing glass stability, together with the structural quantity controlling it.
why: It would sharpen predictions of vibrational damping and anomalous heat transport in glasses, where the crossover physics near the Ioffe–Regel regime governs attenuation.
key_works: Fu et al. (2026), “On the ratio between longitudinal and transverse Ioffe-Regel frequencies in glasses,” [arXiv:2609.22386](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22386).

title: Realizable ideal glass in three dimensions
open: Can an ideal glass — an amorphous solid with vanishing configurational entropy — actually be prepared in three dimensions? The goal is to construct and physically prepare a three-dimensional amorphous solid with demonstrably vanishing configurational entropy under a precisely specified ensemble, or else to establish why proposed preparation routes cannot achieve it.
status: Bolton-Lum et al. (2024, revised 2025; journal 2026), "The Ideal Glass and the Ideal Disk Packing in Two Dimensions," [arXiv:2404.07492](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07492), constructed special two-dimensional ideal packings; this does not establish a physical preparation route for three-dimensional atomic glasses.
solved_when: A three-dimensional amorphous solid is experimentally prepared whose configurational entropy demonstrably vanishes under a precisely specified ensemble, or a rigorous argument is given that no proposed preparation route can achieve this.
why: It would test ideal-glass predictions directly, independently of extrapolated relaxation times.
key_works: Bolton-Lum et al. (2024, revised 2025; journal 2026), “The Ideal Glass and the Ideal Disk Packing in Two Dimensions,” [arXiv:2404.07492](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07492).

title: Tenfold cheaper validated discovery
open: Can automated materials discovery be made an order of magnitude cheaper than conventional practice, measured end to end? Formally, achieve a tenfold reduction in total cost per independently reproduced, application-qualified material relative to a declared contemporary manual baseline, demonstrated across multiple chemistry families.
status: Currently a proposed census moonshot. Individual automated tasks accelerate, but component speedups do not establish the complete discovery-cost target. Key work: Tom et al. (2024), “Self-Driving Laboratories for Chemistry and Materials Science,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055).
solved_when: A demonstration shows total cost per independently reproduced, application-qualified material reduced tenfold against a declared contemporary manual baseline, across multiple chemistry families.
why: It would make materials exploration accessible beyond highly equipped laboratories.
key_works: Tom et al. (2024), “Self-Driving Laboratories for Chemistry and Materials Science,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055).

title: Tenfold lower-field dielectric-elastomer actuation
open: Can a dielectric-elastomer actuator deliver its full useful performance at an electric field an order of magnitude lower than today's devices require? That is, can required field be reduced tenfold while maintaining matched useful stress, strain, bandwidth, and cycling lifetime in a complete device including electrodes and encapsulation — and, in particular, can increased permittivity achieve this gain without offsetting dielectric loss, stiffening, or breakdown?
status: Large-strain dielectric-elastomer artificial muscles are established; the specific experimental baseline is Mao et al.'s report of 125% operable strain at 25 MV/m over 150,000 cycles. This baseline does not constitute proof of the combined lower-field target. Key work: J. Mao et al. (2026), "A self healable dielectric elastomer artificial muscle," [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-72611-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72611-5).
solved_when: An actuator demonstrates a tenfold reduction in required electric field relative to the experimental baseline, while matching the baseline's useful stress, strain, bandwidth, and cycling lifetime (on the order of 150,000 cycles), with electrodes and encapsulation included in the demonstrated device.
why: It would enable compact, efficient soft actuators driven by simpler, lower-voltage electronics.
key_works: J. Mao et al. (2026), “A self healable dielectric elastomer artificial muscle,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-72611-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72611-5).

title: Hydrogen-isotope selectivity above five above 200 K
open: Is there a regenerable solid adsorbent that separates H₂ from D₂ with a separation factor above five at temperatures above 200 K? The material must retain adsorption and desorption kinetics fast enough for cyclic operation, with the selectivity demonstrated dynamically and usable capacity and regeneration energy quantified.
status: Yamauchi et al. explicitly identify this selectivity–temperature frontier. Their study, published online in 2025 and in a 2026 journal volume, reports a separation factor of 4.2 at 213 K, a 5.0 kJ mol⁻¹ isotope-dependent adsorption-enthalpy difference, and room-temperature chromatography; room-temperature separation itself is already demonstrated. T. Yamauchi et al. (2026), "Room-temperature chromatographic H₂/D₂ separation via a solid dihydrogen complex with balanced thermodynamics and kinetics," [DOI:10.1039/D5GC04476F](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5GC04476F).
solved_when: A regenerable solid achieves an H₂/D₂ separation factor above 5 at a temperature above 200 K, with dynamic (not just equilibrium) demonstration of selectivity, adsorption/desorption rates compatible with cyclic operation, and quantified usable capacity and regeneration energy.
why: Strong noncryogenic hydrogen-isotope discrimination could cut the energy cost and complexity of hydrogen-isotope processing, which currently relies on cryogenic or energy-intensive methods.
key_works: T. Yamauchi et al. (2026), “Room-temperature chromatographic H₂/D₂ separation via a solid dihydrogen complex with balanced thermodynamics and kinetics,” [DOI:10.1039/D5GC04476F](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5GC04476F).

title: Suppressing BaF₂’s slow scintillation without sacrificing prompt photons
open: Can a bulk barium fluoride scintillator be engineered to suppress its slow self-trapped-exciton afterglow while keeping its prompt core-valence luminescence intact? Formally, can a composition achieve at least 100-fold suppression of slow photon yield while retaining at least 90% of the undoped fast yield under matched excitation and collection calibration?
status: Xu et al.’s 2025 heavily Y-doped crystals reduced slow photon yield to roughly 6–10% of undoped values while retaining roughly 74–87% of fast yield, depending on boule position. These calibrated photon-yield ratios differ from radioluminescence spectral-intensity ratios; the proposed 100-fold/90% combination is not a reported record. Key work: J. Xu et al. (2025), “Influence of Yttrium Concentration on Scintillation Performance of Heavily Y-Doped Barium Fluoride Crystals,” [DOI:10.1109/TNS.2025.3535633](https://doi.org/10.1109/TNS.2025.3535633).
solved_when: A bulk BaF₂ composition demonstrates at least 100-fold suppression of slow photon yield together with at least 90% retention of the undoped fast yield, measured as calibrated photon-yield ratios under matched excitation and collection conditions.
why: More prompt photons with less afterglow would reduce pileup and improve timing in high-rate particle instrumentation and photon-statistics-limited coincidence timing for medical imaging.
key_works: J. Xu et al. (2025), “Influence of Yttrium Concentration on Scintillation Performance of Heavily Y-Doped Barium Fluoride Crystals,” [DOI:10.1109/TNS.2025.3535633](https://doi.org/10.1109/TNS.2025.3535633).

title: Ten-picosecond coincidence timing from clinically useful scintillator volumes
open: Can a scintillator or metascintillator be built that achieves 10 ps FWHM coincidence timing for 511 keV photon pairs while still providing useful stopping efficiency and energy discrimination at realistic detector thicknesses? Any demonstration must report the event-selection efficiency, so the timing figure is not defined by an unusually favorable subset of events.
status: The 10 ps objective remains explicit in Lecoq’s 2025 FAST workshop contribution. Orfano et al.’s 2024 nanocomposite/BGO multilayers demonstrate energy sharing and a 25% timing improvement relative to their monolithic BGO reference, leaving a substantial gap to the complete specification. Key works: M. Orfano et al. (2024), “Fast Emitting Nanocomposites for High-Resolution ToF-PET Imaging Based on Multicomponent Scintillators,” [DOI:10.1002/admt.202302075](https://doi.org/10.1002/admt.202302075); P. Lecoq (2025), “Harnessing the Purcell Effect for Faster Metascintillators,” [FAST2025 contribution](https://indico.cern.ch/event/1445926/contributions/6487549/).
solved_when: A scintillator or metascintillator demonstrates 10 ps FWHM coincidence timing for 511 keV photon pairs, retains useful stopping efficiency and energy discrimination in realistic thicknesses, and reports its event-selection efficiency.
why: Ten-picosecond time-of-flight localization would change PET reconstruction, sensitivity, and dose tradeoffs.
key_works: M. Orfano et al. (2024), “Fast Emitting Nanocomposites for High-Resolution ToF-PET Imaging Based on Multicomponent Scintillators,” [DOI:10.1002/admt.202302075](https://doi.org/10.1002/admt.202302075); P. Lecoq (2025), “Harnessing the Purcell Effect for Faster Metascintillators,” [FAST2025 contribution](https://indico.cern.ch/event/1445926/contributions/6487549/).

title: Five-meV photocathodes at sustained milliampere current
open: Can a photocathode operate in a real electron gun at roughly 5 mA continuous current with mean transverse energy at or below 5 meV, quantum efficiency of at least 5%, and multiweek lifetime — a tenfold MTE reduction from the best cryogenic bialkali results without sacrificing the other operating metrics?
status: Wang et al.’s September 2026 preprint reports cryogenic K₂CsSb with 50 meV MTE, 5.4% quantum efficiency, operation at 5 mA, and an approximately 20-day operational history; this is a recent preprint benchmark, and carrier survival, surface escape, disorder, and gun operation remain coupled constraints. Key work: D. Wang et al. (2026), “Ultralow Mean Transverse Energy and High Quantum Efficiency Cryogenic Bialkali Photocathode for MHz-Repetition-Rate Electron Sources,” [arXiv:2609.18137](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18137), preprint.
solved_when: A cathode demonstrates mean transverse energy ≤ 5 meV together with quantum efficiency ≥ 5%, sustained operation at approximately 5 mA, and multiweek operation in a practical electron gun.
why: Lower intrinsic emittance at high average current would raise beam brightness for continuous-wave free-electron lasers and energy-recovery linacs.
key_works: D. Wang et al. (2026), “Ultralow Mean Transverse Energy and High Quantum Efficiency Cryogenic Bialkali Photocathode for MHz-Repetition-Rate Electron Sources,” [arXiv:2609.18137](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18137), preprint.

title: Identity of the mussel’s DOPA-rich vanadium-storage carrier
open: Which protein holds the vanadium that mussels stockpile in their foot before building the byssus? The goal is to identify and sequence the DOPA-rich storage carrier and characterize its vanadium binding stoichiometry, oxidation-state control, transfer kinetics to byssal proteins, and mechanism for preventing premature crosslinking.
status: Jee and colleagues' 2024 spectroscopy and calculations constrain vanadium uptake and storage; the study explicitly states that the DOPA-containing storage protein remains unidentified, preventing molecular reconstitution of this processing intermediate (S. Jee, M. Rammal, T. Priemel, D. S. Bohle, and M. J. Harrington (2024), “Vanadium uptake and storage in the fabrication and function of mussel byssus,” [DOI:10.1039/D4NJ02546F](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4NJ02546F)).
solved_when: The DOPA-containing storage protein is identified and sequenced, and its vanadium binding stoichiometry, oxidation-state control, and transfer kinetics to byssal proteins — including how premature crosslinking is prevented — are determined, enabling molecular reconstitution of this processing intermediate.
why: It would explain how biological fabrication separates metal acquisition, storage, and triggered curing, a design principle relevant to latent coordination crosslinkers and selective metal trafficking.
key_works: S. Jee, M. Rammal, T. Priemel, D. S. Bohle, and M. J. Harrington (2024), “Vanadium uptake and storage in the fabrication and function of mussel byssus,” [DOI:10.1039/D4NJ02546F](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4NJ02546F).

title: Low-stress elastocaloric cooling with texture-enabled endurance
open: Can an elastocaloric material deliver large cooling while being driven at dramatically lower stress? Formally: retain roughly 15 K adiabatic cooling and 10⁷-cycle endurance in precipitate-engineered TiNi while reducing the approximately 900 MPa actuation stress by an order of magnitude, with all specifications met in the same specimen and protocol.
status: Li and colleagues demonstrated −15.9 K after ten million compressive cycles in 2026 using textured TiNi containing Ti₄Ni₂O precipitates (X. Li, Q. Liang, C. Liang, D. Wang, S. Li, and X. Ding (2026), "Fatigue resistant elastocaloric effect in TiNi via texture-precipitate synergy," [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-68835-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-68835-0)). Those measurements involved unloading from 900 MPa; the proposed combination with much lower stress remains unmet by that result.
solved_when: A single specimen under a single protocol achieves about 15 K adiabatic temperature change, 10⁷-cycle endurance, and actuation stress roughly an order of magnitude below 900 MPa.
why: Driving the effect at much lower force shrinks actuator and structural hardware while preserving the material's cooling density, making elastocaloric cooling practical where bulky loading systems currently dominate.
key_works: X. Li, Q. Liang, C. Liang, D. Wang, S. Li, and X. Ding (2026), “Fatigue resistant elastocaloric effect in TiNi via texture-precipitate synergy,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-68835-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-68835-0).

title: Experimental realization of the predicted tetragonal ZnFe magnet
open: Can the tetragonal ZnFe phase identified by data-driven computational screening actually be made in the laboratory, and does it hold together with the predicted magnetic behavior?
status: Jami, Bhagat, and Bhattacharya’s 2025 journal paper reports these predictions together with phonon and elastic stability calculations. Experimental realization remains open, and negative formation enthalpy alone does not establish stability against all competing phases.
solved_when: The predicted tetragonal ZnFe phase is synthesized and shown to be structurally stable, with measured magnetization above 1 T, anisotropy above 0.5 MJ m⁻³, and Curie temperature above 1,200 K.
why: It would provide a direct experimental test of a specific rare-earth-free permanent magnet candidate and validate the screening criteria that selected it.
key_works: J. Jami, N. Bhagat, and A. Bhattacharya (2025), “Data-driven high-throughput search for the accelerated discovery of rare-earth-free permanent magnets,” [DOI:10.1103/tppf-n3kb](https://doi.org/10.1103/tppf-n3kb); [arXiv:2507.01849](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.01849).

title: An 800-hour Me-PTCDI monolayer continuous-wave laser
open: Can a molecularly thin laser survive months of continuous operation? The goal is to extend the operating half-life of an hBN-encapsulated Me-PTCDI monolayer continuous-wave laser from hours to at least 800 hours — roughly a 100-fold improvement — while preserving low-threshold coherent lasing at room temperature under optical pumping, by suppressing the residual irreversible degradation channel.
status: Zhang et al. demonstrated room-temperature, optically pumped continuous-wave lasing in 2026 with thresholds of 1.4–3.4 W cm⁻² and an operating half-life up to eight hours; suppressed triplet accumulation and hBN heat removal provide the partial result.
solved_when: An hBN-encapsulated Me-PTCDI monolayer laser demonstrates an output half-life of at least 800 hours under the same conditions as the current benchmark — matching the eight-hour result in pump intensity relative to threshold, temperature, and the 50%-output criterion — while retaining low-threshold continuous-wave coherent lasing.
why: Operating lifetimes of hundreds of hours would move molecularly thin lasers from laboratory curiosities toward practical devices, since irreversible photochemical damage under continuous excitation is currently the limiting failure mode.
key_works: L. Zhang et al. (2026), “Continuous-wave organic laser enabled by monolayer molecular crystal,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-73984-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-73984-3).

title: Diamond’s candidate 584.5 nm oxygen-pair center
open: What is the 584.5 nm optical center in oxygen-implanted diamond, atom by atom? A complete answer specifies its atomic geometry, charge state, and optical cycle, and settles whether it is indeed an oxygen pair — two oxygen atoms plus vacancies — and which vacancy arrangement stabilizes it.
status: Neugebauer et al. reported the center in 2026 after approximately 1500 °C annealing. Emission increased with implantation fluence to a power between 1.5 and 1.9, suggesting an oxygen pair; the proposed O₂Vₓ composition and microscopic structure remain unconfirmed. Key works: P. Neugebauer et al. (2026), “Oxygen in diamond: Thermal stability of ST1 spin centres and creation of oxygen-pair complexes,” [DOI:10.1016/j.diamond.2026.113395](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diamond.2026.113395), [arXiv:2601.04418](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04418).
solved_when: The center's atomic geometry, charge state, and optical cycle are determined, and it is established whether the defect contains two oxygen atoms and which vacancy arrangement stabilizes it; the proposed O₂Vₓ composition is confirmed or refuted.
why: A structural assignment would expand the chemically understood family of diamond emitters and explain annealing-induced oxygen-defect conversion.
key_works: P. Neugebauer et al. (2026), “Oxygen in diamond: Thermal stability of ST1 spin centres and creation of oxygen-pair complexes,” [DOI:10.1016/j.diamond.2026.113395](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diamond.2026.113395), [arXiv:2601.04418](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04418).

title: Near-degenerate polymorph free energies
open: Can we predict, from first principles, which polymorph of a compound is stable at a given temperature and pressure when several experimentally competing structures lie close in energy? More precisely, this requires free energies incorporating anharmonic, electronic, magnetic, and configurational contributions whose computational uncertainty is smaller than the free-energy separation between the candidate polymorphs.
status: The problem has been documented for decades. Inexpensive Gibbs-energy descriptors now enable screening, as in Bartel et al. (2018), "Physical descriptor for the Gibbs energy of inorganic crystalline solids and temperature-dependent materials chemistry," [DOI:10.1038/s41467-018-06682-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-06682-4), while rigorous calculations remain demanding and material dependent.
solved_when: A method yields temperature- and pressure-dependent ordering of experimentally competing polymorphs with an uncertainty smaller than their free-energy separation, across materials of practical interest.
why: It prevents selecting a functional phase that turns out to be unstable under actual operating conditions.
key_works: Bartel et al. (2018), “Physical descriptor for the Gibbs energy of inorganic crystalline solids and temperature-dependent materials chemistry,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-018-06682-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-06682-4).

title: Absolute homogeneous crystal-nucleation rates
open: Can we predict absolute crystal-nucleation rates as a function of supersaturation or undercooling from first principles, without fitting the nucleation barrier or kinetic prefactor to the very rate data being predicted?
status: Classical nucleation theory is nearly a century old; rare-event simulations succeed selectively, but quantitative agreement remains system dependent. See Sosso et al. (2016), "Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations," [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744).
solved_when: A predictive theory or simulation method yields absolute homogeneous nucleation rates across the full supersaturation/undercooling range in quantitative agreement with experiment, with no parameter fitted to the measured rates.
why: It would make crystallization processing predictable and let researchers tell apart an incorrect nucleation mechanism from an incorrect force field.
key_works: Sosso et al. (2016), “Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744).

title: Heterogeneous nucleation-site potency
open: Given a chemically heterogeneous surface, can we predict which specific sites will nucleate a chosen crystalline phase and at what rates, starting only from measured local chemistry, defects, and topography?
status: The question has been active for decades; selected substrates are understood, but lattice matching alone does not explain general nucleation potency. A broader perspective appears in Sosso et al. (2016), “Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744).
solved_when: A validated predictive framework exists that takes local chemistry, defect structure, and topography of a heterogeneous surface as input and outputs the identity of nucleating sites for a chosen phase together with their rate distribution, with predictions confirmed experimentally.
why: It would make nucleation an engineering variable rather than a trial-and-error step, enabling reproducible coatings, reliable inoculants, and controlled crystallization.
key_works: Sosso et al. (2016), “Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.5b00744).

title: Predicting particle-attachment crystallization
open: Can we predict, before any synthesis is attempted, which crystallization pathway a given chemistry will follow — classical monomer addition, oriented particle attachment, or precursor transformation — and what defects the resulting crystal will inherit? In formal terms, this is a theory of pathway selection and defect-population prediction spanning arbitrary chemistries.
status: Particle-attachment pathways are experimentally established; the unresolved problem is quantitative pathway selection and defect inheritance across chemistries. Key works: De Yoreo et al. (2015), "Crystallization by particle attachment in synthetic, biogenic, and geologic environments," [DOI:10.1126/science.aaa6760](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaa6760).
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that, for a specified chemistry, quantitatively determines the operative growth pathway and predicts the resulting defect population prior to synthesis, with validity demonstrated across chemistries.
why: Pathway selection and defect inheritance control nanocrystal shape, biomineral structure, and functional interfaces — outcomes that currently can only be observed after the fact.
key_works: De Yoreo et al. (2015), “Crystallization by particle attachment in synthetic, biogenic, and geologic environments,” [DOI:10.1126/science.aaa6760](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaa6760).

title: Metastable-phase lifetime prediction
open: Can we predict how long a metastable solid will survive before transforming, given its temperature, stress state, atmosphere, and defect population? In formal terms, can a theory yield the full survival-time distribution of a metastable phase, accounting for all competing transformation pathways rather than a single induction time?
status: Energy-above-hull statistics are available for assessing thermodynamic metastability (Sun et al. (2016), "The thermodynamic scale of inorganic crystalline metastability," [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.1600225](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.1600225)), and induction-time models for individual transformations exist (Sun and Ceder (2017), "Induction time of a polymorphic transformation," [DOI:10.1039/C7CE00766C](https://doi.org/10.1039/C7CE00766C)), but thermodynamic metastability alone does not determine practical lifetime.
solved_when: For a specified metastable solid under specified temperature, stress, atmosphere, and defect population, a predictive model reproduces the survival-time distribution, including the branching among competing transformation pathways.
why: Thermodynamic metastability alone does not determine whether a material lasts days or decades; a quantitative lifetime prediction is what turns metastable materials from curiosities into usable components of durable products.
key_works: Sun et al. (2016), “The thermodynamic scale of inorganic crystalline metastability,” [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.1600225](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.1600225); Sun and Ceder (2017), “Induction time of a polymorphic transformation,” [DOI:10.1039/C7CE00766C](https://doi.org/10.1039/C7CE00766C).

title: Transferable solid-state reaction-path prediction
open: Can a model predict how a solid-state powder reaction will unfold — which intermediate phases appear, in what fractions, and on what timescale — for a recipe it has never seen before, given the roles of particle contacts, interphase transport, and atmosphere?
status: Karan et al. (2026) reproduced four Ba–Ti–O reaction histories using correlated transport; transfer beyond this demonstrated chemistry remains open. Karan et al. (2026), “Ion correlations explain kinetic selectivity in diffusion-limited solid-state synthesis reactions,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-026-02596-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02596-5).
solved_when: Intermediate phases, phase fractions, and reaction times are predicted accurately for previously unseen powder recipes, with particle contacts, interphase transport, and atmosphere accounted for.
why: It turns predicted compounds into reproducible synthesis instructions, bridging the gap between computational materials discovery and actual laboratory synthesis.
key_works: Karan et al. (2026), “Ion correlations explain kinetic selectivity in diffusion-limited solid-state synthesis reactions,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-026-02596-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02596-5).

title: Recoverability of high-pressure phases
open: Can we predict, from first principles, which functional phases synthesized at high pressure will survive the trip back to ambient conditions — and can we deliberately engineer defects, interfaces, or composition to keep a chosen useful phase metastable at ambient pressure?
status: Many high-pressure phases are known to be recoverable while others transform on decompression, but no general recoverability rule has been established. Recent work on zirconia by Solomon et al. (2025), "Atomic-scale structure of ZrO2: Formation of metastable polymorphs," [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.adq5943](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adq5943), identifies domain-wall stabilization as a mechanism, without establishing a general rule. Structure-prediction methods that drive such discoveries are reviewed in Oganov et al. (2019), "Structure prediction drives materials discovery," [DOI:10.1038/s41578-019-0101-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-019-0101-8).
solved_when: A predictive recoverability rule exists that correctly identifies which high-pressure phases survive decompression, together with a demonstrated design strategy (via defects, interfaces, or compositional constraints) that preserves a specified useful phase fraction at ambient pressure.
why: It would turn the many functional materials discovered under extreme pressures into materials that can actually be made and used in ordinary conditions, rather than being lost on decompression.
key_works: Oganov et al. (2019), “Structure prediction drives materials discovery,” [DOI:10.1038/s41578-019-0101-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-019-0101-8); Solomon et al. (2025), “Atomic-scale structure of ZrO2: Formation of metastable polymorphs,” [DOI:10.1126/sciadv.adq5943](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adq5943).

title: Static order versus dynamical facilitation
open: Can the long-standing contenders for the glass transition — thermodynamic order, dynamical facilitation, and elastic mechanisms — be told apart at all by observation? The goal is to derive predictions for relaxation times and spatial correlations that differ across these frameworks and can be tested against independently chosen glass formers.
status: Competing frameworks developed over decades reproduce overlapping observations; deeply supercooled simulations improve access without settling a universal mechanism. See Berthier and Biroli (2011), “Theoretical perspective on the glass transition and amorphous materials,” [DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.83.587](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.83.587).
solved_when: A set of discriminating predictions for relaxation times and spatial correlations is produced that distinguishes thermodynamic ordering, facilitation, and elastic mechanisms, and is validated across independently chosen glass formers.
why: It would yield transferable predictions of viscosity and kinetic arrest, replacing overlapping, mechanism-ambiguous accounts with an identifiable mechanism.
key_works: Berthier and Biroli (2011), “Theoretical perspective on the glass transition and amorphous materials,” [DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.83.587](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.83.587).

title: Frictional-jamming universality
open: Which features of the jamming transition — its critical exponents and the state variables governing it — survive when particles have friction, non-spherical shapes, adhesion, or preparation-dependent contact histories?
status: The scaling theory of jamming for frictionless spherical particles is mature (van Hecke (2010), "Jamming of soft particles: geometry, mechanics, scaling and isostaticity," DOI:10.1088/0953-8984/22/3/033101); frictional and nonspherical systems, by contrast, require additional history variables and exhibit distinct transition behavior.
solved_when: A characterization exists of which jamming exponents and state variables remain universal across frictional, anisotropic, adhesive, and history-dependent systems, identifying what must be added or modified relative to the frictionless spherical case.
why: It underpins quantitative prediction of powder handling, granular load support, and the arrest of dense suspensions — processes where real particles are rarely frictionless spheres.
key_works: van Hecke (2010), “Jamming of soft particles: geometry, mechanics, scaling and isostaticity,” [DOI:10.1088/0953-8984/22/3/033101](https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-8984/22/3/033101).

title: Defect-tolerant hyperuniform materials
open: How do the unavoidable imperfections of real materials — finite size, vacancies, polydispersity, and processing noise — degrade hyperuniformity, and can we design a scalable preparation route that preserves a specified optical or transport benefit despite them?
status: Hyperuniform constructions and self-organized examples exist; universal tolerance-to-performance relations across material classes remain undeveloped. Key work: Torquato (2018), “Hyperuniform states of matter,” [DOI:10.1016/j.physrep.2018.03.001](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physrep.2018.03.001).
solved_when: A quantitative account exists of how each defect source (finite size, vacancies, polydispersity, processing noise) erodes useful hyperuniformity, together with a scalable preparation method demonstrated to maintain a specified optical or transport benefit.
why: It would make disordered photonic and transport materials manufacturable rather than merely designable in principle.
key_works: Torquato (2018), “Hyperuniform states of matter,” [DOI:10.1016/j.physrep.2018.03.001](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physrep.2018.03.001).

title: Predictive thermal boundary conductance
open: Can thermal conductance across a chemically realistic rough interface be predicted from its measured structure alone — accounting for intermixing, contamination, bonding, and inelastic scattering? Formally, the goal is a structure-to-conductance map that takes as input the measured interfacial structure and returns the thermal boundary conductance.
status: Acoustic/diffuse mismatch models and atomistic calculations capture selected interfaces; the general structure-to-conductance map remains incomplete. Cahill et al. (2014), "Nanoscale thermal transport. II. 2003–2012," [DOI:10.1063/1.4832615](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4832615).
solved_when: A validated predictive framework exists that computes thermal boundary conductance for an arbitrary chemically realistic rough interface directly from its measured structural characterization, without interface-specific fitting.
why: It would enable reliable thermal design of layered devices and composites, replacing empirical fitting with structure-based prediction.
key_works: Cahill et al. (2014), “Nanoscale thermal transport. II. 2003–2012,” [DOI:10.1063/1.4832615](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4832615).

title: Heat transfer across subnanometre gaps
open: Can we build a single quantitative theory of heat transfer between separated solids approaching contact, in which radiation, phonon coupling, electron tunnelling, and the actual surface chemistry are all included and jointly tested against experiment? Formally, the goal is a crossover theory whose predictions are validated across the subnanometre gap regime, not just in the limits where individual mechanisms dominate.
status: Near-field radiative transfer and conductive mechanisms are individually established; their experimentally resolved crossover remains material and geometry dependent. Key works: Cahill et al. (2014), "Nanoscale thermal transport. II. 2003–2012," [DOI:10.1063/1.4832615](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4832615); Miller, Johnson and Rodriguez (2015), "Shape-Independent Limits to Near-Field Radiative Heat Transfer," [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.115.204302](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.115.204302).
solved_when: A theory incorporating radiation, phonon coupling, electron tunnelling, and actual surface chemistry is formulated and its predicted crossover between near-field radiative transfer and conductive mechanisms is quantitatively confirmed by experimental measurements as the gap shrinks to subnanometre distances and contact.
why: It sets the fundamental limits of nanoscale cooling and energy conversion, both of which hinge on how heat crosses the last nanometre between surfaces.
key_works: Cahill et al. (2014), “Nanoscale thermal transport. II. 2003–2012,” [DOI:10.1063/1.4832615](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4832615); Miller, Johnson and Rodriguez (2015), “Shape-Independent Limits to Near-Field Radiative Heat Transfer,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.115.204302](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.115.204302).

title: Useful room-temperature phonon hydrodynamics
open: Can heat be made to flow hydrodynamically — with second-sound and drift behavior — in a patterned, room-temperature device whose boundaries and defects are realistic rather than idealized, and can that flow yield a practical thermal-control advantage over conventional diffusion?
status: Graphite measurements progressed from second sound above 100 K in 2019 (Huberman et al., 2019, "Observation of second sound in graphite at temperatures above 100 K," DOI:10.1126/science.aav3548) to over 200 K (Ding et al., 2022, "Observation of second sound in graphite over 200 K," DOI:10.1038/s41467-021-27907-z), and to room-temperature second sound in isotopically purified specimens in 2026 (Z. Xie et al., 2026, "Room-temperature second sound in isotopically pure graphite," DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-70807-3). Robust patterned-device operation with realistic disorder and boundaries remains open.
solved_when: A reproducible patterned room-temperature material with realistic boundaries and defects exhibits hydrodynamic heat transport, and a demonstrable thermal-control advantage (e.g., routing or timing of heat pulses) is shown.
why: Hydrodynamic heat transport would provide new means to route and time heat pulses, enabling thermal-control functionality that diffusive transport cannot offer.
key_works: Huberman et al. (2019), “Observation of second sound in graphite at temperatures above 100 K,” [DOI:10.1126/science.aav3548](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aav3548); Ding et al. (2022), “Observation of second sound in graphite over 200 K,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-021-27907-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-27907-z); Z. Xie et al. (2026), “Room-temperature second sound in isotopically pure graphite,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-70807-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70807-3).

title: Sharp thermal-diffusivity bounds
open: How slowly can heat actually spread through an interacting material — is there a fundamental floor on thermal diffusivity, and can that floor be attained? More precisely, the goal is a sharp lower bound on thermal diffusivity for specified classes of interacting materials, with explicit assumptions and a rigorous treatment of criticality, disorder, and quantum statistics.
status: Existing proposed bounds describe many liquids, but the liquid bound of Trachenko, Baggioli, Behnia and Brazhkin (2021), "Universal lower bounds on energy and momentum diffusion in liquids," [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.103.014311](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.103.014311), explicitly excludes the neighborhood of the critical point, leaving both the generality and the optimality of such bounds unresolved.
solved_when: A lower bound on thermal diffusivity is established for specified classes of interacting materials under explicit assumptions covering criticality, disorder, and quantum statistics, and shown to be sharp (achievable), thereby resolving the generality and optimality questions left open by existing liquid bounds.
why: It separates insulation targets that materials science can realistically pursue from limits imposed by physics itself, telling engineers when further improvement is impossible.
key_works: Trachenko, Baggioli, Behnia and Brazhkin (2021), “Universal lower bounds on energy and momentum diffusion in liquids,” [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.103.014311](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.103.014311).

title: Long-life high-temperature phase-change stores
open: Can salt-based phase-change composites be engineered to survive an application-representative service life without losing their latent heat, shape, containment integrity, or heat-transfer performance? Formally, the goal is a high-temperature storage composite whose latent capacity, structural containment, and thermal conductivity degrade negligibly under realistic long-term thermal cycling.
status: Encapsulation and conductive scaffolds improve laboratory performance, but coupled segregation, corrosion, and cycling stability remain scale-dependent barriers. A recent review is Wang et al. (2025), "A review of the performance and application of molten salt-based phase change materials in sustainable thermal energy storage at medium and high temperatures," [DOI:10.1016/j.apenergy.2025.125766](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2025.125766).
solved_when: A salt-based thermal-storage composite retains latent heat, shape, containment integrity, and heat-transfer performance through an application-representative service life, demonstrated under realistic cycling conditions.
why: It would make dispatchable industrial heat and solar thermal storage more economical, removing degradation-driven replacement costs as a barrier to deployment.
key_works: Wang et al. (2025), “A review of the performance and application of molten salt-based phase change materials in sustainable thermal energy storage at medium and high temperatures,” [DOI:10.1016/j.apenergy.2025.125766](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2025.125766).

title: Transferable density functionals for strong correlation
open: Construct a computationally practical density functional that simultaneously treats charge localization, static correlation, and bond breaking in solids while respecting relevant exact constraints.
status: A decades-old challenge; hybrid, range-separated, and correction schemes help selected regimes without providing uniform reliability. Key work: Cohen, Mori-Sánchez and Yang (2012), “Challenges for Density Functional Theory,” [DOI:10.1021/cr200107z](https://doi.org/10.1021/cr200107z).
solved_when: A single, computationally practical functional demonstrably handles charge localization, static correlation, and bond breaking in solids uniformly, while satisfying the relevant exact constraints.
why: It improves predictions of redox, magnetism, defects, and phase stability — properties where present-day functionals fail.
key_works: Cohen, Mori-Sánchez and Yang (2012), “Challenges for Density Functional Theory,” [DOI:10.1021/cr200107z](https://doi.org/10.1021/cr200107z).

title: Universal potentials beyond equilibrium configurations
open: Can we build interatomic potentials that remain trustworthy far from the equilibrium configurations on which they were trained? The goal is a broadly transferable potential that predicts defects, transition states, surfaces, and high-energy configurations without systematic curvature or barrier bias.
status: Deng et al. (2025), “Systematic softening in universal machine learning interatomic potentials,” [DOI:10.1038/s41524-024-01500-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-024-01500-6), document systematic softening in three foundation potentials and show efficient corrections; broad reliability in unseen regimes remains open.
solved_when: A broadly transferable interatomic potential is demonstrated to predict defects, transition states, surfaces, and high-energy configurations without systematic curvature or barrier bias, with reliability that holds in unseen regimes rather than only near training data.
why: Without it, simulations of failure, diffusion, and reaction can be confidently but quantitatively wrong, corrupting downstream multiscale predictions.
key_works: Deng et al. (2025), “Systematic softening in universal machine learning interatomic potentials,” [DOI:10.1038/s41524-024-01500-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-024-01500-6).

title: Scalable reactive potentials with nonlocal charge transfer
open: Can we build a reactive interatomic potential that predicts charge redistribution and reactive forces across heterogeneous metal–insulator–electrolyte systems as boundary conditions change, while remaining accurate and computationally scalable enough for large-scale simulations?
status: Fourth-generation neural network potentials address nonlocal charge transfer in demonstrated systems, as in Ko et al. (2021), "A fourth-generation high-dimensional neural network potential with accurate electrostatics including non-local charge transfer," [DOI:10.1038/s41467-020-20427-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-20427-2); however, reactive transferability and large-scale boundary-condition handling remain incomplete.
solved_when: A potential demonstrates nonlocal charge transfer with reactive transferability across heterogeneous metal–insulator–electrolyte interfaces, handles changing boundary conditions, and scales to large simulations with suitable accuracy — the quantitative targets stated in the problem as posed.
why: It enables realistic simulations of interface chemistry and electrically driven materials processing, where charge transfer across dissimilar phases governs the behavior.
key_works: Ko et al. (2021), “A fourth-generation high-dimensional neural network potential with accurate electrostatics including non-local charge transfer,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-020-20427-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-20427-2).

title: Predicting long-trajectory model failure
open: Can we predict, before deployment, whether an interatomic model will remain physically faithful over long molecular-dynamics trajectories — including rare dynamical excursions that never appear in held-out static tests?
status: A 2026 CdSe nanocluster benchmark (Usman et al. (2026), "Benchmarking Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials for Dynamical Stability in Inorganic Semiconductor Nanocrystals: A CdSe Case Study," [arXiv:2609.15299](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15299)) finds that low force error does not rank dynamical robustness; its findings do not yet establish general diagnostics.
solved_when: A checkable diagnostic exists that predicts, prior to simulation, whether a model's long trajectories will stay physically faithful, going beyond static held-out force-error metrics and validated beyond the 2026 CdSe nanocluster benchmark.
why: Without such a predictor, unstable trajectories can silently corrupt the material properties computed from them; with it, model reliability could be certified before expensive simulations are run.
key_works: Usman et al. (2026), “Benchmarking Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials for Dynamical Stability in Inorganic Semiconductor Nanocrystals: A CdSe Case Study,” [arXiv:2609.15299](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15299).

title: Uncertainty on material observables
open: Can we propagate the uncertainty of atomistic models into calibrated confidence intervals for the macroscopic observables that materials simulations actually report — free energies, diffusion constants, nucleation rates, and phase boundaries? The challenge is to do so rigorously even when the observables come from biased sampling schemes and the underlying model errors are correlated.
status: Ensembles and Bayesian approaches currently quantify local prediction uncertainty, but calibrated uncertainty on nonlinear trajectory-derived observables remains substantially harder. Grasselli et al. (2025), "Uncertainty in the era of machine learning for atomistic modeling," [DOI:10.1039/D5DD00102A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5DD00102A).
solved_when: A framework exists that delivers calibrated (e.g., coverage-guaranteed) uncertainty intervals for trajectory-derived observables — free energies, diffusion constants, nucleation rates, and phase boundaries — correctly accounting for biased sampling and correlated model errors.
why: It would make simulation-driven materials decisions quantitatively defensible, replacing point predictions with trustworthy error bars on the quantities experiments and design decisions depend on.
key_works: Grasselli et al. (2025), “Uncertainty in the era of machine learning for atomistic modeling,” [DOI:10.1039/D5DD00102A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5DD00102A).

title: Rare-event simulations without missing pathways
open: Can we drive atomistic simulation to experimental timescales while still guaranteeing that the rare events we observe reflect the true rate distribution — including important transitions missing from whatever event catalogue the method learned or enumerated?
status: Hyperdynamics, parallel replicas, and kinetic Monte Carlo extend simulated timescales, but their validity depends on basin separation and on the event catalogue covering all relevant transitions, as surveyed in Voter, Montalenti and Germann (2002), "Extending the Time Scale in Atomistic Simulation of Materials," [DOI:10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112601.141541](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112601.141541).
solved_when: An accelerated simulation method reaches experimental timescales while provably preserving rate distributions and detecting important pathways omitted from the learned or enumerated event catalogue. (No quantitative targets are stated in the record; this is the natural criterion.)
why: It would let us predict aging, segregation, corrosion, and phase changes before the long experiments needed to observe them finish.
key_works: Voter, Montalenti and Germann (2002), “Extending the Time Scale in Atomistic Simulation of Materials,” [DOI:10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112601.141541](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112601.141541).

title: Predictive phase-field kinetic coefficients
open: Can interface mobilities and evolution laws in phase-field models be derived from atomistic theory with genuine predictive power — that is, transferable across composition, temperature, and driving force without refitting to each new microstructure experiment?
status: Phase-field modeling is mature for many processes, but kinetic inputs, coarse-graining choices, and memory effects often remain phenomenological. Chen (2002), “Phase-Field Models for Microstructure Evolution,” [DOI:10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112001.132041](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112001.132041).
solved_when: A derivation exists that yields coarse-grained kinetic coefficients and evolution laws from atomistics which reproduce observed microstructure evolution across varied compositions, temperatures, and driving forces with no per-experiment refitting.
why: It would connect atomic-scale mechanisms to manufacturing-scale microstructure prediction, replacing phenomenological inputs with predictive ones.
key_works: Chen (2002), “Phase-Field Models for Microstructure Evolution,” [DOI:10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112001.132041](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.matsci.32.112001.132041).

title: Cross-code precision beyond equations of state
open: Can the electronic-structure community extend the kind of reproducible cross-code agreement already achieved for equations of state to other materials observables — defects, magnetic states, forces, response tensors, and excited-state quantities — under equivalent physical assumptions and convergence criteria?
status: Large equation-of-state verification exercises demonstrate substantial agreement among codes, but that success does not certify every materials observable. A leading example is Bosoni et al. (2024; online 2023), "How to verify the precision of density-functional-theory implementations via reproducible and universal workflows," [DOI:10.1038/s42254-023-00655-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42254-023-00655-3).
solved_when: Reproducible cross-code reference results exist for defects, magnetic states, forces, response tensors, and excited-state quantities, with all codes agreeing under equivalent physical assumptions and convergence criteria.
why: It separates numerical implementation disagreement from genuine physical-model error, telling researchers whether a discrepancy reflects a bug or approximation in a code or a limitation of the underlying theory.
key_works: Bosoni et al. (2024; online 2023), “How to verify the precision of density-functional-theory implementations via reproducible and universal workflows,” [DOI:10.1038/s42254-023-00655-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42254-023-00655-3).

title: Reusable negative-synthesis data
open: Can the community build reusable, interoperable datasets of failed and partially successful materials syntheses — complete with full recipes, detection limits, precursor history, and reasons for failure — that enable prospective cross-laboratory learning?
status: Raccuglia et al. (2016), “Machine-learning-assisted materials discovery using failed experiments,” [DOI:10.1038/nature17439](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17439), demonstrated the value of failed experiments, but broad, comparable failure coverage remains sparse.
solved_when: A broadly shared, interoperable failure dataset exists that contains complete recipes, detection limits, precursor history, and failure reasons, and demonstrably supports prospective cross-laboratory learning rather than retrospective analysis alone.
why: Such data reveals the boundaries of synthesizability and reduces repeated failed experiments across labs.
key_works: Raccuglia et al. (2016), “Machine-learning-assisted materials discovery using failed experiments,” [DOI:10.1038/nature17439](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17439).

title: Prospective materials-discovery benchmarks
open: Can we build materials-discovery benchmarks that test algorithms on chemistry they have never seen and on prospective synthesis outcomes, rather than on data already present in training databases? Such a benchmark would separately score stable-crystal prediction, novelty, synthesizability, and useful measured performance.
status: Matbench Discovery, from Riebesell et al. (2025), “A framework to evaluate machine learning crystal stability predictions,” [DOI:10.1038/s42256-025-01055-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-025-01055-1), provides a concrete benchmark for crystal-stability prediction; however, database leakage, experimental validation, and broader discovery utility remain unevaluated and require additional evaluation layers.
solved_when: A public evaluation exists in which discovery algorithms are assessed on genuinely unseen chemistry and prospective synthesis outcomes, with stable-crystal prediction, novelty, synthesizability, and useful measured performance reported as distinct metrics resistant to database leakage.
why: Without it, benchmark leaderboard gains get mistaken for real progress in discovering new, synthesizable, useful materials.
key_works: Riebesell et al. (2025), “A framework to evaluate machine learning crystal stability predictions,” [DOI:10.1038/s42256-025-01055-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-025-01055-1).

title: Specimen-to-process provenance across databases
open: Can a physical specimen's identity — its composition, processing history, microstructure, measurements, uncertainty, and subsequent modifications — be tracked coherently across databases through machine-readable identities and shared semantics?
status: The OPTIMADE standardizes access to materials databases, but comprehensive experimental process and specimen provenance remains a wider interoperability task.
solved_when: A framework of machine-readable specimen identities and semantics exists that links composition, processing history, microstructure, measurements, uncertainty, and modifications for specimens across materials databases.
why: It enables reproducibility and allows researchers to learn from actual manufactured materials rather than isolated database entries.
key_works: Andersen et al. (2021), “OPTIMADE, an API for exchanging materials data,” [DOI:10.1038/s41597-021-00974-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-021-00974-z); Wilkinson et al. (2016), “The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship,” [DOI:10.1038/sdata.2016.18](https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2016.18).

title: Laboratory-independent executable recipes
open: Transfer a materials synthesis protocol between laboratories and robotic platforms while preserving the relevant thermal, mixing, atmosphere, and precursor-state histories within measured tolerances. In other words, can a recipe's nominal settings be translated into equivalent physical histories on a different platform, so the same material outcome is reproduced?
status: Autonomous laboratories can execute specialized workflows, but translating nominal recipe settings into equivalent physical histories across platforms remains unresolved. See Tom et al. (2024), "Self-Driving Laboratories for Chemistry and Materials Science," [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055); related threads include transfer across robotic embodiments and system identification under hidden state in control theory.
solved_when: A synthesis protocol executed on one autonomous laboratory or robotic platform is carried out on a different one such that the thermal, mixing, atmosphere, and precursor-state histories remain within measured tolerances, as specified for the protocol.
why: Turns one laboratory's success into repeatable production knowledge: a synthesis that works in a single lab becomes transferable production knowledge rather than a site-specific artifact.
key_works: Tom et al. (2024), “Self-Driving Laboratories for Chemistry and Materials Science,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.4c00055).

title: Autonomous phase identification with unknown phases
open: Can an autonomous materials laboratory reliably determine, from noisy diffraction data, which phases are actually present — including phases absent from any known structural library — without confusing texture, disorder, mixtures, or instrument artifacts for new phases? Formally, this asks for an automated method that quantifies phase purity and performs open-set phase identification on noisy characterization data.
status: The A-Lab (Szymanski et al. (2023), "An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of inorganic materials" (current corrected title), [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w)) integrates powder synthesis and diffraction analysis, but robust identification beyond known structural libraries remains a separate unresolved requirement; its 2026 correction (Szymanski et al. (2026), "Author Correction: An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of inorganic materials," [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09992-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09992-y)) acknowledges concerns about structural identification and the interpretation of novelty.
solved_when: A method exists that, given noisy characterization data, both quantifies phase purity and identifies genuinely unmodeled phases while distinguishing them from texture, disorder, mixtures, and instrument artifacts, and that has been demonstrated within an autonomous synthesis-and-analysis loop rather than on curated data alone.
why: It prevents autonomous discovery systems from accepting misidentified products, which otherwise undermines the reliability of any materials the system claims to have synthesized.
key_works: Szymanski et al. (2023), “An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of inorganic materials” (current corrected title), [DOI:10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w); Szymanski et al. (2026), “Author Correction: An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of inorganic materials,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09992-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09992-y).

title: Continuous atomic movies of working materials
open: Can we watch atoms in three dimensions, continuously, while a material is actually working — during a nonrepeating reaction or deformation event under realistic conditions? Formally, the goal is continuous operando observation of 3D atomic rearrangements with sufficient chemical and temporal resolution to infer the underlying mechanisms.
status: Four-dimensional atomic tomography has reconstructed nucleation at successive annealing states, as in Zhou et al. (2019), "Observing crystal nucleation in four dimensions using atomic electron tomography," [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1317-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1317-x); continuous operando observation remains a more demanding target.
solved_when: A single nonrepeating event (reaction or deformation) under realistic conditions is captured as a continuous three-dimensional atomic movie in which transient intermediates and mechanisms can be inferred from the chemical and temporal resolution achieved.
why: It resolves transient intermediates and the causal evolution of defects, which are invisible to snapshots taken before and after an event.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2019), “Observing crystal nucleation in four dimensions using atomic electron tomography,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-019-1317-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1317-x).

title: Artifact-controlled hydrogen atom-probe maps
open: Can we measure how much hydrogen actually occupies specific defects in a sample, distinguishing the hydrogen that was there originally from the hydrogen introduced by specimen preparation, residual gas, field-driven migration, and detection artifacts?
