status: Isotope labeling and cryogenic transfer enable valuable observations; accurate site populations remain difficult to establish across materials and instruments. Gault et al. (2021), "Atom probe tomography," [DOI:10.1038/s43586-021-00047-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43586-021-00047-w).
solved_when: Hydrogen site occupancies at specific defects can be quantified with controlled, quantified contributions from preparation contamination, residual gas, field-driven migration, and detection artifacts, yielding accurate site populations.
why: It tests hydrogen-embrittlement and hydrogen-storage mechanisms directly.

title: Unique structure inference for disordered nanomaterials
open: What combination of scattering, spectroscopy, and microscopy suffices to identify the relevant atomic correlations of an amorphous or nanocrystalline material — and when uniqueness is impossible, what are the defensible equivalence classes of structures consistent with the data?
status: Pair-distribution analysis and joint modeling constrain structures, but multiple configurations can fit the same limited measurements. Key work: Billinge and Levin (2007), "The Problem with Determining Atomic Structure at the Nanoscale," [DOI:10.1126/science.1135080](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1135080).
solved_when: A characterization exists of which measurement combinations determine the relevant atomic correlations, together with explicit equivalence classes for the non-unique cases, validated on amorphous or nanocrystalline systems.
why: It establishes which structural claims the data can actually support, preventing overinterpretation of nanoscale structure from limited measurements.
key_works: Billinge and Levin (2007), “The Problem with Determining Atomic Structure at the Nanoscale,” [DOI:10.1126/science.1135080](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1135080).

title: Causal mechanical effect of chemical short-range order
open: Does chemical short-range order by itself measurably strengthen CrCoNi, or do the mechanical changes seen across heat treatments come from everything else that changes along the way? Formally: determine how much varying chemical short-range order alone changes yield stress, slip localization, and work hardening in CrCoNi while holding grain size, dislocation density, segregation, and contamination fixed.
status: An explicit controversy since at least 2020. Atom-probe measurements by M. He et al. (2024), "Quantifying short-range order using atom probe tomography," [DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1), quantify heat-treatment-dependent ordering, but measuring order does not itself establish its mechanical contribution. Related simulation capability comes from Y. Cao, K. Sheriff, R. Freitas (2024), "Capturing short-range order in high-entropy alloys with machine learning potentials," [arXiv:2401.06622](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.06622).
solved_when: Matched heat-treated specimens are shown to differ in ordering — independently measured, not assumed — and blinded, pre-registered predictions of the mechanical response are confirmed against experiment, isolating order as the causal variable.
why: A causal answer would make atomic-scale chemical order a controllable alloy-design variable rather than an unavoidable microstructural side effect.
key_works: M. He et al. (2024), “Quantifying short-range order using atom probe tomography,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1); Y. Cao, K. Sheriff, R. Freitas (2024), “Capturing short-range order in high-entropy alloys with machine learning potentials,” [arXiv:2401.06622](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.06622).

title: Cross-instrument short-range-order ground truth
open: Can a set of reference specimens and a shared inference benchmark be built so that atom-probe, electron, X-ray, and neutron measurements all recover the same species-resolved pair correlations, each with quantified uncertainties and identifiable detection limits?
status: The 2024 atom-probe approach of M. He et al. (2024), "Quantifying short-range order using atom probe tomography" ([DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1)), explicitly maps the regimes where neighborhood information survives detection losses and trajectory errors; equivalent reliable comparisons across measurement modalities remain a separate target.
solved_when: Reference specimens exist and a common inference benchmark demonstrates agreement in species-resolved pair correlations recovered from atom-probe, electron, X-ray, and neutron measurements, with reported uncertainties and identifiable detection limits for each modality.
why: It prevents incompatible definitions or instrument artifacts from becoming alloy-design labels.
key_works: M. He et al. (2024), “Quantifying short-range order using atom probe tomography,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-01912-1).

title: Equilibrium ordering versus segregation in refractory multicomponent alloys
open: Can we predict, from first principles, which ordered phases and decomposition products are thermodynamically stable in non-equiatomic Ti–Nb–Mo–Ta–W refractory alloys, and at what transition temperatures they appear? A complete answer must also let us tell true equilibrium apart from slow decomposition across the intended service-temperature range.
status: A 2024 electronic-structure study resolves competing ordering and segregation tendencies in specific Ti-containing systems — C. D. Woodgate and J. B. Staunton (2024), "Competition between phase ordering and phase segregation in the TiₓNbMoTaW and TiₓVNbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloys," [arXiv:2401.16243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16243) — but complete experimentally validated composition–temperature maps are still lacking.
solved_when: Experimentally validated composition–temperature maps of the stable ordered phases, decomposition products, and transition temperatures exist for non-equiatomic Ti–Nb–Mo–Ta–W alloys, covering the intended service-temperature range and distinguishing genuine equilibrium from slow decomposition.
why: It prevents the selection of alloys that appear strong initially but decompose during prolonged service at temperature.
key_works: C. D. Woodgate and J. B. Staunton (2024), “Competition between phase ordering and phase segregation in the TiₓNbMoTaW and TiₓVNbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloys,” [arXiv:2401.16243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.16243).

title: Grain-boundary segregation beyond dilute binary spectra
open: Can we predict how temperature controls which solutes occupy which grain-boundary sites across the full distribution of sites in a real multicomponent polycrystal — accounting for solute–solute interactions and structural changes of the boundaries themselves — without fitting a separate segregation constant for each alloy?
status: Tuchinda and Schuh computed entropy spectra for 155 dilute binary systems in 2024 (N. Tuchinda and C. A. Schuh, 2024, "Computed entropy spectra for grain boundary segregation in polycrystals," DOI:10.1038/s41524-024-01260-3); non-dilute interactions and dynamically changing boundaries extend beyond that benchmark.
solved_when: A predictive theory yields temperature-dependent site occupancies for competing solutes over the full boundary-site distribution of multicomponent polycrystals, incorporating non-dilute interactions and dynamically evolving boundary structures, with no per-alloy fitted segregation constants — thereby extending beyond the 155 dilute binary systems benchmarked by Tuchinda and Schuh (2024).
why: It connects alloy chemistry to embrittlement, grain growth, and corrosion through the actual interfaces where these phenomena occur, enabling alloy design against intergranular failure.
key_works: N. Tuchinda and C. A. Schuh (2024), “Computed entropy spectra for grain boundary segregation in polycrystals,” [DOI:10.1038/s41524-024-01260-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-024-01260-3).

title: Nanocrystalline stability under simultaneous heat and load
open: Can we design nanocrystalline alloys that keep their grain-size distribution and ductility when simultaneously subjected to prolonged heating and cyclic deformation? The design problem requires treating segregation at grain boundaries and, especially, triple junctions as part of the stabilization mechanism, rather than relying on annealing stability alone.
status: A 2024 Pt–Au study by A. K. Barnett et al. demonstrates a strong role for triple-junction segregation in grain coarsening (“Triple Junction Segregation Dominates the Stability of Nanocrystalline Alloys,” DOI:10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c02395). Its model-system result does not establish long-term stability across alloy chemistries and mechanical histories.
solved_when: An alloy is produced whose grain-size distribution and ductility remain stable under combined prolonged heating and cyclic deformation, with stabilization demonstrably arising from segregation at boundaries and triple junctions rather than annealing stability alone.
why: It preserves nanoscale strengthening in operating components, where heat and mechanical loading act together.
key_works: A. K. Barnett et al. (2024), “Triple Junction Segregation Dominates the Stability of Nanocrystalline Alloys,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c02395](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c02395).

title: Long-life strength–ductility balance in refractory alloys
open: Can a refractory concentrated alloy retain useful tensile ductility and fracture resistance after prolonged high-temperature exposure, creep, and realistic oxygen uptake — and can the same composition be qualified across this entire service envelope?
status: Huang et al. (2026) reported Nb₄Ta₄V₃Ti with about 1 GPa room-temperature yield strength, nearly 20% uniform strain, and 500 MPa tensile strength at 1,000 °C ("Achieving high tensile strength and ductility in refractory alloys by tuning electronic structure," DOI:10.1038/s41563-025-02464-8). These are tensile benchmarks; long-life service qualification remains open.
solved_when: One alloy composition is qualified across the full service envelope — prolonged high-temperature exposure, creep, and realistic oxygen uptake — while retaining useful tensile ductility and fracture resistance.
why: It enables hotter load-bearing components without sacrificing manufacturability.
key_works: H. Huang et al. (2026), “Achieving high tensile strength and ductility in refractory alloys by tuning electronic structure,” [DOI:10.1038/s41563-025-02464-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-025-02464-8).

title: Repeated high-grade aluminium recycling with variable impurities
open: Can mixed automotive aluminium scrap be recycled through repeated closed loops while keeping fracture, fatigue, corrosion, and forming performance under control as the Fe, Cu, Zn, and Si inventories shift from cycle to cycle, without requiring more primary-metal dilution each time around? Formally, this asks for a recycling route in which product properties remain within specification over multiple loops despite evolving impurity composition, at constant or decreasing primary-metal input.
status: Krall et al. (2026) demonstrated direct whole-vehicle-scrap upcycling under industrially relevant processing conditions ("Direct aluminium-alloy upcycling from entire end-of life vehicles," [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-69492-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69492-z)). Repeated-loop impurity evolution and the full product-property envelope remain open targets.
solved_when: Repeated closed recycling loops of mixed automotive aluminium are demonstrated in which the full product-property envelope — fracture, fatigue, corrosion, and forming performance — stays controlled as Fe, Cu, Zn, and Si inventories change, without increasing primary-metal dilution per cycle.
why: It would convert the demonstrated single-pass upcycling route into a durable circular material system for automotive aluminium, so that scrap streams do not progressively lose value or demand growing primary-metal inputs.
key_works: P. Krall et al. (2026), “Direct aluminium-alloy upcycling from entire end-of life vehicles,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-69492-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69492-z).

title: Recrystallization prediction with competing solute drag and precipitation
open: Can we predict recrystallized fraction and grain-size distributions in microalloyed steels across changing thermomechanical schedules using only independently measured inputs — boundary mobilities, segregation behavior, and precipitation kinetics — rather than parameters fitted to the recrystallization data itself?
status: Physically based models coupling precipitation and recrystallization exist as of 2025, but they rely on mobilities and interaction parameters that are difficult to measure; transferability across residual-element inventories remains an open validation problem. Key work: M.-I. T. Tzini and G. N. Haidemenopoulos (2025), “A Physically Based Mean Field Model for Strain-Induced Precipitation and Recrystallization in High-Strength Low-Alloy Steels,” [DOI:10.1002/srin.202400493](https://doi.org/10.1002/srin.202400493).
solved_when: A model with independently determined boundary mobilities, segregation, and precipitation kinetics reproduces recrystallized fraction and grain-size distributions across changing thermomechanical schedules, including across varying residual-element inventories.
why: It would let recycled steel chemistries be accommodated through controlled processing, rather than requiring scrap-dependent revalidation of every schedule.
key_works: M.-I. T. Tzini and G. N. Haidemenopoulos (2025), “A Physically Based Mean Field Model for Strain-Induced Precipitation and Recrystallization in High-Strength Low-Alloy Steels,” [DOI:10.1002/srin.202400493](https://doi.org/10.1002/srin.202400493).

title: Full-stress-tensor screw-dislocation mobility
open: Can screw-dislocation mobility laws for body-centred-cubic alloys be derived and validated over the full applied stress tensor, across temperature and solute distributions, including non-Schmid effects at experimentally relevant rates?
status: Non-Schmid behavior is longstanding. Allera et al. calculated activation free energies in Fe and W in 2025, but explicitly restricted their treatment to resolved shear stress in the glide plane (A. Allera et al. (2025), "Activation entropy of dislocation glide in body-centered cubic metals from atomistic simulations," [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-62390-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-62390-w)).
solved_when: A mobility law is derived and validated that accounts for the full applied stress tensor (not only the resolved shear stress in the glide plane), arbitrary temperature and solute distributions, and non-Schmid effects at experimentally relevant rates.
why: It improves predictions of low-temperature brittleness and rate-dependent plastic flow in these alloys.
key_works: A. Allera et al. (2025), “Activation entropy of dislocation glide in body-centered cubic metals from atomistic simulations,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-62390-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-62390-w).

title: Intrinsic inverse Hall–Petch crossover
open: Is there a true, intrinsic grain size below which nanocrystalline metals get softer rather than stronger, and if so, what is it for a specified metal? More precisely, can the crossover between dislocation-mediated strengthening and boundary-mediated softening be measured in a way that separates it from grain growth, porosity, impurities, and strain-rate effects?
status: Atomistic predictions of softening date to 1998 (J. Schiøtz, F. D. Di Tolla, K. W. Jacobsen (1998), “Softening of nanocrystalline metals at very small grain sizes,” [DOI:10.1038/35328](https://doi.org/10.1038/35328)), and recent models still predict condition-dependent crossovers; work on triple-junction segregation (A. K. Barnett et al. (2024), “Triple Junction Segregation Dominates the Stability of Nanocrystalline Alloys,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c02395](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c02395)) addresses specimen stability, but there is still no composition- and rate-independent critical grain size that could be inserted into a universal law.
solved_when: A stable nanocrystalline specimen of a specified metal is prepared and measured under matched conditions such that the critical grain size at the strengthening–softening crossover is determined with grain growth, porosity, impurities, and strain-rate effects experimentally excluded.
why: It identifies the usable lower grain-size limit for strengthening, telling designers how fine a grain size can usefully be targeted before softening takes over.
key_works: J. Schiøtz, F. D. Di Tolla, K. W. Jacobsen (1998), “Softening of nanocrystalline metals at very small grain sizes,” [DOI:10.1038/35328](https://doi.org/10.1038/35328); A. K. Barnett et al. (2024), “Triple Junction Segregation Dominates the Stability of Nanocrystalline Alloys,” [DOI:10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c02395](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.nanolett.4c02395).

title: Quantitative competition among hydrogen-embrittlement mechanisms
open: Can we predict where a crack will initiate, how fast it will grow, and how much ductility will be lost in a given steel, starting from measured hydrogen content, microstructure, stress state, and loading rate? In formal terms, this asks for a validated mechanism-selection law that quantitatively partitions embrittlement among decohesion, localized plasticity, and vacancy generation.
status: More than a century of research has produced multiple proposed mechanisms, but none is generally validated as a mechanism-selection law. Interface protection demonstrated in 2025 (G. Hachet et al. (2025), "Protection of metal interfaces against hydrogen-assisted cracking," [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6)) improves resistance but does not resolve which mechanism dominates under given conditions.
solved_when: For a specified steel and measured inputs (hydrogen, microstructure, stress, loading rate), the framework predicts crack-initiation location, growth rate, and ductility loss with quantitative resolution of the competing contributions of decohesion, localized plasticity, and vacancy generation, and this prediction is generally validated.
why: It would replace broad susceptibility labels with usable failure predictions, enabling real design and lifetime decisions for hydrogen-exposed steels.
key_works: G. Hachet et al. (2025), “Protection of metal interfaces against hydrogen-assisted cracking,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67310-6).

title: Stress-corrosion initiation under heterogeneous salt deposits
open: Can we predict when and where stress-corrosion cracks will initiate beneath spatially heterogeneous salt deposits during wet–dry cycling? Formally, the goal is a predictive distribution of initiation times and locations that accounts for local electrolyte chemistry, residual stress, and surface microstructure.
status: The 2025 study by Elsherkesis et al. isolates deposit-pattern effects [M. Elsherkisi et al. (2025), “Effect of salt deposition patterns on stress corrosion cracking,” DOI:10.1038/s41529-025-00650-2], but extrapolating from uniformly coated laboratory coupons to irregular service deposits remains a separate, unsolved problem.
solved_when: A validated predictive model reproduces the observed distribution of crack-initiation times and locations under irregular, service-representative salt deposits subjected to wet–dry cycling, incorporating local electrolyte chemistry, residual stress, and surface microstructure.
why: It would make exposure-specific corrosion management possible for real components, replacing extrapolations from idealized laboratory conditions.
key_works: M. Elsherkisi et al. (2025), “Effect of salt deposition patterns on stress corrosion cracking,” [DOI:10.1038/s41529-025-00650-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41529-025-00650-2).

title: Rare-event fatigue initiation from measured microstructure
open: Can we predict the low-probability tail of fatigue-initiation life for components whose microtextured regions, inclusions, and residual stresses have actually been measured — and keep that calibration valid when the component volume or the loading waveform changes?
status: A 2026 multiscale platform connects location-specific microstructure to probabilistic dwell-fatigue nucleation in titanium; general tail calibration across manufactured populations remains the target. Key work: S. Ghosh and collaborators (2026), “Parametrically upscaled model-based predictive platform for fatigue with location-specific microstructural linkages,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-72037-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72037-z).
solved_when: A validated model predicts the rare-event tail of fatigue-initiation life from measured microstructural inputs, with tail calibration retained under changes in component volume and loading waveform.
why: It reduces uncertainty in allowable lifetimes without overlooking rare early failures.
key_works: S. Ghosh and collaborators (2026), “Parametrically upscaled model-based predictive platform for fatigue with location-specific microstructural linkages,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-72037-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72037-z).

title: Microstructurally short-crack arrest under changing loads
open: Can we predict, from the actual microstructure, whether a microstructurally short fatigue crack will arrest at, deflect along, or escape a grain-scale barrier when the applied load amplitude varies over time? A successful theory would use the real microstructure and the evolving crack-closure state rather than a long-crack threshold alone.
status: Short cracks have long been known to grow below long-crack thresholds. In 2025, surface-strain and roughness indicators improved prospective path prediction in nickel (Valiollahi et al. (2025), "Combining Effective Plastic Strain and Surface Roughness for Predicting Future Propagation Path of Microstructure-Sensitive Crack (MSC) in Polycrystalline Nickel," [DOI:10.1111/ffe.14462](https://doi.org/10.1111/ffe.14462)); load-history-dependent arrest remains an additional requirement beyond that state of the art.
solved_when: A predictive criterion or model determines arrest, deflection, or escape of a short crack at a grain-scale barrier under variable-amplitude loading, incorporating the actual microstructure and evolving crack closure rather than relying solely on the long-crack threshold; in particular, load-history-dependent arrest must be captured.
why: It connects inspection-sized defects to the early fatigue damage that controls structural life, making short-crack behavior predictable where long-crack thresholds fail.
key_works: Valiollahi et al. (2025), “Combining Effective Plastic Strain and Surface Roughness for Predicting Future Propagation Path of Microstructure-Sensitive Crack (MSC) in Polycrystalline Nickel,” [DOI:10.1111/ffe.14462](https://doi.org/10.1111/ffe.14462).

title: Ductile fracture after non-proportional loading
open: Can ductile failure after non-proportional loading — compression followed by tension, or shear paths that change direction — be predicted from the underlying micromechanics of void nucleation, growth, and strain localization rather than from a fracture locus recalibrated for each path? In other words, when does a single evolving-damage model of void populations and particle cracking transfer across load histories?
status: A 2025 computational study shows why modeling growth from an initial void fraction alone misses some compression-before-tension behavior, and identifies void nucleation and loading history as essential unresolved ingredients for transfer. Key work: M. Kristoffersen et al. (2025), “Ductile failure by strain localisation: A computational study of materials and structures subjected to highly non-proportional load histories,” [DOI:10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2024.113128](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2024.113128).
solved_when: A predictive model exists that reproduces both the failure strain and the fracture location for compression–tension and changing shear histories from evolving void populations, particle cracking, and strain localization, without fitting a separate fracture locus to each loading path.
why: It would put forming limits, crashworthiness prediction, and the integrity assessment of dented structures on a transferable footing, replacing case-by-case calibration with a mechanism-based prediction.
key_works: M. Kristoffersen et al. (2025), “Ductile failure by strain localisation: A computational study of materials and structures subjected to highly non-proportional load histories,” [DOI:10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2024.113128](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2024.113128).

title: Creep-cavity nucleation over service timescales
open: Can we predict when and where creep cavities nucleate and coalesce on grain boundaries — from the local grain-boundary character, precipitate population, stress state, and aging history — and can those predictions be transferred from accelerated tests to the long, low-stress exposures of real service? Formally, this asks for a validated nucleation-rate model whose extrapolation across the large gap between test and service conditions is quantitatively reliable.
status: Correlative microscopy in 2024 linked cavities in ex-service 316H steel to local microstructure statistically (T. L. Martin and collaborators, 2024, “A correlative approach to evaluating the links between local microstructural parameters and creep initiated cavities,” [DOI:10.1016/j.matdes.2024.112905](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2024.112905)). Correlation maps still need validated nucleation rates and time extrapolation.
solved_when: A model exists that predicts cavity emergence and coalescence from grain-boundary character, precipitates, local stress, and aging, with validated nucleation rates and demonstrated time extrapolation from accelerated tests to long low-stress service exposures.
why: It would let engineers defensibly extend the life of high-temperature structures instead of relying on conservative correlation maps alone.
key_works: T. L. Martin and collaborators (2024), “A correlative approach to evaluating the links between local microstructural parameters and creep initiated cavities,” [DOI:10.1016/j.matdes.2024.112905](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2024.112905).

title: Adhesive-wear transition with real surface chemistry
open: Can we predict, from measurable interfacial properties, when sliding contact on oxidized, chemically heterogeneous engineering surfaces shifts from plastic smoothing of asperities to detachment of wear debris? The prediction should rest on real surface chemistry rather than on tuned model potentials.
status: Aghababaei et al. established a critical-junction-length framework in 2016 (R. Aghababaei, D. H. Warner, J.-F. Molinari (2016), “Critical length scale controls adhesive wear mechanisms,” [DOI:10.1038/ncomms11816](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms11816)); realistic oxidation, lubrication, and evolving tribomaterial layers were outside its explicit simulation scope. Work on weak interfaces has since offered insight via an amorphous model system (T. Brink and J.-F. Molinari (2019), “Adhesive wear mechanisms in the presence of weak interfaces: Insights from an amorphous model system,” [arXiv:1901.07466](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.07466)).
solved_when: A quantitative criterion for the transition between plastic asperity smoothing and debris detachment is derived that uses only measurable interfacial properties and is validated for oxidized, chemically heterogeneous surfaces.
why: It identifies when contact causes permanent material loss, which underpins surface durability in engineering components.
key_works: R. Aghababaei, D. H. Warner, J.-F. Molinari (2016), “Critical length scale controls adhesive wear mechanisms,” [DOI:10.1038/ncomms11816](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms11816); T. Brink and J.-F. Molinari (2019), “Adhesive wear mechanisms in the presence of weak interfaces: Insights from an amorphous model system,” [arXiv:1901.07466](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.07466).

title: Predictive steady-state wear without an empirical wear coefficient
open: Can wear volume and debris-size distributions at steady state be predicted from contact geometry and material properties alone, with no empirically fitted wear coefficient? A complete theory would have to account for debris aggregation, recirculation, escape, and surface renewal within the third-body layer.
status: Archard-type wear coefficients remain useful empirical quantities. Pham-Ba and Molinari modeled formation and aggregation regimes in a third-body layer in 2023 (S. Pham-Ba and J.-F. Molinari (2023), “Role of minimum adhesive wear particle size in third-body layer properties,” [arXiv:2304.14783](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14783)), but scale and dimensionality limit direct transfer to real components. The empirical baseline traces to J. F. Archard (1953), “Contact and Rubbing of Flat Surfaces,” [DOI:10.1063/1.1721448](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1721448).
solved_when: A validated predictive model outputs macroscopic wear volume and debris-size distributions from contact geometry and material properties alone, with no empirically fitted wear coefficient, and captures debris aggregation, recirculation, escape, and surface renewal.
why: It would allow material selection for sliding contacts without repeating every sliding experiment, replacing trial-and-error wear testing with first-principles prediction.
key_works: J. F. Archard (1953), “Contact and Rubbing of Flat Surfaces,” [DOI:10.1063/1.1721448](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1721448); S. Pham-Ba and J.-F. Molinari (2023), “Role of minimum adhesive wear particle size in third-body layer properties,” [arXiv:2304.14783](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14783).

title: Separating chemical and mechanical frictional aging
open: How much of the observed strengthening of a frictional contact with time comes from chemical bond formation at the interface, from creep-driven growth of real contact area, and from capillary bridges — and can we predict the resulting rate-and-state friction parameters from independently controlled humidity, temperature, and load histories?
status: Li et al. directly demonstrated chemical-bond contributions to frictional aging in 2011 (Q. Li, T. E. Tullis, D. Goldsby, R. W. Carpick (2011), "Frictional ageing from interfacial bonding and the origins of rate and state friction," [DOI:10.1038/nature10589](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10589)). Later nanoindentation and humidity studies show that the operative mechanism depends on material and contact conditions.
solved_when: A quantitative decomposition of frictional aging into bond-formation, contact-area creep, and capillary-bridge contributions is obtained over controlled humidity, temperature, and load histories, and the resulting rate-and-state parameters are predicted from that decomposition.
why: It would connect empirical friction laws to surface treatments and environmental control, letting aging behavior be engineered rather than merely fitted.
key_works: Q. Li, T. E. Tullis, D. Goldsby, R. W. Carpick (2011), “Frictional ageing from interfacial bonding and the origins of rate and state friction,” [DOI:10.1038/nature10589](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10589).

title: Load-bearing superlubricity in contaminated ambient conditions
open: Can a structurally superlubric interface keep its near-zero friction over macroscopic sliding distances and realistic loads when exposed to dust particles, humidity cycling, misalignment, and progressive wear?
status: A 2026 graphite–silica device (C. Chen et al. (2026), “Structural superlubricity triboelectric nanogenerator with negligible wear and high triboelectrification efficiency,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-74450-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-74450-w)) reported a friction coefficient of 0.0034 and stable electrical operation beyond 110,000 cycles, but at a specially prepared microscopic interface; general macroscopic-bearing performance remains open.
solved_when: A device maintains superlubricity over macroscopic travel under practical loads despite particles, humidity cycling, misalignment, and wear, with a specified lifetime and independently repeated friction measurements.
why: It would cut frictional energy losses and wear in practical moving interfaces, enabling durable low-loss bearings outside laboratory-perfect conditions.
key_works: C. Chen et al. (2026), “Structural superlubricity triboelectric nanogenerator with negligible wear and high triboelectrification efficiency,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-74450-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-74450-w).

title: Predicting protective tribofilm growth and failure
open: Can we predict when a lubricant chemistry forms, repairs, or loses a protective tribofilm under realistic pressure, temperature, and intermittent sliding histories? In particular, this calls for a theory that accounts for antagonistic interactions among additives across the full formulation-to-lifetime chain.
status: Single-asperity experiments have resolved tribofilm growth mechanisms (N. N. Gosvani et al. (2015), “Mechanisms of antiwear tribofilm growth revealed in situ by single-asperity sliding contacts,” [DOI:10.1126/science.1258788](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1258788)), and 2025 diester experiments generated graphitic films with reduced friction and wear (W. Song et al. (2025), “In-situ catalysis of green lubricants into graphitic carbon by iron single atoms to reduce friction and wear,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58292-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58292-6)). These are mechanistic building blocks for a still-incomplete formulation-to-lifetime prediction method.
solved_when: A validated formulation-to-lifetime prediction method exists that forecasts tribofilm growth, repair, and failure under realistic pressure, temperature, and intermittent sliding histories, including antagonistic additive interactions.
why: It would enable lubricant design that predicts service protection and depletion, rather than relying on empirical trial-and-error for durability.
key_works: N. N. Gosvami et al. (2015), “Mechanisms of antiwear tribofilm growth revealed in situ by single-asperity sliding contacts,” [DOI:10.1126/science.1258788](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1258788); W. Song et al. (2025), “In-situ catalysis of green lubricants into graphitic carbon by iron single atoms to reduce friction and wear,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58292-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58292-6).

title: Coupled fretting wear and fatigue across slip regimes
open: Can crack-initiation life be predicted as a fretting contact transitions between partial and gross slip, while wear continuously reshapes the contact geometry, friction, and residual stress — and can such a model be validated on joint geometries it has never seen?
status: Comparative 2024 critical-plane studies and coupled damage models improve selected fretting tests, but rankings and predictive accuracy depend on the contact regime and model choices; see Shu et al. (2024), “A comparative study of several life prediction models based on the critical plane approach for fretting fatigue crack initiation,” [DOI:10.1111/ffe.14256](https://doi.org/10.1111/ffe.14256).
solved_when: A coupled wear–fatigue model predicts crack-initiation life across the partial-to-gross-slip transition on previously unseen joint geometries, with accuracy that does not degrade from the contact regime or model choices.
why: It turns fretting-fatigue life prediction from a regime-dependent curve fit into a transferable tool, improving lifetime estimates for joints, connectors, and contacting structural components.
key_works: Shu et al. (2024), “A comparative study of several life prediction models based on the critical plane approach for fretting fatigue crack initiation,” [DOI:10.1111/ffe.14256](https://doi.org/10.1111/ffe.14256).

title: Detecting crack-like lack-of-fusion defects in complex parts
open: Can we reliably detect thin, crack-like lack-of-fusion defects buried deep in thick or geometrically inaccessible metal additively manufactured parts, even when the defects lie in unfavorable orientations and the surfaces are realistically rough? The goal is to establish calibrated probability-of-detection curves for such defects across realistic part geometries and conditions.
status: NIST's ongoing 2026 program explicitly targets reference anomaly images, nondestructive testing, and probability-of-detection measurements; nominal density alone does not certify defect absence. Key work: NIST (updated 2026), "Measurement Science for Additive Manufacturing Program," [program](https://www.nist.gov/programs-projects/measurement-science-additive-manufacturing-program).
solved_when: Calibrated detection probabilities exist for thin, irregular lack-of-fusion defects throughout thick or geometrically inaccessible metal-AM parts, covering unfavorable defect orientations and realistic surface roughness.
why: It makes inspection results usable in component qualification and reliability calculations, so that nominal density measurements alone no longer stand in for certified defect absence.
key_works: NIST (updated 2026), “Measurement Science for Additive Manufacturing Program,” [program](https://www.nist.gov/programs-projects/measurement-science-additive-manufacturing-program).

title: Hot-cracking-resistant AM alloys without lost service performance
open: Can an alloy's composition and its additive-manufacturing processing path be co-designed so that solidification (hot) cracking is eliminated in demanding multicomponent systems, without sacrificing the creep, corrosion, or fatigue performance the alloy needs after heat treatment? In other words, can printability and in-service properties be treated as joint design objectives rather than competing constraints?
status: Sheikh et al. screened 3,876 Co–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ni compositions in 2025 using printability and phase criteria; validation concentrated on a particular alloy and simplified processing conditions.
solved_when: A multicomponent alloy is demonstrated, through combined compositional screening and process design, to print free of solidification cracking under the intended processing conditions while retaining the required creep, corrosion, or fatigue properties after heat treatment.
why: It expands the range of high-performance alloys that can be reliably printed, rather than restricting additive manufacturing to alloys chosen for printability alone.
key_works: S. Sheikh et al. (2025), “High-throughput alloy and process design for metal additive manufacturing,” [DOI:10.1038/s41524-025-01670-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41524-025-01670-x); [arXiv:2304.04149](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.04149).

title: Predicting residual stress through cutting and heat treatment
open: Can we predict the full spatial residual-stress tensor field and resulting distortion in an additively manufactured part as it moves through the entire process chain — deposition, support removal, machining, and heat treatment — with quantified uncertainty that holds up on part geometries not used to calibrate the model? In formal terms, the goal is a validated forward model of path-dependent stress evolution over the complete manufacturing sequence, not merely over selected stages.
status: AM Bench provides measured stresses and released-part deflections that can serve as validation targets, including 2025 synchrotron measurements of IN718 artifacts reported by T. Phan et al. (2025), "Elastic residual strain measurements of 3D additively manufactured builds of nickel alloy 718 AM Bench 2022 artifacts using energy dispersive synchrotron X-ray diffraction," [NIST bibliography and data](https://www.nist.gov/ambench/direct-am-bench-data-links-and-referencing-guidance). These data validate selected stages of the process chain; full-sequence transfer to new geometries remains open.
solved_when: Predicted residual-stress tensors and released-part deflections agree with measurements across the complete deposition-to-heat-treatment sequence, with stated uncertainty bounds verified on new part geometries rather than only on the calibration artifacts.
why: Without full-sequence prediction, dimensional control and structural-integrity assessments after manufacture rest on partial stage validations; with it, distortion can be managed and load-bearing integrity meaningfully certified.
key_works: T. Phan et al. (2025), “Elastic residual strain measurements of 3D additively manufactured builds of nickel alloy 718 AM Bench 2022 artifacts using energy dispersive synchrotron X-ray diffraction,” [NIST bibliography and data](https://www.nist.gov/ambench/direct-am-bench-data-links-and-referencing-guidance).

title: Joint surface–pore control of AM fatigue
open: Can fatigue life in additively manufactured parts be predicted from the coupled effects of surface valleys, near-surface pores, microstructure, and residual stress — and can we identify the point at which polishing or pore removal stops helping because a different initiation mechanism has taken over?
status: Qu et al. demonstrated high fatigue resistance through near-void-free titanium printing in 2024; however, transferable defect-to-fatigue relations across surfaces and component volumes remain incomplete. Key work: Z. Qu et al. (2024), "High fatigue resistance in a titanium alloy via near-void-free 3D printing," [DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07048-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07048-1).
solved_when: A transferable model is available that predicts fatigue life from interacting surface and pore (defect) populations together with microstructure and residual stress, and that identifies when further polishing or pore removal yields no further life improvement because another initiation mechanism dominates.
why: It directs processing and finishing effort toward the defects that actually limit lifetime, rather than wasting resources on mechanisms that no longer control failure.
key_works: Z. Qu et al. (2024), “High fatigue resistance in a titanium alloy via near-void-free 3D printing,” [DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07048-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07048-1).

title: Powder-reuse retirement criteria based on properties
open: When should reused Ti–6Al–4V powder be refreshed or retired? Establish property-based criteria — using oxygen content, morphology, contamination, and process signatures — that predict fracture and fatigue performance of built parts, replacing the current reliance on a fixed reuse count.
status: Zhuo et al. (2025) tracked powder morphology, oxygen uptake, and mechanical property changes during reuse in laser powder bed fusion. Existing reuse-count results depend on handling history and cannot automatically transfer among machines or replenishment policies. Key work: Z. Zhuo, R. Ji, L. Wang, J. Mao (2025), "Reusability of Ti-6Al-4V powder in laser powder bed fusion: Influence on powder morphology, oxygen uptake, and mechanical properties," [DOI:10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2024.118672](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2024.118672).
solved_when: A validated criterion exists that determines refresh-or-retire decisions from measurable powder properties (oxygen, morphology, contamination, and process signatures) that demonstrably predict fracture and fatigue properties, rather than a reuse count.
why: It would reduce powder waste without accepting an unmeasured loss of component reliability.
key_works: Z. Zhuo, R. Ji, L. Wang, J. Mao (2025), “Reusability of Ti-6Al-4V powder in laser powder bed fusion: Influence on powder morphology, oxygen uptake, and mechanical properties,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2024.118672](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2024.118672).

title: Transferable AM qualification across machines
open: Which calibrated machine observables and material descriptors are sufficient to let a qualified additive-manufacturing process be transferred between machines and sites while preserving the part property distributions — that is, can transfer be demonstrated without repeating the entire original qualification campaign?
status: NIST’s 2026 program still identifies machine calibration, variability, and process/part qualification as research needs, and parameter-name equivalence alone does not establish process equivalence. Key work: NIST (updated 2026), “Measurement Science for Additive Manufacturing Program,” [program](https://www.nist.gov/programs-projects/measurement-science-additive-manufacturing-program).
solved_when: A demonstrated set of calibrated machine observables and material descriptors is shown to suffice for transferring a qualified process between machines and sites while preserving property distributions, without redoing the full original qualification campaign.
why: It cuts the cost of requalification and makes distributed production across sites credible.
key_works: NIST (updated 2026), “Measurement Science for Additive Manufacturing Program,” [program](https://www.nist.gov/programs-projects/measurement-science-additive-manufacturing-program).

title: Shared AM sensor-to-defect-to-lifetime benchmarks
open: Can we build a shared benchmark that links in-situ monitoring signals, ex-situ tomography and microstructure data, and measured component lifetimes for the very same additively manufactured specimens — so that the full sensor-to-defect-to-lifetime chain can be evaluated on common ground?
status: AM Bench 2025 has added public tensile and rotating-bending fatigue datasets, including "AMB2025-03 High-Cycle Rotating Bending Fatigue Tests of PBF-L Ti-6Al-4V," NIST (2025), [DOI:10.18434/mds2-3734](https://doi.org/10.18434/mds2-3734); see also NIST, [AM Bench data and referencing guidance](https://www.nist.gov/ambench/direct-am-bench-data-links-and-referencing-guidance). The remaining target is joined evidence spanning monitoring through failure across sites and alloys.
solved_when: Interoperable, time-registered datasets covering monitoring, tomography, microstructure, and lifetime data exist for the same specimens, including machine and powder histories and reserved cross-site evaluation cohorts.
why: Such a benchmark tests whether manufacturing observations actually predict useful component properties, turning process monitoring from a heuristic into a validated predictor of failure.
key_works: NIST (2025), “AMB2025-03 High-Cycle Rotating Bending Fatigue Tests of PBF-L Ti-6Al-4V,” [DOI:10.18434/mds2-3734](https://doi.org/10.18434/mds2-3734); NIST, [AM Bench data and referencing guidance](https://www.nist.gov/ambench/direct-am-bench-data-links-and-referencing-guidance).

title: Simultaneous closed-loop geometry and microstructure control
open: Can a closed-loop controller drive both melt-pool geometry and the final microstructure of a printed part at the same time? Formally, the goal is a control strategy with explicit constraints ensuring that a correction which improves dimensions cannot degrade porosity, texture, or mechanical properties.
status: Bayesian controller autotuning was demonstrated for LPBF in 2025 (B. Kavas et al. (2025), "In-situ controller autotuning by Bayesian optimization for closed-loop feedback control of laser powder bed fusion process," [DOI:10.1016/j.addma.2025.104641](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2025.104641); [arXiv:2406.19096](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19096)). A melt-pool control objective is still an imperfect proxy for the final material state.
solved_when: A controller is demonstrated that simultaneously regulates melt-pool geometry and final microstructure during printing, with explicit constraints that provably prevent geometry-improving corrections from worsening porosity, texture, or mechanical properties.
why: It would make real-time process control optimize component function as well as geometry, rather than shape alone.
key_works: B. Kavas et al. (2025), “In-situ controller autotuning by Bayesian optimization for closed-loop feedback control of laser powder bed fusion process,” [DOI:10.1016/j.addma.2025.104641](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2025.104641); [arXiv:2406.19096](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19096).

title: Predictable steel–copper interfaces in multimaterial printing
open: Can we design a printed steel–copper interface whose bonding and fatigue behavior are predictable rather than empirical? Formally, the goal is a 316L–copper-alloy interface with reproducible bonding and fatigue resistance, where dilution, cracking, and brittle-phase formation can be predicted across interface orientations and thermal histories.
status: Bulloch et al. (2025) combined depth profiling, microscopy, and thermodynamic modeling for 316L–CuSn10 interfaces; transferable prediction across orientations and processing histories remains open.
solved_when: A 316L–copper-alloy interface design is demonstrated with reproducible bonding and fatigue resistance, and dilution, cracking, and brittle-phase formation are predicted transferably across interface orientations and processing histories.
why: It enables integrated printed structures that combine structural strength with thermal conduction and electrical function in a single part, removing the need to join dissimilar metals after printing.
key_works: A. Bulloch et al. (2025), “Fundamental Investigation of the Interface Formation of Multi-material Additive Manufactured 316L-CuSn10 Structures,” [DOI:10.1007/s11661-025-07817-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11661-025-07817-1).

title: Weld-local hydrogen-cracking prediction
open: Can we predict, from a weld's thermal history, local phase composition, residual stress, and hydrogen transport, which crack path will be weakest and at what load it will fail — including the uncertainty arising in the heat-affected zone? A complete answer would couple these fields into a quantified prediction of the critical crack path and failure load for a heterogeneous steel weld.
status: Wijnen and collaborators linked welding simulations to heterogeneous phase-field integrity analysis in 2025, in the computational framework “A computational framework to predict weld integrity and microstructural heterogeneity: Application to hydrogen transmission” ([arXiv:2412.08217](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08217); [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264127524009080)). Broad experimental validation across weld procedures and hydrogen histories remains the target.
solved_when: A validated predictive framework exists that, given the weld's thermal history, phases, residual stress, and hydrogen transport, outputs the weakest crack path and failure load with quantified uncertainty in the heat-affected zone, and is confirmed experimentally across a broad range of weld procedures and hydrogen histories.
why: It would make weld qualification sensitive to the actual local failure mechanisms rather than conservative blanket criteria, directly informing hydrogen-pipeline integrity.
key_works: J. Wijnen and collaborators (2025), “A computational framework to predict weld integrity and microstructural heterogeneity: Application to hydrogen transmission,” [arXiv:2412.08217](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08217); [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264127524009080).

title: Hot tearing from evolving mushy-zone topology
open: Can we predict where and when hot tears nucleate and coalesce during solidification directly from measurable quantities — dendrite and interdroplet intermetallic geometry, liquid feeding, and imposed contraction — accounting for the evolving permeability of the mushy zone as solidification proceeds?
status: Han et al. directly imaged hot-tear formation in Al–Cu and Al–Cu–Fe in 2024; conventional susceptibility correlations failed to capture the influence of second phases. Key work: I. Han, S. Feng, F. Wilde, P. S. Grant, E. Liotti (2024), "Revealing hot tear formation dynamics in Al–Cu alloys with X-ray radiography," [DOI:10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119421](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119421).
solved_when: A validated model predicts hot-tear nucleation and coalescence locations from measured dendrite/intermetallic geometry, liquid feeding, and imposed contraction, including the evolution of local permeability during solidification.
why: It would reduce casting defects and enable robust use of more complex recycled alloys in casting.
key_works: I. Han, S. Feng, F. Wilde, P. S. Grant, E. Liotti (2024), “Revealing hot tear formation dynamics in Al–Cu alloys with X-ray radiography,” [DOI:10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119421](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2023.119421).

title: Room-temperature tensile ductility in bulk structural ceramics
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can a bulk, macroscopic hard oxide or covalent ceramic be made to exhibit reproducible distributed tensile plasticity at room temperature, while still retaining useful stiffness, hardness, and resistance to subcritical cracking?
status: Room-temperature deformation has been demonstrated in selected ceramics, micropillars, and nanofibers; 2025 ceramic-nanofiber results do not establish bulk tensile ductility in general structural ceramics. Key works: S. Qiang et al. (2025), “Integration of high strength, flexibility, and room-temperature plasticity in ceramic nanofibers,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58240-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58240-4); L. Liu et al. (2025), “Nanotwinned CrN ceramics with enhanced plasticity,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-61275-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61275-2).
solved_when: Macroscopic hard oxide or covalent ceramic specimens are produced that display reproducible distributed tensile plasticity at room temperature without sacrificing stiffness, hardness, or subcritical-crack resistance.
why: It would combine the environmental resistance of ceramics with substantially improved damage tolerance, opening structural uses now blocked by brittleness.
key_works: S. Qiang et al. (2025), “Integration of high strength, flexibility, and room-temperature plasticity in ceramic nanofibers,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58240-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58240-4); L. Liu et al. (2025), “Nanotwinned CrN ceramics with enhanced plasticity,” [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-61275-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61275-2).

title: True toughness design for high-entropy carbides
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can we design dense multicomponent carbide compositions whose resistance to crack growth is genuinely improved — predicted from composition and bonding while hardness is retained, and confirmed by actual fracture-mechanics tests rather than elastic-modulus proxies alone?
status: Valence-electron tuning has provided computational design directions since 2021 (D. G. Sangiovanni et al. (2021), "Enhancing plasticity in high-entropy refractory ceramics via tailoring valence electron concentration," [DOI:10.1016/j.matdes.2021.109932](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2021.109932)); 2025 UHTC potential studies broaden compositional screening (S. J. Magorrian et al. (2025), "Computational tuning of the elastic properties of low- and high-entropy ultra-high temperature ceramics," [arXiv:2512.13204](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13204)), but elastic constants alone do not determine fracture toughness.
solved_when: A composition predicted computationally to have enhanced crack-growth resistance (without loss of hardness) is synthesized dense and validated through fracture-mechanics testing, not merely elastic-constant calculations.
why: It would make compositional screening predict resistance to actual crack growth, turning elastic-design guidelines into verified toughness design.
key_works: D. G. Sangiovanni et al. (2021), “Enhancing plasticity in high-entropy refractory ceramics via tailoring valence electron concentration,” [DOI:10.1016/j.matdes.2021.109932](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2021.109932); S. J. Magorrian et al. (2025), “Computational tuning of the elastic properties of low- and high-entropy ultra-high temperature ceramics,” [arXiv:2512.13204](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13204).

title: Ceramic strength tails from actual flaw populations
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can we predict the failure probability of a full-size ceramic component from independently measured surface and volume flaw populations, when those defects are clustered, multimodal, or correlated with processing history? Formally, the question asks for a statistical framework whose extrapolation beyond coupon-size specimens to component scales is defensible rather than merely a fitted Weibull distribution.
status: Weibull statistics provide a longstanding baseline. Lamon's 2024 SiC study shows variability among inferred flaw-strength distributions and testing configurations, indicating that tail transfer requires more than fitting a distribution. Key work: J. Lamon (2024), “Investigation of Variability of Flaw Strength Distributions on Brittle SiC Ceramic,” [DOI:10.3390/ceramics7020050](https://doi.org/10.3390/ceramics7020050).
solved_when: A method exists that takes measured surface and volume flaw populations as input and yields component failure probabilities with a defensible, validated extrapolation beyond coupon sizes, demonstrably handling clustered, multimodal, or processing-correlated defects.
why: It would make reliability claims credible for large, brittle components, where coupon-scale statistics cannot be trusted to carry over directly.
key_works: J. Lamon (2024), “Investigation of Variability of Flaw Strength Distributions on Brittle SiC Ceramic,” [DOI:10.3390/ceramics7020050](https://doi.org/10.3390/ceramics7020050).

title: Thermal-shock damage with an evolving flaw network
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can we predict the residual strength of a ceramic component after repeated thermal shocks, starting from the evolving three-dimensional population of cracks, realistic heat-transfer boundary conditions, and crack–crack interactions, rather than from a single critical temperature difference? Formally, this asks for a theory that propagates damage through multiple quench cycles and outputs the retained strength as a functional of the evolving flaw network.
status: Classical thermal-shock criteria distinguish initiation and propagation, following D. P. H. Hasselman (1969), "Unified Theory of Thermal Shock Fracture Initiation and Crack Propagation in Brittle Ceramics," [DOI:10.1111/j.1151-2916.1969.tb15848.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1151-2916.1969.tb15848.x). Current ceramic-composite experiments, e.g. R. Mitra and collaborators (2025), "Resistance to cyclic oxidation and evolution of oxide scale in 2.5D and 3D Cf/SiC composites with Si-B-C added matrix," [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S095522192500487X) (2026 corrigendum should also be consulted), reveal coupled oxidation and thermal-shock degradation, making repeated-exposure prediction a separate, unresolved challenge.
solved_when: A validated predictive framework exists that computes residual strength after repeated thermal-shock exposures from the evolving 3D crack population, heat-transfer boundary conditions, and crack interactions — replacing single-critical-temperature-difference criteria.
why: It underpins the design of reusable furnaces, heat exchangers, and rapidly cycled ceramic components, where repeated-exposure lifetimes rather than first-shock thresholds govern serviceability.
key_works: D. P. H. Hasselman (1969), “Unified Theory of Thermal Shock Fracture Initiation and Crack Propagation in Brittle Ceramics,” [DOI:10.1111/j.1151-2916.1969.tb15848.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1151-2916.1969.tb15848.x); R. Mitra and collaborators (2025), “Resistance to cyclic oxidation and evolution of oxide scale in 2.5D and 3D Cf/SiC composites with Si-B-C added matrix,” [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S095522192500487X) (2026 corrigendum should also be consulted).

title: Zirconia aging-front kinetics under coupled stress and moisture
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can we predict how deep the tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation front penetrates engineered zirconia, and what it does to mechanical performance, when humid exposure and cyclic stress act together? A complete theory should account for grain-boundary dopant segregation and heterogeneous grain sizes under these coupled conditions.
status: A 2024 study by H. Reveron and collaborators, “Aging behavior of a 1.5 mol% yttria doped zirconia exhibiting optimized toughness and strength” (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0955221923007422), resolved multiple kinetic regimes in strong, tough 1.5Y-TZP using water vapor and air exposure, showing that a single accelerated-aging conversion factor cannot represent all these conditions.
solved_when: A predictive model reproduces the transformation depth and mechanical consequences of the tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation in 1.5Y-TZP under combined water vapor and air exposure with cyclic stress, resolving all observed kinetic regimes rather than relying on a single accelerated-aging conversion factor.
why: It preserves transformation toughening in zirconia components while avoiding unexpected aging damage in service — the failure mode that current single-factor accelerated tests cannot foresee.
key_works: H. Reveron and collaborators (2024), “Aging behavior of a 1.5 mol% yttria doped zirconia exhibiting optimized toughness and strength,” [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0955221923007422).

title: Uniform flash sintering of complex thick ceramics
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can complex, thick ceramic shapes be fully densified by flash sintering while keeping temperature, density, grain-size, and stoichiometry gradients bounded throughout the part — including near electrodes and geometric constrictions?
status: Ong et al. (2025), "Low-furnace-temperature flash sintering of tetragonal 1.5-mol% YSZ: Role of particle necking on grain growth," [DOI:10.1111/jace.20490](https://doi.org/10.1111/jace.20490), achieved over 99% relative density in 1.5YSZ at furnace temperatures as low as 600 °C using controlled current ramps; however, furnace temperature differs from specimen temperature, and shape-independent uniformity remains unestablished.
solved_when: A flash-sintering protocol densifies a complex, thick ceramic shape while demonstrating bounded temperature, density, grain-size, and stoichiometry gradients throughout the part, including near electrodes and geometric constrictions.
why: It cuts ceramic-processing time and furnace demands while preserving part quality; without it, flash sintering of nontrivial geometries risks gradient-driven defects that undermine reliability.
key_works: Ong et al. (2025), “Low-furnace-temperature flash sintering of tetragonal 1.5-mol% YSZ: Role of particle necking on grain growth,” [DOI:10.1111/jace.20490](https://doi.org/10.1111/jace.20490).

title: Long-duration UHTC recession under realistic oxidizing flow
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can we predict — and then suppress — how quickly an ultrahigh-temperature ceramic erodes when held above 2,000 °C in high-enthalpy oxidizing flow through repeated heating cycles? The challenge is to model the coupled physics of oxide volatilization, mechanical shear removal of the oxide scale, and evolving surface emissivity, and use that model to design materials that survive it.
status: Tsuganezawa et al. performed arc-jet exposures above 2,000 °C for 60 seconds in 2025, linking protection to oxide chemistry (M. Tsuganezawa, Y. Arai, R. Inoue (2025), "Thermodynamic Analysis on Complex Oxides Formed by Aerodynamic Heating for Ultrahigh-Temperature Ceramic Matrix Composites," [DOI:10.3390/jcs9020087](https://doi.org/10.3390/jcs9020087)). Long-duration reusable-service qualification remains open.
solved_when: A validated model reproduces measured recession of a UHTC above 2,000 °C under high-enthalpy oxidizing flow with repeated heating, and a material or protection strategy grounded in that model demonstrably suppresses recession over long-duration, reusable-service conditions.
why: It underpins durable components and reusable thermal protection systems that must survive repeated extreme-heat exposures; without it, qualification of reusable service above 2,000 °C remains empirical and out of reach.
key_works: M. Tsuganezawa, Y. Arai, R. Inoue (2025), “Thermodynamic Analysis on Complex Oxides Formed by Aerodynamic Heating for Ultrahigh-Temperature Ceramic Matrix Composites,” [DOI:10.3390/jcs9020087](https://doi.org/10.3390/jcs9020087).

title: Environmental-barrier coatings against combined steam and molten deposits
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can an environmental-barrier coating on a ceramic-matrix composite hold its adhesion and resist recession when steam, molten calcium–magnesium–aluminosilicate (CMAS) deposits, thermal cycling, and erosion act at the same time? In formal terms, the goal is a coating that survives this full coupled environment and a validated failure map that predicts degradation under the combined conditions, rather than resistance to any single exposure in isolation.
status: Rare-earth silicate coatings and chemically modified bond coats already provide substantial protection. Lee’s 2019 work addresses bond-coat oxidation, which is one of several interacting failure processes: K. N. Lee (2019; online 2018), “Yb2Si2O7 Environmental barrier coatings with reduced bond coat oxidation rates via chemical modifications for long life,” [DOI:10.1111/jace.15978](https://doi.org/10.1111/jace.15978).
solved_when: A coating demonstrates preserved adhesion and low recession under simultaneous steam, molten CMAS deposits, thermal cycling, and erosion, and the coupled failure map is validated against these combined exposures rather than isolated ones.
why: It would make ceramic-matrix composites reliable in contaminated high-temperature gas flows, where failure currently emerges from interacting degradation processes that single-exposure tests do not capture.
key_works: K. N. Lee (2019; online 2018), “Yb2Si2O7 Environmental barrier coatings with reduced bond coat oxidation rates via chemical modifications for long life,” [DOI:10.1111/jace.15978](https://doi.org/10.1111/jace.15978).

title: Multiaxial matrix-cracking laws in woven ceramic composites
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can we predict how matrix cracks multiply, how fibers bridge them, and how stiffness degrades in a woven ceramic-matrix composite under combined tension and shear? Formally, the goal is a predictive law for crack multiplication, fiber bridging, and residual stiffness under multiaxial, off-axis loading, incorporating measured woven architectures and evolving interface friction.
status: Fiber-bridging theory dates to the 1980s and remains foundational, anchored by B. Budiansky, J. W. Hutchinson, A. G. Evans (1986), "Matrix fracture in fiber-reinforced ceramics," [DOI:10.1016/0022-5096(86)90035-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-5096(86)90035-9); however, general loading in three-dimensional woven architectures requires more than the original aligned-fiber tensile model. Related directions include homogenization with evolving discontinuities and inverse identification of bridging laws.
solved_when: A theory or validated model predicts crack multiplication, fiber bridging, and residual stiffness under combined tension and shear — including off-axis loading and changing interface friction — for measured woven CMC architectures, without treating each layup and load path as a new material.
why: It allows component design without treating every layup and load path as a new material.
key_works: B. Budiansky, J. W. Hutchinson, A. G. Evans (1986), “Matrix fracture in fiber-reinforced ceramics,” [DOI:10.1016/0022-5096(86)90035-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-5096(86)90035-9).

title: Defect-free dimensional compensation in printed ceramics
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can a printed ceramic part be made to come out of sintering or pyrolysis at the right shape and size, with no cracking or closed porosity, by predicting and compensating its anisotropic shrinkage through drying, debinding, and densification? In formal terms, the goal is a compensation method — model- or data-driven — that maps a target geometry to a printable green-body geometry whose densified result meets tolerance without internal defects.
status: Eckel et al. (2016) demonstrated complex printed polymer-derived ceramics ("Additive manufacturing of polymer-derived ceramics," DOI:10.1126/science.aad2688). Subsequent processing advances reduce shrinkage in selected systems, but transferable compensation across shapes and feedstocks remains unsolved.
solved_when: A complex ceramic part produced with the compensation approach meets its geometric tolerances after drying, debinding, and sintering or pyrolysis while remaining free of internal cracks and closed porosity, and the compensation transfers across shapes and feedstocks rather than holding only for a single selected system.
why: Success would make ceramic additive manufacturing suitable for precision structural parts, where today's unpredictable shrinkage and defect formation block dimensional control.
key_works: Z. C. Eckel et al. (2016), “Additive manufacturing of polymer-derived ceramics,” [DOI:10.1126/science.aad2688](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aad2688).

title: Slag–refractory corrosion rates under evolving microstructure
subfield: Structural ceramics, ceramic composites, and refractories
open: Can we predict how fast an industrial slag corrodes a refractory lining when the slag chemistry itself is changing over the campaign — that is, derive penetration, dissolution, and spalling rates from measurable quantities such as pore connectivity, wetting behavior, reaction-layer growth, and thermal stress? A satisfactory answer would also include in situ measurement protocols capable of separating these coupled mechanisms.
status: Recent rotating-finger and high-temperature imaging studies resolve parts of the corrosion process, and 2026 digital-image-correlation work by C. Liu et al. (2026), “In-situ assessment of slag corrosion on refractories based on HT-DIC: A novel multi-dimensional index with corrosion severity,” measures coupled corrosion severity — but this severity index is not yet a transferable kinetic law. Related degradation of MgO-based linings by tundish fluxes is documented by S. C. Duan et al. (2025), “Effect of tundish fluxes on the degradation of MgO-based refractory linings in continuous casting process,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jmrt.2025.09.274](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmrt.2025.09.274).
solved_when: A validated, transferable kinetic law exists that predicts penetration, dissolution, and spalling rates under evolving slag chemistries from pore connectivity, wetting, reaction-layer growth, and thermal stress, supported by in situ measurements that separate the individual mechanisms.
why: Longer furnace-lining life with less contamination and fewer unplanned shutdowns, turning lining replacement from a reactive expense into a schedulable design decision.
key_works: C. Liu et al. (2026), “In-situ assessment of slag corrosion on refractories based on HT-DIC: A novel multi-dimensional index with corrosion severity,” [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0010938X26000569); S. C. Duan et al. (2025), “Effect of tundish fluxes on the degradation of MgO-based refractory linings in continuous casting process,” [DOI:10.1016/j.jmrt.2025.09.274](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmrt.2025.09.274).

title: Composition-resolved calcium-silicate-hydrate structure
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Can we determine the full ensemble of atomic and mesoscale structures of calcium-silicate-hydrate (C–S–H) as a function of its composition and environment — Ca/Si ratio, aluminium substitution, water activity, and age — rather than a single representative structure? Formally, the goal is a predictive ensemble that jointly reproduces scattering, spectroscopy, density, and mechanical observations.
status: R. J.-M. Pellenq et al. (2009), “A realistic molecular model of cement hydrates,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.0902180106](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0902180106), supplied a validated structural archetype, but it does not uniquely determine the full heterogeneous, composition-dependent ensemble present in practical binders.
solved_when: A predictive model of C–S–H structures exists that resolves variation across Ca/Si ratio, aluminium substitution, water activity, and age, and simultaneously reproduces scattering data, spectroscopy, density, and mechanical properties.
why: Such a structure would connect binder chemistry directly to transport, shrinkage, and mechanical performance, allowing these properties to be predicted and engineered rather than inferred empirically.
key_works: R. J.-M. Pellenq et al. (2009), “A realistic molecular model of cement hydrates,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.0902180106](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0902180106).

title: Mechanistic concrete creep under changing humidity
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Can we predict how concrete creeps and recovers over a structure's lifetime when both humidity and applied stress vary repeatedly? Formally, the goal is a mechanistic model that derives long-term creep and recovery under humidity and stress cycling from C–S–H rearrangement, water transport, and chemical aging, cleanly separating irreversible structural change from reversible poroelastic effects.
status: Vandamme and Ulm (2009), "Nanogranular origin of concrete creep" [DOI:10.1073/pnas.0901033106](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0901033106), linked creep to nanogranular packing; more recently, large-scale environmental testing — W. Bachofner et al. (2025; online 2024), "Influence of environmental conditions on the creep behavior of large-scale concrete specimens," [DOI:10.1002/suco.202401042](https://doi.org/10.1002/suco.202401042) — continues to show the importance of moisture history. Prediction across changing lifetime histories remains incomplete.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that forecasts creep and recovery across changing humidity and stress histories over a structure's lifetime, attributing each contribution to its underlying mechanism, with the irreversible structural component distinguished from reversible poroelastic response.
why: It would sharpen dimensional-stability predictions and service-life estimates for concrete structures, which currently degrade under unmodeled moisture-history effects.
key_works: M. Vandamme and F.-J. Ulm (2009), “Nanogranular origin of concrete creep,” [DOI:10.1073/pnas.0901033106](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0901033106); W. Bachofner et al. (2025; online 2024), “Influence of environmental conditions on the creep behavior of large-scale concrete specimens,” [DOI:10.1002/suco.202401042](https://doi.org/10.1002/suco.202401042).

title: Alkali–silica reaction swelling pressure from gel chemistry
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Can the swelling pressure — and the concrete cracking it drives — be predicted from the composition and environment of the alkali–silica reaction product itself? A satisfactory theory would connect gel chemistry, nanoscale confinement, water uptake, and external restraint to a quantitative pressure, and would identify the regimes in which colloidal osmotic pressure dominates over other gel-swelling mechanisms.
status: The chemistry of ASR is established, but the expansion mechanism remains debated. Giebson and Seyfarth's 2025 study (C. Giebson and K. Seyfarth, 2025; online 2024, "The colloidal nature and osmotic potential of alkali-silica reaction products and their role for the ASR expansion mechanism," DOI:10.1617/s11527-024-02542-4) quantifies colloidal properties and osmotic potential in synthetic ASR products.
solved_when: A predictive model yields expansive pressure (and resulting cracking) from ASR-product composition, nanoscale confinement, water uptake, and restraint, and correctly identifies when colloidal osmotic pressure versus other gel-swelling mechanisms dominates.
why: It would enable aggregate-specific prevention of ASR damage and reliable assessment of already-damaged structures.
key_works: C. Giebson and K. Seyfarth (2025; online 2024), “The colloidal nature and osmotic potential of alkali-silica reaction products and their role for the ASR expansion mechanism,” [DOI:10.1617/s11527-024-02542-4](https://doi.org/10.1617/s11527-024-02542-4).

title: Transport-law transfer across carbonated low-clinker binders
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Can we predict how carbonation changes the transport of water, oxygen, and chloride through low-clinker binders, using only independently measured pore structure and chemistry as inputs? A successful theory would cover partial carbonation and realistic curing histories, not just fully carbonated, ideally cured specimens.
status: Dudi and collaborators compared several low-clinker binders and water/binder ratios in 2025 [L. Dudi and collaborators (2025), "Revealing the relationships between transport properties and microstructure characteristics in low-clinker binders before and after carbonation," https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S000888462500225X]; general relationships that remain valid across binder families and exposure states are still being established.
solved_when: A validated predictive relationship exists that quantifies changes in water, oxygen, and chloride transport after carbonation for low-clinker binder compositions across binder families, water/binder ratios, partial carbonation states, and realistic curing histories.
why: Without it, the lower initial emissions of low-clinker binders risk being offset by unpredicted durability loss over the service life.
key_works: L. Dudi and collaborators (2025), “Revealing the relationships between transport properties and microstructure characteristics in low-clinker binders before and after carbonation,” [paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S000888462500225X).

title: Steel-interface moisture and carbonation-induced corrosion
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Can we predict the corrosion rate — and the cumulative loss of steel cross-section — from the actual moisture and oxygen conditions present at the steel–concrete interface when carbonated low-clinker concrete undergoes wet–dry cycling?
status: Experiments by C. Albert and collaborators (2025), “Moisture as a key factor in the corrosion of steel in carbonated low-clinker materials,” identify moisture as a key controller of corrosion across binder types, showing that carbonation-front position alone is an insufficient proxy for corrosion kinetics.
solved_when: A validated model or measurement framework predicts corrosion rates and cumulative section loss as a function of the evolving interfacial moisture and oxygen state under wet–dry cycling in carbonated low-clinker concrete, across the binder types tested.
