why: It would let durability design accommodate low-carbon binders rather than relying on carbonation depth alone, which the experiments show is an insufficient proxy for corrosion kinetics.
key_works: C. Albert and collaborators (2025), “Moisture as a key factor in the corrosion of steel in carbonated low-clinker materials,” conference contribution, [ETH repository record](https://www.research-collection.ethz.ch/entities/publication/012f55e9-29d9-4fef-a4a3-1e859df5b979).

title: Water-durable earthen construction with genuine recyclability
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Can we design an earthen building material that keeps its structural performance through repeated rain and wet–dry cycling, yet can afterwards be crushed and reprocessed into material of equivalent quality — without adding progressively more binder or resorting to thermal firing? Formally, water durability and genuine closed-loop recyclability must be achieved in the same material system.
status: A 2025 study (M. Audren, S. Guihéneuf, T. Le Borgne, D. Rangeard, A. Perrot (2025), "Recycling or downcycling? The difference between raw and stabilised earth explained," [DOI:10.1617/s11527-025-02721-x](https://doi.org/10.1617/s11527-025-02721-x)) recycled cement- or lime-stabilized compressed-earth blocks but found residual cement no longer supplied the original water resistance. Strong initial stabilization and repeated equivalent recycling remain different, unreconciled achievements.
solved_when: An earthen material is demonstrated that retains its specified structural properties after repeated rain and wet–dry exposure and can be reprocessed into equivalent material without progressive binder addition or thermal firing.
why: It preserves the low-energy and circular advantages of locally available earth; without it, each stabilization strategy tends to trade away either water resistance or the ability to recycle the material at end of life.
key_works: M. Audren, S. Guihéneuf, T. Le Borgne, D. Rangeard, A. Perrot (2025), “Recycling or downcycling? The difference between raw and stabilised earth explained,” [DOI:10.1617/s11527-025-02721-x](https://doi.org/10.1617/s11527-025-02721-x); A. Perrot, D. Rangeard, E. Courteille (2018), “3D printing of earth-based materials: Processing aspects,” [DOI:10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2018.04.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.conbuildmat.2018.04.017).

title: Glass crack-growth kinetics under realistic humidity histories
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Can we predict, from first principles, how long a stressed silicate glass part will survive when its surface flaws grow under a humidity, temperature, and aqueous chemistry that keep changing? Formally, the goal is a theory of crack-growth kinetics — including arrest and restart of cracks after exposure changes — that yields full lifetime distributions for realistic fluctuating environments and evolving flaw populations.
status: Wiederhorn established in 1967 that water vapor controls crack propagation in soda-lime glass (S. M. Wiederhorn (1967), "Influence of Water Vapor on Crack Propagation in Soda-Lime Glass," [DOI:10.1111/j.1151-2916.1967.tb15145.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1151-2916.1967.tb15145.x)). Extrapolating from such steady laboratory environments to arbitrary fluctuating exposure and flaw populations remains a practical mechanistic problem.
solved_when: A predictive theory reproduces lifetime distributions of stressed silicate glass starting from evolving surface flaws under variable humidity, temperature, and aqueous chemistry, explicitly accounting for crack arrest and restart after changing exposure, without requiring steady laboratory conditions.
why: It would let engineers certify the reliability of glass structures, containers, and protective surfaces under real service environments rather than extrapolated steady-state laboratory data.
key_works: S. M. Wiederhorn (1967), “Influence of Water Vapor on Crack Propagation in Soda-Lime Glass,” [DOI:10.1111/j.1151-2916.1967.tb15145.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1151-2916.1967.tb15145.x).

title: Durable reversible protection of unstable heritage glass
subfield: Cement, concrete, earthen materials, and glass durability
open: Can chemically unstable heritage glass be protected against atmospheric leaching and crizzling by a treatment that is fully removable, preserves the object's appearance, and withstands long-term humidity cycling? The central difficulty is achieving durable protection without trapping damaging salts or water beneath the coating.
status: Centenaro et al. (2025), “Sol–Gel Thin Films for the Protection of Ancient Glass Artifacts: A Performance Comparison Between Inorganic and Hybrid Silica Compositions,” [DOI:10.1002/admi.202500061](https://doi.org/10.1002/admi.202500061), compared inorganic and hybrid silica protective films under artificial aging. Long-term compatibility and reversibility across historical compositions remain separate conservation targets.
solved_when: A treatment exists that prevents atmospheric leaching and crizzling through long humidity cycles, leaves appearance unchanged, can be removed reversibly, and traps no damaging salts or water — demonstrated as compatible and reversible across historical glass compositions.
why: It would preserve irreplaceable glass objects without the risk of irreversible alteration by the conservation treatment itself.
key_works: Centenaro et al. (2025), “Sol–Gel Thin Films for the Protection of Ancient Glass Artifacts: A Performance Comparison Between Inorganic and Hybrid Silica Compositions,” [DOI:10.1002/admi.202500061](https://doi.org/10.1002/admi.202500061).
